en: *Saṃghakarmavastu*, Volume One, with Preface, excerpted from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of the Western Taiyuan Monastery.
Preface: Originally, at the Deer Park and the Dragon City, the wondrous traces of the *śīla* (precepts) were initiated; at the Elephant Rock and Vulture Peak, they were further opened.
The profound essence of liberation:
thus, throughout the trichiliocosm, beings receive the cooling breeze and emerge from the burning house;
from the heavens above to the earth below, they board the raft of precepts and cross the ford of delusion.
Consequently, the inner assembly flourished, and external followers thereby attained peace and happiness.
Later, when the fine cotton of hidden truth was folded away, there arose the anxiety of the "breaking axle" of extensive learning;
when the subtle words of the Correct Dharma were concealed, few could witness the firmness of the "life-preserving bag."
Thereupon, Kāśyapa emerged preeminent, repairing the severed threads of the Dharma and seeking it in its emptiness;
Upāli arose, shaking up the collapsed net and providing profound assistance.
Thus, the torch of wisdom shone forth once more, and the ocean of precepts was thereby restored to its clarity.
The Vinaya teachings are vast and profound, making it truly difficult to enumerate them all exhaustively.

This *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure), however, is the orthodox method for perpetuating the tradition and the grand standard for its preservation; its lineage culminates in the Five Sections (*pañcavarga*), and its source originates from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. It is indeed the essential pivot of Bodhi and the very ford for crossing over to Nirvana.

Having long applied my keen intellect since youth to this profound purpose, I have contemplated the ultimate teachings and examined the path of their meaning; through the passage of many seasons, I hope to be free from major errors.
However, since ancient times, various virtuous masters have held differing interpretations and each has expounded divergent traditions; in total, there are five versions:
one version consists of one fascicle, compiled by the Vinaya Master Kai of the Cao Wei dynasty at the capital of Xu, titled "The Miscellaneous Karmavācanas of the Mahīśāsaka."

Beginning with the establishment of the *sīmā* (boundary), the procedures for receiving the precepts, the additional days, and the petitions not included in the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) underwent frequent increases and decreases, deviating from the Vinaya texts;
one version in a single fascicle was compiled in Luoyang by Fandi of the Cao Wei dynasty and titled "One Fascicle of Karmavācanā," which is found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Beginning with the establishment of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā), this manual details the procedures for receiving [the precepts], the increasing of days, and the formal motion for entry into the ritual (karmavācanā).
Master Lì of Wèijùn received and upheld this text;
though he applied his mind keenly to its regulations, although he eliminated many errors, he had not yet dispelled all minor faults.
It is divided into two fascicles and includes a commentary on the meaning;

one version consists of a single fascicle, compiled by the Vinaya Master Guang of the Northern Wei at Ye, which was based on the edition compiled by Tan-di, though its recorded notes do not accord with the main text;
another version consists of two fascicles, composed by the Vinaya Master Yuan of the Sui dynasty at Bingzhou, titled "Karmavācanā, Fascicle One," and derived from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Although Yuan himself claimed that his work followed the text exactly without adding or omitting a single word,
a detailed examination of the Vinaya canon reveals that it is not without its own deletions and additions.
Furthermore, he composed commentaries and sub-commentaries which became widely circulated throughout the Bing and Fen regions.
This consists of one fascicle; it was composed in the Imperial Court by Vinaya Master Xuán of Jīngzhào, with the title *Shānbǔ Suíjí Jiémó* (Excerpts and Supplements to the *Suiji Karmavācanā*).
It discards the formal texts of its own school in the near term, while drawing upon the peripheral doctrines of other traditions in the distant term.
Since the teachings have thus become disordered, there are frequent contradictions when applied to specific matters.
He also composed commentaries on their meanings, which circulated widely during his time.

Sui had thoroughly researched the various collections compiled by different schools; yet, when he compared their principles and sought out their texts, he found that they were largely inconsistent and erroneous.

Thus, despite my lack of talent, I have ventured to describe these profound and subtle matters, dividing them into three fascicles and binding them into a single work. I hope that by avoiding any additions or omissions, this may suit the needs of the times; I have merely sought to produce a coherent text and did not dare to engage in forced interpretation.
I only pray that the pearl of the precepts may increase its radiance, shining as brightly as the sun and moon;
and that the fragrance of the bound grasses may be transmitted, decaying only when heaven and earth do.
May those who read this in the future understand this resolve.
1. Chapter on Expedient Means (Part One). Chapter One: Expedient Means. Regarding the assembly of the Saṃgha, the Vinaya states:
"Those who ought to come, let them come."
It is further stated:
"There are four kinds of Saṃghas: those consisting of four, five, ten, or twenty persons.

As for the Saṃgha of four persons, with the exception of the full ordination, the invitation for self-examination (pravāraṇā), and the absolution of offenses, all other karmavācanās should be performed."

Regarding a community of five monks: with the exception of receiving full ordination and the formal act for absolution from offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*) in the Central Land, all other *karmavācanā* (formal acts) should be performed.
Regarding a community of ten monks: with the exception of the formal act for absolution from offenses, all other *karmavācanā* should be performed.
Regarding a community of twenty monks: all *karmas* (formal acts) should be performed;
how much more so when there are more than twenty.
If, within any of the four types of assemblies, there is even one person missing, the ritual act is not accomplished; it is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya.
Regarding "being in harmony" (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*):

the Vinaya states that they perform the same *karma* together, having assembled in one place; those who have not come must have given their authorization (*anuśrāvaṇā*), and those present who ought to be censured are not censured.
Furthermore, it is said: five things should be in concord:

if one acts in accordance with the Dharma; if one remains silent and acquiesces; if one has granted consent (*chanda*); if one has heard from a trustworthy person; or if one was previously sitting silently among them. These five matters should be in concord.
"Those who have not yet received the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) must leave.
The Vinaya states:
"One should not perform a formal act (karmavācanā) or recite the precepts (poṣadha) in the presence of those who have not received the full ordination."
It is further stated:
"Allow that those who have not yet received the full ordination (upasampadā) be excluded; for all others, perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) and recite the precepts in their presence.
It is also stated:
There are four cases regarding the fulfillment of the quorum:

there is one who has attained the quorum and should not be censured; there is one who has not attained the quorum and should be censured; there is one who has not attained the quorum and should not be censured; and there is one who has attained the quorum and should be censured.
What kind of person, when reaching the full number [of the assembly], should not be censured?

One who is subject to the formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), or the formal act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople (*pratisedha-gṛhapraveśa-karman*).
What kind of person, though not completing the quorum, should be censured?
It is one who intends to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
What kind of person neither completes the quorum nor should be censured?

If a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is being performed for a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī may not count toward the required quorum, nor may she voice an objection; the same applies to a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī; those who claim to have committed one of the thirteen offenses such as the "borderline offense" (*antarakṛta-āpatti*); those who have been suspended (*utkṣipta*); those who have been expelled (*pravāsanīya*) or are subject to expulsion; those undergoing a period of separate residence (*parivāsa*); those on the boundary platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*); those traveling through the air by supernormal power (*ṛddhi*); those who have vanished; those who are out of sight or hearing; and the person for whom the *karmavācanā* is being performed.
What kind of person fulfills the required number and yet may be censured?

It is a virtuous bhikṣu who dwells within the same boundary, who does not use supernormal powers to remain in the air, who does not conceal himself, and who does not move beyond the range of sight or hearing, even as far as speaking to a bystander.
"Which bhikṣus who have not arrived may announce their *chanda* (consent) and *pāriśuddhi* (purification)?
With the sole exception of those within a defined boundary (*sīmā*), they may not announce their *chanda*.
Their *chanda* must be announced together with their *pāriśuddhi*."
When it is time for the *pravāraṇā*, one should say, "I grant my consent for the *pravāraṇā*.
If there are matters concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha; matters concerning illness; or circumstances involving the care of the sick, it is permitted to grant one's consent.
The Vinaya states:
There are five ways of giving consent (*chanda*):

saying "I give you my consent," saying "I speak on behalf of my consent," saying "I give my consent for the sake of [another]," manifesting the physical signs of giving consent, or speaking at length to give consent.
If one does not manifest their physical presence or verbally express their consent (*chanda*), the giving of consent is not accomplished; one should instead give consent to another.

If the person holding the consent dies after receiving it, or departs for another place, or ceases the religious life, or joins a group of non-Buddhists, or joins a separate faction, or arrives at the boundary of the *sīmā* (ordination site), or when the dawn appears, or if they themselves claim to have committed one of the thirteen offenses such as the "borderline offenses" (*antarakṛtya*), or if they have been suspended, or have been expelled, or are subject to expulsion, or if they are in the air by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), or if they are outside the range of sight or hearing—the giving of consent is not accomplished, and one should instead give consent to another.
If one reaches the midst of the assembly or the midst of the Sangha, it is also like this.
If one wishes to communicate a formal proposal (*chanda*) in detail, one should go to the person who is to transmit the proposal, perform the proper ritual gestures, and speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!"
"I, bhikṣu [Name], regarding a matter of the Saṃgha that accords with the Dharma, grant my consent and purity.
If the bhikṣu holding this consent has personal business arise and is unable to go to the Saṃgha, it is permitted for him to transfer his consent to another person."
When performing the transfer, one should say:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am conveying the consent and purity of the bhikṣu [Name]."
Both he and myself, regarding the affairs of the Dharma and the Saṃgha, grant our consent and purity.
When the bhikṣu holding the consent arrives at the assembly and speaks, if he is able to recall their names, he shall address the Saṃgha one by one, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The bhikṣu so-and-so and the bhikṣu so-and-so grant their consent and purity for the legal business of the Saṃgha.
If one cannot record their names, simply say "many."

If a person who has received the consent (*chanda*) falls asleep, enters meditative absorption, forgets, or does not intentionally speak [of it] in such a manner, it is called "having granted the consent";
if one intentionally fails to speak of it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
What is the Sangha currently doing?
There are three kinds of activities:
first, those concerning human affairs, such as receiving repentance and so forth;...
The second concerns matters pertaining to insentient things, such as the tying together of various boundaries;
the third concerns matters pertaining to both sentient and insentient things, such as the assignment of locations or the separation from one's robes.

Since these matters to be performed must be deliberated upon by the Sangha to determine what is appropriate, it is necessary to question those involved before the assembly regarding their proposed actions.
Regarding *karmavācanā*:
in terms of its essential nature, there are only three types, namely:
the single motion (*jñapti*), the motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*), and the motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*).
The Vinaya states: There are seven kinds of *karmavācanā* that should not be performed:

an illegal and non-Vinaya *karmavācanā*; an illegal *karmavācanā* of a divided assembly; an illegal *karmavācanā* of a harmonious assembly; a legal *karmavācanā* of a divided assembly; a legal-like *karmavācanā* of a divided assembly; a legal-like *karmavācanā* of a harmonious assembly; and a *karmavācanā* that continues despite being censured.
One should perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
One should perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* by making the motion according to the rules for the motion and performing the formal act according to the rules for the formal act;
the same applies to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
This constitutes a formal act (kamma) that is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
These six expedients apply universally to all other dharmas, with the sole exception of the delimitation of boundaries (sīmā-bandha); if any are missing, the act is not validly accomplished.
2. Chapter on Establishing Boundaries (Part One). Chapter Two: Establishing Boundaries. Regarding the legal rules for establishing the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*):
one should spread out seats, strike the *gandī* gong, and everyone should assemble together.
Having gathered in one place, they shall not receive the *karmavācanā* for the formal consent (*chanda*).

Among them, the resident monks (*pūrvasthita-bhikṣu*) should proclaim the characteristics of the four boundaries of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*): if there is a mountain in the east, they should call it a mountain; if there is a moat, they should call it a moat; or a village, a city, a field boundary, a garden, a grove, a pond, a tree, a rock, a wall, or a shrine.
As with the characteristics in the east, so it is for the other directions as well.

However, at the place where boundaries are demarcated, two boundaries must not touch one another; a space should be left between them. One must not demarcate boundaries across a rapid stream, except where there is a permanent bridge or boat service.
Regarding the method for announcing the boundaries (*sīmā*): one should rise and pay homage to the Saṃgha, and declare:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], who am a resident monk; if one is not a resident monk but is familiar with the boundaries, when making the announcement, the two words 'resident' (*jùzhù*) should be omitted."
For the sake of the Saṃgha, one should chant the characteristics of the four boundaries of the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā).
Having made the formal announcement (jñapti), one should then chant them in sequence, starting from the southeast corner and so forth, up to three recitations.

From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā*—whether he be a senior elder (*sthavira*), a junior elder (*anusthavira*), one who recites the Vinaya, or one who does not recite the Vinaya—should act in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣus residing here have proclaimed the marks of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions.

If it is the time for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now establish a great boundary within these marks of the four directions as a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu residing here proclaims the marks of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions."
The Sangha now establishes a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) within these four directional markers, as a single residence and for a single recitation of the precepts.

Those elders who consent to the Sangha’s establishment of a great boundary within these four directional markers, as a single residence and for a single recitation of the precepts, remain silent; those who do not consent, please speak.

The Saṃgha has already consented that within these four boundaries, there shall be a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa; the formal establishment of the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) is now complete.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
When the method for dissolving the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) was being performed, some bhikṣus wished to make the boundary wider while others wished to make it narrower.
The Buddha said:
"If you wish to alter it, first dissolve the previous boundary; thereafter, you may make it wider or narrower according to your intention."
One should perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) for its dissolution; it should be performed as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now, these bhikṣus residing in this dwelling place share the same residence and recite the Prātimokṣa together."
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha, out of compassion, grant its consent to dissolve the boundary.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Sangha, listen!
The bhikṣus residing at this monastery, who share the same dwelling place and the same recitation of the precepts, now dissolve the boundary (*sīmā*).

Those elders who consent to the Sangha dissolving the boundary for those sharing the same dwelling place and the same recitation of the precepts should remain silent; whoever does not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to hear this: the boundary for a common residence and a common recitation of the Prātimokṣa is hereby dissolved.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

When the rules for establishing a boundary for a common recitation of the precepts and a common distribution of offerings were being enacted, there were two distinct locations with separate distributions of offerings and separate recitations of the precepts; the bhikṣus then wished to establish a single boundary for both a common recitation of the precepts and a common distribution of offerings.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow you to each dissolve the boundary yourselves, and then perform the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to re-establish it.
The arrangement of seats and so forth shall be as previously described.
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Regarding the characteristics of the boundary as they have been described, if the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now establish at this place and that place a single boundary for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a single boundary for the distribution of offerings."
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Sangha, listen!

According to the characteristics of the boundary as described, the Sangha now establishes at this place and that place a single boundary for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a single boundary for the distribution of material offerings.

"Whichever elders among you consent to the Saṃgha binding a boundary at this place and that place for a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a single distribution of offerings, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak."

The Saṃgha has already consented that, in this place and that place, there shall be a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a single distribution of offerings, and the boundary has been established.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the method for establishing a single boundary for the recitation of the *Poṣadha* and separate boundaries for the distribution of offerings (*lābha*), there are two types of residences where the *Poṣadha* is recited separately and the offerings are distributed separately; yet, the bhikṣus desire to establish a single boundary for the recitation of the *Poṣadha* and separate boundaries for the distribution of offerings.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to dissolve the boundaries individually, and then re-establish them.
The method for establishing them is the same as before, with the exception of changing one phrase, which says:
"Same *poṣadha*, separate *lābha* (offerings).
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

When the boundary for "separate *poṣadha* and same *lābha*" is being established, two residences were previously holding separate *poṣadhas* and separate *lābhas*. At that time, the bhikṣus desired to have a separate *poṣadha* and a common *lābha* in order to protect their respective dwellings.
The Buddha has permitted the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) for this purpose; it should be performed as follows:

"Listen, venerable Saṃgha! If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now establish separate *poṣadha* ceremonies at these two respective residences, while sharing a common distribution of offerings (*lābha*), for the sake of protecting and maintaining the dwellings."
It is announced as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now the Saṃgha shall, at this and that residence, establish a separate *poṣadha* ceremony while sharing the same *lābha*, for the purpose of protecting the residence."

"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha’s formal establishment of separate recitation of the Prātimokṣa at this and that residence, while sharing the same communal offerings for the sake of protecting the residences, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."

The Saṃgha has already consented to this; at that and those residences, the separate recitation of the Prātimokṣa has been established with a common distribution of offerings for the purpose of guarding the residences.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding these and the two preceding cases, the Vinaya provides no method for their dissolution. If one wishes to dissolve them, the dissolution should follow the reverse of the procedure for their establishment; this reversal should be understood accordingly.

At the time of the formal act for establishing a *sīmā* (boundary), various monks may require a quorum of four, five, ten, or twenty monks for a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual); in such instances, the large assembly gathers together and becomes utterly exhausted.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to demarcate a *sīmā* (boundary zone).
You shall declare the characteristics of the four boundaries, whether they be wooden stakes, stones, field ridges, or fixed limits."
Regarding the boundaries therein, one should establish three layers of marks:
the innermost layer is the mark of the *śīma* (precept-field);

the middle layer is the mark of the interior of the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary). These two—the mark of the *śīma* and the mark of the *mahā-sīmā*—must not overlap or run parallel; a space must be left between them.
The outermost layer is the boundary marker for the great precinct (*mahā-sīmā*).
First, the boundary markers for the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) are proclaimed; the ritual procedure is as described above.
It should be performed in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These bhikṣus residing here have proclaimed the boundary markers for the small four-sided boundary.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now establish a *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept-platform) within these boundary markers of the small four-sided boundary.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These bhikṣus residing here proclaim the boundary markers for a small four-sided boundary."
The Saṃgha now intends to establish a *sīmā-śīla-kṣetra* (precept field) within these boundaries of the small four-sided area.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of this *sīmā-śīla-kṣetra* within these four-sided boundaries, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already consented to the completion of the demarcation of the *kṣetra* (precept-field) within these four boundaries.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Next, the internal and external boundaries of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) are proclaimed; the proclamation and the formal act of demarcation are as described above.

The text for the procedure of dissolving the *sīmā* (boundary) is abbreviated and does not include the dissolution itself; if one wishes to dissolve it, one should reverse the formula for its establishment as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This is the *śīla-sīmā* (precept boundary) for the monks at this residence."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the boundary of the training ground (śikṣāmaṇḍala) be dissolved.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This is the boundary for the *śīma* (precept zone) at this monastery; the Saṃgha now dissolves this *śīma*.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha dissolving the *śīma* here remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented to the conclusion of this dissolution of the *karmavācanā* boundary.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

At the time of establishing a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) to confer the precepts, there was one who wished to receive the precepts and arrived outside the boundary; the group of six bhikṣus went to obstruct him.
The Buddha said: "Listen well!

From this day forward, for those who do not agree [to the formal act] and have not yet left the boundary, I permit them to quickly assemble in one place outside the boundary and establish a small boundary (kṣudrasīmā)."
"It should be done in this manner:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha has gathered in one place to establish a small boundary (sīmā). "
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let us establish a small boundary (sīmā).
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now this Saṃgha assembles in one place to establish a small boundary (sīmā).
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s assembly in one place to establish a small boundary should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented; the demarcation of the small boundary is concluded.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the legal procedure for releasing a difficult-to-bind small boundary for the purpose of bestowing the precepts, the Vinaya states:
From this day forward, one should depart only after having dissolved the boundary; one must not depart without having dissolved the boundary.
It should be dissolved in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
Now the community of monks has assembled to dissolve the boundary.
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha consents, let the boundary be dissolved.
The motion is as follows.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now the community of monks has assembled to dissolve the boundary.
Those elders who consent to the community dissolving the boundary remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented; the delimitation of the boundary is concluded.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the legal procedure for establishing a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, the Vinaya states:

If, on the day of the *poṣadha*, one is traveling through a wilderness area where there is no village, the community of monks (*saṃgha*) should gather together in one place to recite the precepts collectively.

If the community cannot achieve such harmony, then according to the principle of "harmonious groups" (*samavāya*), they should descend from the road at each point, assemble in separate locations, establish a minor boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), and recite the precepts.
The boundary should be marked in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now there are this many bhikṣus assembled."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to establish a small boundary.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now, so many bhikṣus have gathered to establish a small boundary (sīmā).
Those elders who consent to these so many bhikṣus gathering to establish the small boundary should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented; the assembly of so many bhikṣus has completed the binding of the small boundary (sīmā).
Because the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the method for releasing the small boundary when difficulties arise during the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, one should not depart without first releasing the boundary.
It should be understood in this way:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now there are this many bhikṣus assembled."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha hear this: I announce that this small boundary (sīmā) at this place is hereby dissolved.
Thus is the formal motion (jñapti).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now that this many bhikṣus have assembled, we shall dissolve the small boundary (sīmā) at this location.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha dissolving the small boundary at this location should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented to the resolution of this small boundary.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the legal procedure for establishing a small boundary for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) during times of difficulty, the Vinaya states:
If a large number of bhikṣus, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, are traveling on a road in a place that is neither a village nor an *araṇya* and where boundaries have not yet been established:
if they can perform the *pravāraṇā* together in harmony, it is well;
if they cannot achieve harmony, they should, according to their respective groups, move to another location, establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), and perform the *pravāraṇā*.
It should be done in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The seating places for the bhikṣus are already full, extending as far as these seating places of the bhikṣus."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now establish a small boundary (sīmā) at this place.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"Marking off the area where these bhikṣus are seated, the Saṃgha shall establish a small boundary (sīmā) at this spot.
Those elders who consent to marking off the area where these bhikṣus are seated and for the Saṃgha to establish a small boundary here, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak."
The Saṃgha has already consented; the small boundary (sīmā) for the seating places of these bhikṣus has been established.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus maintained.
Regarding the method for releasing a difficult-to-bind small boundary for the *pravāraṇā*, one should not depart without first relinquishing the boundary.
It should be relinquished in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Within the area marked by the sitting places of these bhikṣus."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now dissolve this small boundary at this location.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The monks are gathered at this place where these bhikṣus are seated; the Saṃgha now dissolves the small boundary (sīmā) at this location.
Those elders who consent to the dissolution of the small boundary at this place where these bhikṣus are seated, let them remain silent; those who do not consent, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has consented; the small boundary (kṣudrasīmā) for the seating places of these bhikṣus is hereby dissolved.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the method for establishing the boundary for not losing one's robes (acīvarāpanāśasīmā): at that time, there was a bhikṣu who felt a sense of renunciation. Seeing a fine cave in an araṇya, he thought to himself:
"If I am permitted to stay overnight separated from my robe, I may then dwell here in this cave.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you shall establish the *akopya-cīvara-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robe) by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*)."
"It shall be done thus:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This place is a single residence with a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.'"
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let us establish the boundary for not losing one's robes.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
In this place, which is a single dwelling and a single recitation of the *Poṣadha*, the Saṃgha now establishes a boundary for not losing one's robes (*akālacīvara-sīmā*).

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of a boundary for not losing one's robes in this place, which is a single dwelling and a single recitation of the *Poṣadha*, should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented; this boundary for not losing one’s robes, established within this same dwelling place and for the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa, is now concluded.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held as such.
At that time, the bhikṣus removed their robes and left them in the houses of laypeople; while they were putting them on again, their bodies were exposed.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to establish a 'boundary for not losing robes' (akṣaya-sīmā), with the exception of villages and the areas outside of villages."
The ritual for the formal act (*karmavācanā*) is as described above, with the addition of one sentence:
"excluding the village and the area outside the village.
The motion (*jñapti*) is as follows.

The text for the procedure of dissolving the *acīvarāpatti-sīmā* (the boundary where one is not liable for losing one's robe) is abbreviated and does not include the dissolution; it should be translated from the formal act of establishing it as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This place constitutes a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the *akalpiya-cīvara-sīmā* (the boundary of not losing one's robe) be dissolved.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
In this place, which constitutes a single residence and a single recitation of the *Poṣadha*, we now dissolve the *akalacīvara-sīmā*.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s dissolution of the *akalacīvara-sīmā* in this place, which constitutes a single residence and a single recitation of the *Poṣadha*, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already consented that at this place, within this same dwelling and for the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa, the boundary for not losing one's robe is hereby dissolved.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
There was a village where the rules for formal acts were understood; the procedure for establishing a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*) was likewise the same.

At the time of the formal act for establishing a pure area, there was a monk suffering from vomiting and diarrhea. While people in Śrāvastī were cooking gruel, due to certain circumstances the city gates opened late; he did not reach the gruel and died.
The Buddha said:

"I allow you to establish a pure ground within the monastery by means of a formal motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). You should announce whether it is a room, a location, a warm chamber, or a place for walking meditation."

A single bhikṣu should rise, assume the proper demeanor, and announce within the Saṃgha: "I designate such-and-such a courtyard and the locations for various fruits, vegetables, and so forth as pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*).
Having made this announcement, he should act accordingly.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now demarcate a certain place as a pure ground (śuddhasthāna).
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now demarcates a certain place as a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*).
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s demarcation of this certain place as a pure ground should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented to demarcate a certain area as a purified site (śuddhasthāna).
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The Vinaya states:
There are four kinds of pure grounds (*śuddhasthāna*).
First, when a donor or a manager constructs a monastery (*saṃghārāma*), they designate it by saying:
"This place shall be made a pure ground for the Saṃgha."
Second, if one builds a monastery for the Saṃgha but has not yet offered it to the Saṃgha.
Third, if it is half-fenced, or mostly unfenced, or entirely unfenced; the same applies to walls or moats.

Fourth, the method for the Saṃgha to perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to demarcate a pure area (*śuddha-sthāna*) is abbreviated in the text as there is no procedure for its dissolution; one should reverse the formula for demarcation as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now revoke the designation of the pure ground at such-and-such a place.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now releases the pure ground at such-and-such a place.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s release of the pure ground at such-and-such a place remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented and completed the release of the pure ground at such-and-such a place.
The Saṃgha consents, as they remain silent; thus this matter is upheld as such.
Chapter Three: Bestowing the Precepts (Part One) The Method for Bestowing the Precepts by the "Welcome" Formula (*Ehi-bhikṣu*) According to the Vinaya:

At that time, those who heard the Dharma had all their defilements wiped away while still on their seats; they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, saw the Dharma, realized the Dharma, accomplished all dharmas, and having already obtained the fruit, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to go forth under the Tathāgata to practice the holy life.
The Buddha said, "Come, bhikṣu!"
"Within my Dharma, you shall find great joy; practice the holy life and bring an end to the source of suffering.

As soon as these words were spoken, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, the saffron robes were upon his body, and the alms bowl was in his hand; he was thus called one who has gone forth and received full ordination.

At the time of bestowing the precepts through the Three Refuges, there were those who heard the Dharma and attained faith; when they wished to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), the bhikṣus led them to the Buddha’s presence, but along the way they lost their faith and were unable to receive full ordination.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to grant them immediate ordination and bestow the full precepts (upasampadā).
He instructed them to shave their hair, don the saffron robes, remove their leather sandals, place their right knees on the ground, join their palms, and speak these words:
I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
I now go forth in the presence of the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One.
Recite this three times:
"I, [Name], have taken refuge in the Buddha, have taken refuge in the Dharma, and have taken refuge in the Saṅgha.
I go forth under the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One."
[This is] said three times.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* for conferring the precepts and the method of ordaining others: if a bhikṣu, being foolish, should suddenly ordain others without knowing how to instruct them, then because he does not provide instruction, they do not maintain dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*).

They beg for food improperly, accepting impure food in various places, or accepting food in an impure bowl, and they shout loudly during the morning and midday meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to confer full ordination upon him through a formal motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
He shall go before the Saṃgha, perform the proper ritual observances, and make this request.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], seek the Saṃgha’s permission to ordain a person and bestow the full precepts upon them; may the Saṃgha grant me, the bhikṣu [Name], permission to ordain a person and bestow the full precepts.
This is said three times.
The Saṃgha should examine this person; if he is incapable of providing instruction and cannot be sustained by the two dharmas, they should say to him: "Stop!"
"Do not ordain others.
If there is one who possesses wisdom capable of providing instruction and who can embrace them through the two dharmas, they should grant the dharma in this manner:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!"
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, now requests from the Saṃgha the authorization to confer full ordination upon another.
If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now authorize this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to confer full ordination upon another.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, please listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, now requests from the Sangha that another person be granted full ordination."
The Saṃgha now intends to grant full ordination to the bhikṣu so-and-so on behalf of another person.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting full ordination to the bhikṣu so-and-so for the sake of another person, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has already granted its consent that the bhikṣu so-and-so has completed the bestowal of full ordination upon another person.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The same rule applies to the *upādhyāya* (preceptor).

Regarding the ordination of śrāmaṇeras by means of the "formal act" (jñapti-carma), at one time a son of a skilled craftsman came to the saṃghārāma and requested the bhikṣus to allow him to leave the household life to follow the Path; the bhikṣus immediately granted him the going forth to follow the Path.
The parents came weeping to the saṃghārāma and asked the bhikṣus,
"Have you seen such and such a small child coming?
Those who had not seen him replied:
“I did not see it.
He then searched through the various rooms and found it; the elders criticized and disparaged him.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if you wish to have your hair shaved within the saṃghārāma, you should inform the entire Saṃgha.
If the assembly cannot be gathered together, you must go from room to room and let them know."
If the Saṃgha is in harmony, they should make this formal announcement (jñapti):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, wishes to seek the tonsure from such-and-such a person."
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha consents, let them grant [the hair-cutting] to so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this motion, one may then cut the hair.

Regarding the ordination of a śrāmaṇera, the invitation of the upādhyāya is identical to the [ordination] ritual for a bhikṣu. If one wishes to go forth within a saṃghārāma, one must first invite an upādhyāya.
Having prepared the proper deportment, one should make the invitation as follows.
Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to serve as my Preceptor for the Ten Precepts; may the Venerable One act as my Preceptor for the Ten Precepts.
"Relying upon the Venerable One, I receive the śrāmaṇera precepts; out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.
The respondent should reply:
It may be so. Please perform the ritual for requesting the *ācārya* according to the proper procedure as follows: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind!
I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to serve as my *daśa-śīla-ācārya*. May the Venerable One act as my *daśa-śīla-ācārya*."
"Relying upon the Venerable One, I have received the śrāmaṇera precepts; out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.
The respondent should reply:
It may be so. Regarding the procedure for announcing to the Saṃgha: if harmony cannot be achieved, one should inform the entire Saṃgha;
if harmony is achieved, one should make the announcement as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to go forth from the household life under so-and-so.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let the Saṃgha allow so-and-so to go forth.
The announcement is thus made.
Regarding the method for conferring the precepts, one puts on the *kāṣāya* robe, assumes the proper deportment, and speaks as follows:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Saṃgha."
Following the Tathāgata into homelessness, with [Name] as my preceptor, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One.
(Recite this three times.)
I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
Having completed my going forth following the Tathāgata, with [Name] as my preceptor, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One.
Recite this three times.
To confer the characteristics of the ten precepts, say:
"For as long as life lasts, you shall not kill living beings."
"Can you uphold these śrāmaṇera precepts?
He replied, "I can."
"For as long as life lasts, one shall not steal.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?
He replied:
Yes. To refrain from sexual misconduct for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept; are you able to uphold it?
He replied, "I can.
For as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from false speech."
"Can you uphold these śrāmaṇera precepts?
He replied, "I can."
"For as long as life lasts, one shall not drink alcohol.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?
He replied:
"Yes. For as long as life lasts, you must not wear flower garlands or smear your body with scented oils.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?"
He replied: "I can.
For as long as life lasts, I shall not engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor shall I go to witness or listen to them."
"Can you uphold these śrāmaṇera precepts?
He replied, "I can."
"For as long as life lasts, one must not sit upon high and wide beds.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?
He replied:
Yes. For as long as life lasts, one must not eat at improper times.
This is a śrāmaṇera precept; can you uphold it?
He replied: "I can.
For as long as life lasts, I shall not take hold of or possess gold, silver, or precious objects, whether in their natural state or as images."
"Can you uphold these śrāmaṇera precepts?
He replied, "I can."
These are the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera.
For as long as life lasts, you must not violate them. Can you uphold them?
Answer: Yes.
Yes. You have now completed receiving the precepts; you should make offerings to the Triple Gem and diligently cultivate the three types of action:
practicing seated meditation, reciting the sutras, and zealously performing communal duties.
Having bestowed [the precepts], he instructed him to recite ten items.

These ten are: first, all sentient beings depend upon food and drink; second, name-and-form; third, the three feelings; fourth, the four noble truths; fifth, the five aggregates; sixth, the six sense bases; seventh, the seven factors of enlightenment; eighth, the eightfold noble path; ninth, the nine abodes of sentient beings; and tenth, the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
The Buddha addressed the non-Buddhist practitioners, saying:

"From this day forward, I authorize the performance of a formal motion with a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for a period of four months of communal residence among the community of monks for those who are non-Buddhists.
It should be granted in this manner:"
Having first shaved his hair and donned the *kāṣāya*, and so forth until he has joined his palms, he is instructed to say these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, [name], a former follower of another path, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha."
"I seek to go forth from the household life under the World-Honored One to follow the Path; the World-Honored One is my Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.
(This is said three times.
"I, [Name], a follower of an external path, having taken refuge in the Buddha, having taken refuge in the Dharma, and having taken refuge in the Saṅgha..."
"I have gone forth from the Tathāgata to study the Path; the Tathāgata is my Truly Realized One, the Perfectly Awakened One.
This is said three times.
Next, the precepts are conferred, the ritual for which is the same as that for the Dharma.
Regarding the method for dwelling together for four months, one should next instruct them to speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the outsider [name], request from the Saṃgha to dwell together for four months."
"May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me four months of co-residence.
This should be stated three times. [The candidate] should remain in a place where they are within sight but beyond earshot. The Saṃgha should perform the ritual in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
That certain outsider now requests from the community of monks four months of co-residence.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant it, let the Saṃgha grant that certain outsider four months of co-residence.
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
That certain outsider now requests from the community of monks a four-month period of co-residence.
The Sangha now grants him a four-month period of co-residence.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha granting him a four-month period of co-residence should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to grant that outsider four months of probation;
the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus this matter is upheld.
Once he has completed his probation, he shall cause the minds of the bhikṣus to be joyful, and only then should he receive full ordination within the Saṃgha.
Why is it that these non-Buddhists cannot gladden the hearts of the bhikṣus?

Because those non-Buddhists, by their very nature, cling tenaciously to the ways of the non-Buddhist laypeople; they do not associate with the bhikṣus but associate with the non-Buddhists, and instead of following the bhikṣus, they recite and study heterodox doctrines.
If they hear people speak ill of the non-Buddhists, they immediately give rise to anger; if they hear people disparage the teachings of their non-Buddhist masters, they likewise give rise to anger.

If heterodox practitioners come and praise the excellent qualities of their own path, they rejoice and leap for joy; if a teacher of a heterodox school comes and hears praise for the matters of his own path, he too rejoices and leaps for joy;
even if they hear it said that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are not the true Dharma, they likewise rejoice and leap for joy.
This is called "the heterodox being unable to cause the bhikṣus to feel delight."
How can non-Buddhists cause the bhikṣus to rejoice?
It is precisely the reverse of the above.
This is called dwelling together with non-Buddhists, harmonizing their minds and intentions, so as to cause the bhikṣus to rejoice.
The procedure for requesting a preceptor when receiving full ordination involves baring one shoulder, and so forth, and making this request:
"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind!
I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to be my preceptor; may the Venerable One act as my preceptor."
"By relying on the Venerable One, I have received full ordination; out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.
The response is:
"It may be so. Or he says:
"It is thus."
Some said: "We shall instruct you. Others said: [We shall instruct you].
"Be pure and do not be negligent.
To request the Preceptor, one should perform the ritual with the proper form as follows:
"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind!"
I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to serve as my *karmācārya*. May the Venerable One act as my *karmācārya* for me.
Relying upon the Venerable One, I shall receive the full ordination; out of compassion, please grant this.
After he has spoken three times,
one should reply: "So be it."
Request the Preceptor according to the ritual procedure as follows:
"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind!
I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to serve as my Preceptor for Instruction (avavādācārya). May the Venerable One deign to act as my Preceptor for Instruction."
"By relying on the Venerable One, I have received full ordination; out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.
The response should be:
It may be so. Regarding the procedure for establishing the location of the person receiving the precepts, it should be established in a place where they are visible but not audible.
If the person receiving the precepts is in the air, or hidden, or outside the range of sight and hearing, or outside the boundary, it is not called the conferral of full ordination.
The same applies to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the bhikṣus who complete the quorum.
Regarding the procedure for appointing a teacher of instruction, the Vinaya provides this teaching:
"No one who has brought disgrace upon the Saṃgha shall receive full ordination (*upasampadā*)."

At that time, there was one who wished to receive the precepts; when the bhikṣus led him outside the boundary and removed his clothes to examine him, the candidate felt ashamed and abashed, which delayed the matter of receiving the precepts.
The Buddha said:
"You must not look upon them thus with their bodies naked.
From this day forward, I allow that one first inquire about the thirteen impediments before conferring the precepts."
In this regard, the preceptor asks:
"Who among the assembly is able to act as the instructor for so-and-so?
If there is one who will act as the instructor, they should respond as follows:
"I, [Name], am able.
Having answered thus, the Preceptor of the Precepts should make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Sangha, please listen!"
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Name].
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let [Name] serve as the preceptor for instruction.
This is the formal motion.
When going there to inquire about the prohibitions and obstacles, the preceptor goes there and says:
"This is the *antarvāsa*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, the *saṃghāṭī*, and the bowl."
"Is this robe and bowl yours?
Having answered "Yes," one should further say to him:
"Good son, listen attentively!"

Now is the time for ultimate sincerity, the time for truthful speech. I now question you; answer according to my questions. If it is not true, you should say it is not true; if it is true, say it is true.
"Have you not committed an offense involving a pārājika?
Have you not committed an offense with a bhikṣuṇī?
Have you not entered the path with a thieving mind?"
Are you not one who has broken the precepts of either the inner or outer paths? Are you not a eunuch?
Are you not one who has killed his father?
Have you not killed your mother?
Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
"Did you not, with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha?
Are you not a non-human being? Are you not an animal?"
Are you not of both sexes?
What is your name? And what is the name of your preceptor?
"Are you twenty years of age?
Are your robes and bowl complete?
Have your parents given their permission?"
Are you not in debt to others?
Are you not a slave?
Are you not a government official?
Are you a man? A man may have such diseases as leprosy, carbuncles, white leprosy, consumption, or insanity.
"Do you currently have these various ailments?
If he answers "No" to each question according to the facts, one should further say to him:
"Just as I have questioned you now, the Saṃgha shall also question you in this same manner."
Just as you have answered me previously, so too should you answer within the Saṃgha.

Having finished questioning, the instructor returns to the midst of the Saṃgha and, maintaining his usual dignified demeanor, stands at a distance where he can reach others with an outstretched hand, making this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Preceptor Name].
If the Sangha is ready and the Sangha permits, I have finished my inquiry; please allow him to be brought forward.
The formal motion is as follows.
To request the Dharma of ordination from the Saṃgha, he should be called by saying, "Come.
Once he has come, one should take hold of his robe and bowl and instruct him to pay homage to the Saṃgha.
Having performed the prostrations, he stands before the Preceptor and, assuming the proper posture, is instructed to speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, [Name], seek to receive full ordination from [Name]."
I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the full ordination, with [Name] acting as my preceptor.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me deliverance.
(Recite this three times.)

Whether one requests the precepts or does not request them; if one is wearing secular clothing and so forth; or if one is asleep, intoxicated, insane, naked, angry, unconscious, physically incomplete, borrowing another’s robes and bowl, or if there is no preceptor or multiple preceptors—in all such cases, it is not termed the "reception of full ordination."
The Preceptor’s Announcement: The Preceptor wishes to question [the candidate]; first, he makes this announcement. He says:
"May the Venerable Saṃgha listen!"
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Name].
This person, [Name], now requests the Sangha to grant him full ordination, with [Name] acting as preceptor.
If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me leave; I shall inquire about various difficult matters.
Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
The Preceptor asks regarding the Dharma, saying:
"Listen, son of good family!
Now is the time for sincerity, the time for truthful speech. Regarding what you are now asked, you should answer according to the truth.
Have you not committed a pārājika offense?"
Have you not committed an offense against a bhikṣuṇī?
Have you not entered the path with a thieving mind?
Have you not damaged the two paths?
Are you not a eunuch? Are you not one who has killed his father?
Are you not one who has killed his mother?
Have you not killed an arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Sangha?
Have you not, with a malicious mind, shed the blood of a Buddha?
Are you not a non-human? Are you not an animal?
Are you not of dual gender?
"What is your name?
What is the name of your preceptor?
Have you reached the age of twenty?"
Are your robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents given you permission?
Are you not indebted to others?
Are you not a slave?
Are you not an official? Are you a man?
"A man may have such diseases as leprosy, abscesses, white leprosy, consumption,
or insanity. Do you now have any of these diseases?"
Furthermore, one must respond with "no" to each question according to the facts.

When the formal rite for bestowing the precepts is performed, the arising of the precepts is difficult; all necessary conditions must be fulfilled. One should guide them through the Dharma so that they give rise to the highest grade of resolve and receive the precepts with utmost sincerity and truthfulness.
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from such-and-such a person."
This person, [Name], now requests from the Sangha the full ordination, with [Name] acting as the preceptor.
[Name] has declared himself pure, free from all obstacles, twenty years of age, and possessed of the three robes and alms bowl.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let [the name] so-and-so receive full ordination with so-and-so as preceptor.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Name].
This person, [Name], now requests the Sangha for full ordination, with [Name] acting as preceptor.
So-and-so has declared himself pure, free from obstacles, twenty years of age, and possessed of the three robes and bowl.
The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as the preceptor.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha granting full ordination to [Name], with [Name] acting as preceptor, should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This is said three times."
The Sangha has already consented to grant full ordination to [Name], with [Name] acting as preceptor;
this matter is concluded. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, it shall be held thus.
Having performed this rite, one should announce the time.
Receiving it from a border region is no different from this.
Regarding the procedure for conferring the characteristics of the precepts: at that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), had the entire Saṃgha depart.
The person receiving the precepts had a former consort not far away, and at that time, the recipient of the precepts engaged in unchaste conduct with her together.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one must first recite the four *pārājika* rules."
It should be said thus:
"Listen, son of good family!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed the four *pārājika* rules. If a bhikṣu commits even one of these offenses, he is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a scion of the Śākya."
"You must all refrain from committing sexual misconduct and engaging in impure practices.
If a bhikṣu commits an impure act and indulges in the practice of sexual desire— even with an animal—
he is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke a parable for him: "It is just as if someone were to have their head cut off; they would never return to life.
So it is with a bhikṣu: once he has committed a pārājika offense, he can no longer restore his status as a bhikṣu."
"You must not do this for as long as you live; can you maintain it?
He replied, "I can."
Under no circumstances shall one steal, even down to a blade of grass or a leaf.

If a bhikṣu steals five coins or more than five coins from another person—whether taking it himself or inciting others to take it, whether breaking it himself or inciting others to break it, whether cutting it himself or inciting others to cut it, or by burning it, burying it, or altering its color—he is no longer a śramaṇa;
he is no longer a son of the Śākya.
Just as when the heartwood of a tāla tree is severed, it never again grows or flourishes;
so it is with a bhikṣu who has committed a pārājika offense—he can never again restore his status as a bhikṣu.
"You must not do this for as long as you live; can you maintain this?
He replied, "I can."
Under no circumstances shall one intentionally take the life of a living being, even down to an ant.

If a bhikṣu intentionally takes a human life with his own hand, or seeks out a knife to give to another, or instructs someone to die, praises death, encourages death, gives another a non-medicinal substance, causes an abortion, or kills by means of incantations;
or if he himself employs such means or instructs another to do so—he is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"Just as a needle with a broken eye is no longer fit for use, so it is with a bhikṣu who has committed a pārājika offense; he can never again fulfill the conduct of a bhikṣu."
"You must not do this for as long as you live; can you maintain this?
He replied, "I can."
No one shall speak falsely, even in jest.

If a bhikṣu, being untrue to the facts and lacking such qualities himself, should say of himself: "I have attained the state of a superior man; I have attained dhyāna; I have attained liberation; I have attained meditative concentration; I have attained the four formless attainments; I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat; devas, nāgas, and yakṣas come to make offerings to me"—he is not a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
Just as a great rock split into two parts can never be joined back together again, so it is with a bhikṣu;
once he has committed a pārājika offense, he can never again fulfill the conduct of a bhikṣu.
"You must not do this for as long as you live; can you maintain this?
He replied, "I can."

Regarding the conferral of the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*): A young non-Buddhist ascetic came seeking ordination. The bhikṣus immediately granted him ordination and first gave him the four reliances.
That non-Buddhist replied, "Venerable Sirs!..."
I am able to accept two supports:
begging for food and sitting under a tree.
However, I am not able to accept these two things: wearing robes made of discarded rags and using medicine that has gone rotten.
"Why is this? For who can touch their own body?
Thereupon he abandoned the path and did not go forth into homelessness.
The Buddha said:
"If this non-Buddhist had not left the household life, he would have suffered a great loss;
had he become a renunciant, he would have attained the realization of the Way."
"From this day forward, after you have first received the precepts, you shall subsequently receive the four reliances.
One should say:
"Listen, son of good family!"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances; by relying upon these, a bhikṣu attains renunciation and full ordination, thereby fulfilling the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Regarding the refuse-rag robe: by relying on this, a bhikṣu is able to go forth and receive full ordination, thereby becoming a bhikṣu.
Are you able to maintain this for as long as life lasts?
He replied:
"I am able.
If he should obtain extra benefits:
One may accept robes offered by a donor or robes that have been cut and torn.
By relying on alms-gathering, a bhikṣu relies upon this to go forth and receive full ordination, thereby perfecting the dharma of a bhikṣu.
"Can you maintain this throughout your entire life?
He replied, "I can."
If one obtains long-term benefits—

such as food assigned by the Sangha, food sent by a donor, food on the eighth day of the month, food on the fifteenth day of the month, food on the first day of the month, the regular food of the Sangha, or food invited by a donor— one may accept it.
Sitting under a tree: by relying on this, a bhikṣu attains renunciation and full ordination, thereby establishing the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?
He replied:
"I am able.
If he should obtain extra provisions:
If there is a separate room, a pointed-roofed hut, a small house, a stone chamber, or two rooms with a single door, one may accept [residence].
Relying on fermented medicines, a bhikṣu may, by depending on these, leave the household life and receive full ordination, thereby perfecting the dharma of a bhikṣu.
"Can you maintain this throughout the remainder of your life?
He replied, "I can."
If you obtain long-term benefits—such as ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar—you may accept them.

Having received the precepts, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been accomplished according to the Dharma; you have obtained a proper dwelling; your preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is according to the Dharma; your instructors (*ācārya*) are according to the Dharma; and the community of monks (*saṃgha*) is complete and sufficient.
You should properly receive these teachings: you ought to exhort others to perform meritorious deeds, repair stupas, and make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
You must not disobey any instruction given by your preceptors and ācāryas that accords with the Dharma.

One should study, inquire, and recite the sūtras, diligently seeking skillful means so as to attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship within the Buddha-dharma.
Since you have first resolved to leave the household life, your efforts will not be in vain and their karmic fruition will never cease.
As for other matters you do not yet know, you should inquire of your Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
From this day forward, let those receiving full ordination proceed ahead.

Regarding the method for requesting the *karmācārya* to confer the higher ordination (*mahānāśī*) upon a *bhikṣuṇī*: the candidate for ordination, together with the community of *bhikṣuṇīs*, shall go before the community of *bhikṣus*. Standing in the presence of the *ācārya*, they shall perform the formal ritual and make this request:
"Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!"
I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to serve as my *karmācārya*. May the Venerable One act as my *karmācārya*.
Through reliance upon the Venerable One, may I receive the full ordination; out of compassion, please do so.
After it has been said three times, he should reply: "So be it."
Regarding the method for requesting ordination: after she has paid homage to the Saṃgha and performed the formal ritual, she speaks as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
I, [Name], am seeking to receive the full ordination from the Preceptor Nun [Name]."
I, [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the conferral of the full ordination, with the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] as my preceptor.
May the Saṃgha rescue me out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.)
The Ritual of the Preceptor’s Announcement: In this procedure, the preceptor first makes an announcement and subsequently asks questions.
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
This [person], so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun so-and-so.
This [person], so-and-so, now requests the Sangha to grant her the full ordination, with the preceptor nun so-and-so as her preceptor.
If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha listen with forbearance as I inquire about matters concerning obstacles.
Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
The Preceptor asks the candidate regarding the Dharma, saying:
Listen attentively!
Now is the time for truth, the time for speaking the reality. I now question you: if you have [committed such an act], you should say you have; if you have not, you should say you have not.
Have you not committed a pārājika offense?
Have you not committed an offense against a bhikṣu?
Are you not one who has taken up the path with a thief’s intent?
Are you not one who has broken away from either the inner or outer paths?
Are you not a eunuch? Are you not one who has killed his father?
Are you not one who has killed his mother?
Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Have you not, with a malicious mind, shed the blood of a Buddha?
Are you not a non-human? Are you not an animal?
Are you not of both sexes?
What is your name?
What is the name of your preceptor-ni?
Have you reached the required age?
Are your robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents or husband given you permission?
Are you not indebted to anyone?
Are you not a slave?
Are you a woman? Women have such various ailments as these:
"Leprosy, abscesses, consumption, insanity, the two channels being joined, narrowness of the birth canal, constant leakage of urine and feces, and constant discharge of mucus and saliva—
do you have any such ailments?"
Answer "No" according to the facts.
One should then ask again:
"Have you trained in the precepts?"
One should immediately reply:
"I have studied the precepts.
One should then ask again:
"Are you pure? One should then answer:
"I am pure."
Furthermore, one should ask the other nuns:
"Has so-and-so already trained in the precepts?
The other nuns should reply:
Having already learned the precepts,
he is asked again:
"Are you pure?"
He answers again, saying:

"Pure. Once the preparatory procedures for the formal bestowal of the precepts have been completed, he provides guidance as before, instructing him to receive them with utmost sincerity and truthfulness.
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
This [person], so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so."
This [person], so-and-so, now requests from the Saṃgha the full ordination (upasampadā), with the preceptor nun so-and-so.
So-and-so declares herself pure, free from all obstacles, of age, fully possessed of robes and bowl, and having already trained in the purity of the precepts.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now confer the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor-ni.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This [name], from the preceptor nun [name], seeks to receive the full ordination.
This [name] now requests the Sangha to grant her the full ordination, with [name] as the preceptor nun.
So-and-so has declared herself pure, free from obstacles, of full age, complete with robes and bowl, and having trained in the purity of the precepts.
The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon So-and-so, with Preceptor Nun So-and-so.
"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha conferring the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor nun, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
This is said three times."
The Sangha has already consented; the full ordination for [Name] has been completed, with [Name] as the preceptor nun.
Because the Sangha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya states:
"She declares herself pure and states that she has reached twenty years of age; the Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon [Name].
Since both parties recite these words together, there is no error in following this recitation.
Having performed this rite, one should announce the time.
This is no different from the procedure for receiving the precepts on the outskirts [of the community].
The method for conferring the characteristics of the precepts should be spoken to them as follows:
Listen attentively, virtuous woman!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed the eight pārājika rules; if a bhikṣuṇī violates them, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
One must not engage in impure conduct or practice the dharma of sexual desire.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in impure conduct or practices the dharma of sexual desire, even with an animal, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī;
she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not steal even so much as a blade of grass or a leaf.

If a bhikṣuṇī takes five coins or more than five coins from another person—whether she takes it herself or instructs another to take it; whether she cuts it herself or instructs another to cut it; whether she breaks it herself or instructs another to break it;
or whether she burns it, buries it, or alters its color—she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not take the life of any living being, even so small as an ant.

If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes a human life with her own hand, provides a person with a weapon, instructs them to die, praises death, encourages death, gives someone non-medicinal substances, causes an abortion, performs incantations or sorcery, or employs such means herself or teaches others to do so;
she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not utter false speech, even in jest.

If a bhikṣuṇī, being untrue and without such qualities herself, claims for herself that she has attained the state of a superior person—saying she has attained dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, or meditative absorption (samāpatti); or that she has attained the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat;
or that devas, nāgas, or yakṣas have come to make offerings to her—that woman is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate the precepts regarding conduct and life within this [community].
Can you maintain them? He replied, "I can."
One must not engage in physical contact, even with an animal.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, engages in physical contact with a man who has a defiled mind—between the armpits and above the knees—whether by rubbing, pressing, stroking upward, stroking downward, pulling, pushing, lifting up, lowering down, grasping, or pressing firmly;
she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not commit these eight acts, even with an animal.
