If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, accepts the hand-grasping, the garment-grasping, entering a secluded place, standing together in a secluded place, speaking together, walking together, physical leaning against one another, or making a rendezvous with a man who has a defiled mind;
if she commits these eight acts, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
He replied, "I can."
One must not conceal another's grave offenses, even down to a minor offense of wrong speech (*dukkaṭa*).
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a *pārājika* offense, she must not fail to report it herself, nor inform the Saṃgha, nor speak to others so that they may know.
At a later time, if this bhikṣuṇī has left the religious life, or has been expelled, or has been barred from participating in the communal affairs of the Saṃgha, or has entered a non-Buddhist sect;
she should then say:
"I previously knew that this person had committed such and such an offense."
"She is not a bhikṣuṇī; she is not a daughter of the Śākya clan, because she has concealed another's grave offense.
You must not commit this for as long as you live—can you uphold it?"
He replied, "I can.
[The Buddha said: "You must not follow the words of the monk who has been suspended, nor even those of a śrāmaṇera."

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a bhikṣu has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions— having committed an offense regarding proper conduct, yet not having confessed it, and not being permitted to live in communal residence—
and she nevertheless follows and accords with that bhikṣu’s words.
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister!

That bhikṣu has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's instructions; he has violated the rules of decorum and has not yet confessed his offense, nor does he agree to live in communal residence."
"Do not comply with the words of that bhikṣuṇī.
When the bhikṣuṇīs admonish this bhikṣuṇī and she persists in her refusal to relinquish [her position],
those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her up to three times so that she may relinquish this matter.
Up to three admonitions, if she relinquishes [the offense], it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan, because she has committed the offense of following a formal accusation.
You must not commit this for as long as you live; can you maintain this?
He replied, "I can.
"Listen attentively, virtuous woman!"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has spoken four similes:

if one commits the eight offenses, it is like severing a person's head so that they can never rise again; like cutting the heart of a tāla tree so that it will not grow further; like breaking the eye of a needle so that it can no longer be used; like splitting a great stone into two parts so that they can never be joined back together.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits the eight grave offenses, she cannot return to the practice of a bhikṣuṇī.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you maintain it?
He replied, "I can."
When conferring the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*), one should say to her:
"Listen attentively, virtuous woman!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances; by relying upon these, a bhikṣuṇī goes forth and receives full ordination, thereby perfecting the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī."
To go forth and receive the full precepts by relying on rag robes is the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?
Answer: Yes.
Yes. If one obtains long-term benefits—
such as robes offered by a donor or robes made from cut pieces— one should accept them.
"Living by alms-gathering, going forth, and receiving full ordination—this is the Dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
Can you uphold this for as long as life lasts?
She answers, saying:
Yes. If one obtains long-term benefits—

such as food assigned by the Saṃgha, food sent by a donor, food on the eighth day of the month, food on the fifteenth day, food on the first day of the month, the regular food of the community, or food invited by a donor— one should accept it.
"Sitting under a tree and receiving the full ordination (upasampadā) as a renunciant—this is the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?
She replies:
Yes. If one obtains additional benefits—
such as a separate room, a gabled house, a small room, a stone chamber, or two rooms with a single door— one should accept them.
"Going forth and receiving full ordination by means of fermented medicinal drugs is the rule for bhikṣuṇīs.
Can you maintain this throughout your entire life?
She replies:
Yes. If one obtains long-term benefits—
namely, clarified butter, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar— one should accept them.

You have completed receiving the precepts; the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been accomplished in accordance with the Dharma; you have obtained the proper standing; the Upādhyāya is in accordance with the Dharma; the Ācārya is in accordance with the Dharma; and the Sangha of both divisions is fully complete.
"You should properly receive these instructions on the Dharma: you ought to exhort others to perform meritorious deeds, repair stupas, and make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Regarding all lawful instructions and commands from your preceptors and ācāryas, you must not disobey them."
One should study, inquire, and recite the sutras, diligently seeking skillful means so as to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat within the Buddha-dharma.
Since you have first resolved to leave the household life, your efforts will not be in vain, and their karmic fruition will be unceasing.
As for other matters you do not yet know, you should inquire of your Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
He ordered that those receiving the precepts should go ahead.

4. Chapter on Teacher and Disciple (Part One). Chapter Four: On the Rules for Establishing Harmonious Conduct. At that time, there were bhikṣus who had not yet received instruction; they did not observe the rules of decorum, their robes were not properly adjusted, and they behaved even like the assemblies of Brahmins.
At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu who had no disciples and no one to attend to him; he passed away.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the existence of preceptors."
A preceptor should regard his disciples as his own children, and disciples should regard their preceptor as their father;
thus, through mutual respect and care for one another, the True Dharma shall endure for a long time, increasing and expanding.
He requested the Dharma as before.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I authorize bhikṣus who have ten years of seniority and possess wisdom to confer the full ordination upon others."
Furthermore, the preceptor is enjoined to practice the duties of a preceptor toward his disciple; he should act in this manner.

If the Saṃgha intends to perform one of the seven types of formal acts (*karmas*), such as censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) and so forth, the preceptor must manage the matter according to the Dharma within that process so that the Saṃgha does not perform the *karman* against the disciple;
if they do perform it, he must ensure it is done in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, if the Saṃgha performs one of the seven types of formal acts (*karmans*), such as censure, against a disciple, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) should manage the matter according to the Dharma so that the disciple becomes compliant and does not oppose the Saṃgha; he should cause the disciple to seek the removal of the offense so that the Saṃgha may quickly grant the lifting of the formal act.
Furthermore, if a disciple commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, the preceptor shall attend to him according to the Dharma:
if he ought to be granted the parivāsa probation, he shall grant the parivāsa, and so on, up to granting him the rehabilitation from the offense (ābṛti).
Furthermore, if a disciple falls ill, the preceptor should attend to him; if he has another person look after him, he must do so until the disciple recovers or passes away.
If the disciple is dissatisfied with his dwelling place, the preceptor should either move him himself or instruct someone else to move him.
If a disciple has any matter of doubt, it should be resolved according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings.
If wrong views arise, they should be instructed to abandon those wrong views and abide in right view.
One should protect them by means of two things:
by means of the Dharma and by means of food and clothing.

Regarding protection by means of the Dharma, one should instruct them in the increase of virtue, the increase of concentration, and the increase of wisdom, and teach them scholarship and the recitation of the scriptures.

Regarding the protection of food and clothing therein, one should provide them with food, clothing, seats, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness and debility, arranging these according to what one's capacity allows.
From this day forward, the rules for the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) are established as follows.
The preceptor must act accordingly;
if he fails to do so, he shall be dealt with according to the law.
Regarding the rules for the conduct of relying upon an *ācārya*: at that time, there were newly ordained bhikṣus whose preceptors had passed away and who had no one to instruct them;
because they lacked instruction, their conduct was no different from that of a gathering of Brahmins.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the existence of ācāryas and disciples.
An ācārya should regard his disciple as a son, and a disciple should regard his ācārya as a father; they should respect one another and serve one another in turn."
"In this way, within the Buddha-dharma, may it be further increased and widely disseminated.
One should make this request with the full ritual protocol, saying:
"Virtuous One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!"
I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to be my preceptor. May the Venerable One grant me his preceptorship; I shall dwell in dependence upon the Venerable One.
(Recite three times.)
He replied, "So be it.
Or he said:
"I grant you my reliance," or he says,
"Do not be negligent."
The ritual procedures for an ācārya are in all respects the same as those for an upādhyāya.

When the rules governing the conduct of disciples were established, various disciples did not practice the duties of a disciple; they would enter villages and other places without first informing their upādhyāya.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the rules for disciples shall be established, requiring that a disciple practice the duties toward his preceptor as follows.
The eight rules to be observed together are as previously stated.

Furthermore, without informing one’s preceptor, one must not enter a village, go to another person’s house, or travel with other bhikṣus or take other bhikṣus as companions. One must not give, nor receive; one must not assist in communal affairs, nor accept assistance in communal affairs from others. One must not shave another’s hair, nor cause another to shave one’s hair. One must not enter a bathhouse, nor rub or massage another’s body, nor have one’s own body rubbed or massaged by another. One must not go to a dwelling during the daytime, go to a cemetery, go outside the boundary, or travel to another region.

At dawn, he should enter the preceptor’s room to receive and recite the Dharma scriptures, inquire about their meaning, and remove the urinal; he should announce that the time has arrived, and so forth, as explained in detail.
He should inquire after his preceptor’s well-being three times each day—at dawn, at midday, and at dusk.
He should perform two services for the preceptor, never declining them even if they are laborious: first, the maintenance and repair of the dwelling; second, the mending and washing of robes.
Whatever the Upādhyāya instructs according to the Dharma, you shall fully and respectfully carry out.
If he sends you to travel in various directions, you must not decline or make excuses by invoking some pretext;
if you do so decline, you shall be dealt with according to the law.
From this day forward, I establish the rules for the practice of disciples;
if one does not practice them, they shall be dealt with according to the law.
This same rule applies to the practice performed under an ācārya, as the text is identical and thus not repeated here.

Regarding the method for rebuking disciples: at that time, the disciples did not serve or revere their preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and instructors (*ācārya*), nor did they follow the proper conduct of disciples. They were shameless and lacked a sense of moral dread; they did not accept instruction, acted with improper decorum, and were disrespectful. They were difficult to speak with, befriended evil people, and took pleasure in visiting the houses of courtesans, married women, unmarried girls, and eunuchs, as well as the monasteries of *bhikṣuṇīs*, *śikṣamāṇās*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*. They also delighted in going to watch turtles and tortoises.
When such faults exist, one should administer a formal reprimand.
There are three factors that must be present:
first, the disciple; second, the manifestation of the fault; and third, the words of the reprimand.
There are five forms of censure, which should be spoken as follows:
"I now reprove you! Depart!
Do not enter my room! Do not perform services for me! Do not come to where I am! I will not speak with you."
This is called the method for a preceptor (upādhyāya) to reprove a disciple.
The method for an ācārya to reprove a disciple is also fivefold; the wording is identical, except that the fourth phrase, "Do not come to my place," is changed to:
"Do not rely upon me."
He censured [the practice] for as long as he lived.
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
Even at the conclusion of the *varṣā* retreat, one should not reprimand in such a manner;
furthermore, one should not reprimand those who are ill.
Regarding the method for a disciple’s confession: after having been reprimanded, the disciple does not confess to their *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*.
The Buddha said:
"Once you have been reprimanded, you should confess to your upādhyāya and ācārya.
You should perform the confession according to the proper ritual, speaking as follows:"
"Venerable Sir!
I now repent and shall not do it again.
If you will accept my repentance, that would be well."
If they do not grant forgiveness, one should further perform repentance three times each day—at dawn, at midday, and at dusk.
If they accept the repentance, it is well;
if they do not accept it, one should humble oneself and comply, seeking skillful means to resolve the offense committed.
If that disciple humbles his mind and complies, showing no opposition, yet the preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) still refuses to accept him, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
There are five kinds of unrighteous conduct by which a preceptor causes a disciple to depart; in such cases, the disciple should offer a confession and then leave.
One should say to the preceptor:
"If I am acting in accordance with the Dharma, you do not know it;
if I am not acting in accordance with the Dharma, you likewise do not know it."
If I have transgressed the precepts, I neglect to admonish or rebuke them;
if they have transgressed, I do not even recognize it;
and if they have transgressed and offer repentance, I still do not recognize it.
In this manner, one should offer an apology with gentle words.
If [the preceptor] does not accept it,
the upādhyāya should depart and leave him at a distance.

The preceptor (niśrayācārya) should take his robes and bowl and go beyond the boundary; having stayed there overnight, he shall return on the following day and rely upon another bhikṣu for his residence.

Chapter Five: The Exposition of the Uposatha (Sūtra-pāṭha). Regarding the Dharma of the Saṃgha’s Uposatha: On the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day, the bhikṣus did not know on which day the Uposatha was to be observed.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the senior monk.
On the day of the poṣadha, he should announce:

Having thus announced this, when the time for the recitation arrives, the junior bhikṣus should go first to the hall where the recitation is held to sweep and sprinkle it, spread out the seats, prepare the water-pitcher for rinsing, the water-pitcher for washing the feet, light the lamps, and provide the śalākās (voting sticks).
If a junior bhikṣu does not know [the rules], the senior bhikṣu should instruct him;
if the senior bhikṣu does not instruct him, he commits a duṣkṛta offense;
if the junior bhikṣu does not follow the senior bhikṣu’s instruction, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
The same applies to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
At that time, the laypeople asked the bhikṣus,

Because he did not know this, the bhikṣu felt ashamed.

Although he counted them repeatedly, he still forgot.

"You should prepare counting-slips (śalākā)."
The *śalākā* (voting sticks) should be made of copper, iron, bamboo, wood, or similar materials; they should not be made of precious gems.

When the Saṃgha assembles, those sitting nearby should examine one another to ascertain whether everyone has arrived;
they should first announce this, and only then recite the precepts.

Regarding the method for instructing the bhikṣuṇīs: at the time of the recitation of the precepts, the elder asks, "Whom has the community of bhikṣuṇīs sent?

Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The community of bhikṣuṇīs at [place name] is in harmony; they have appointed the bhikṣuṇī [name] to pay homage at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha and to request instruction.
After it has been stated three times,
the Elder should further ask:
"Who will provide instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs?"
If there are [such persons], they should be appointed.

If that nun says, "I have invited this person," then she should be appointed based on that invitation.
If, however, she replies:
Regarding the phrase "I shall follow the community's assignment," the community should assign [a monk] according to the regular order of those who instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
The Buddha said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who is endowed with ten qualities..."

1. Being fully endowed with the precepts; 2. Being learned; 3. Having mastered the recitation of the two sets of precepts; 4. Being capable of making decisive judgments without doubt; 5. Being skilled in preaching the Dharma; 6. Having left the household life from a noble family; 7. Having a handsome appearance such that the community of bhikṣuṇīs feels joy upon seeing him; 8. Being capable of preaching the Dharma to the community of bhikṣuṇīs and encouraging them to feel joy; 9. Not having committed a grave offense after donning the dharma robes for the sake of leaving the household life under the Buddha; 10. Being at least twenty years of age or more than twenty years of age—one such as this should be appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
The appointment should be made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs."
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs."
"Whichever elders approve of appointing the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Sangha has approved and completed the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs."
The Saṃgha having consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The one appointed shall take a companion bhikṣu and go to the residence of the bhikṣuṇīs.
One should arrive at the appointed time, and the bhikṣuṇī should also go out to meet her at the appointed time.
If the bhikṣu does not arrive at the appointed time, it is a duṣkṛta;
if the bhikṣuṇī does not go out to meet her at the appointed time, it is likewise.
At that time, having observed the assembled multitude, the instructor spoke to them regarding the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed, as well as the Dharma teaching.
As for the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed:
although she may be a bhikṣuṇī of a hundred years' standing, upon seeing a newly ordained bhikṣu, she should rise to meet him, pay homage, and arrange a clean seat for him to sit upon.
This Dharma should be respected, revered, and praised; for as long as life lasts, one must not transgress it.
A bhikṣuṇī should not revile or scold a bhikṣu, nor should she slander him by saying:
"He has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his dignified conduct."
This Dharma should be respected, etc., as stated above.

A bhikṣuṇī should not perform an *ukkhepana* (formal accusation), an *anusmāraṇa* (reminding), or a *paccāropana* (self-accusation) against a bhikṣu; she should not obstruct another’s search for an offense, obstruct the *poṣadha*, or obstruct the *pravāraṇā*. A bhikṣuṇī should not reprimand a bhikṣu; rather, it is the bhikṣu who should reprimand the bhikṣuṇī.
This Dharma should be respected, etc., as stated above.
Once a śikṣamāṇā has completed her training in the precepts, she shall request the full ordination from the community of bhikṣus;
this rule regarding respect and so forth is as stated above.
When a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must perform the mānatva penance before both communities of monks and nuns.
This rule should be respected, etc., as stated above.
A bhikṣuṇī shall request instruction from the Saṃgha every half-month;
this rule should be respected, etc., as stated above.
A bhikṣuṇī should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where no bhikṣus are present;
such rules should be respected as described above.
When the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha has completed the summer retreat, they should go before the bhikṣu-saṃgha and request the three matters for the invitation to admonish (pravāraṇā).
"Seen, heard, or suspected;
such dharmas should be respected," and so forth,
as above.
Next, he shall preach the Dharma for them, instructing and guiding them according to their capacities.

Regarding the brief instructions on the Dharma, if there is no nun available to provide instruction and she cannot be found despite a general invitation, the bhikṣu who received the entrustment shall return before the senior monk (upādhyāya) and report the matter in full.
The Elder should say to them:
"This person provides no instruction for bhikṣuṇīs, nor is there anyone capable of preaching the Dharma.
Tell the community of bhikṣuṇīs: 'Exert yourselves in practice; do not be negligent!'"
On the following day, when the nuns arrive, this bhikṣu shall convey the words of the Elder.

Regarding the dharma of *pārisuddhi* (purification): if the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day [of the half-month] arrives and the resident bhikṣus wish to recite the *Prātimokṣa*, and guest bhikṣus arrive—whether they be few or equal in number—the resident bhikṣus should recite the *Prātimokṣa* again from the beginning.
Otherwise, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If the visiting monks are more numerous, the resident monks should seek reconciliation with them;
if this cannot be achieved, they should go outside the boundary to recite the precepts.

If the resident monks have already finished reciting the precepts and visiting monks arrive wishing to recite them, whether they are fewer or equal in number, the visiting monks should seek reconciliation with the resident monks.
If it cannot be obtained, one should go outside the boundary to recite the precepts.
If the visiting bhikṣus are more numerous, one should follow the visiting bhikṣus and recite the precepts again;
otherwise, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If the day is the same but the time is different, and the resident bhikṣus have already assembled and finished reciting the introduction (nidāna), while the visiting bhikṣus arrive in small numbers, they should announce their purity.
They should make this announcement as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
"I, bhikṣu [name], am pure.
Having made this announcement, the others should listen in succession.
If the recitation of the precepts is finished, whether the entire assembly has not yet risen, or most have not yet risen, or all have already risen, one should likewise announce their purity.
If not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If, after the introduction has been recited, the number of visiting monks is equal to or greater than that of the resident monks, the resident monks shall recite the precepts again;
if not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If, after the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* has concluded, the entire assembly has not yet risen, or most have not yet risen, or all have already risen, one should recite it again.
If visiting *bhikṣus* have assembled and recited the introduction (*nidāna*) and so forth, and resident *bhikṣus* subsequently arrive, it is to be treated in the same manner.
Regarding the rules for the abbreviated recitation of the precepts (*saṃkṣipta-poṣadha*), the Vinaya states:
"If there are the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) or other circumstances, the abbreviated recitation of the precepts is permitted.
As for the "eight difficulties":
Whether it be due to a king, a thief, fire, water, illness, humans, non-humans, or malevolent insects;
as for other circumstances:
if a great assembly has gathered but there are few seats, or if many members of the assembly are ill, one is permitted to perform a brief recitation of the precepts.

If a great assembly has gathered, but the seating is not fully covered, or if it rains, or if the *poṣadha* has lasted many nights and become long, or if there is a matter of dispute, or if they are discussing the *Abhidharma* or the *Vinaya*, or if the night of preaching the Dharma has already been long—provided that the entire assembly has not yet risen and the dawn-sign (*āloka-lakṣaṇa*) has not yet appeared—one should perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts. There is no other expedient means by which one may receive the consent (*chanda*) and purity (*śuddhi*) while staying overnight.
Omitting the preliminary procedures, follow exactly the extensive method.

Regarding the measurement of distance—whether it is far or near—if the recitation of the preface to the *Prātimokṣa* and the inquiry into purity have been completed and the distance becomes difficult to traverse, one should say:
"Venerable sirs!"
These four *pārājika* rules have been regularly recited by the Saṃgha;
the same applies up to the *śaikṣa* rules.
From the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) onwards, they are to be recited at length according to the text.
If adverse conditions approach so closely that there is no time to recite the introduction, one should depart immediately on account of those conditions.
Regarding the method for reciting the *Poṣadha* in the presence of others: if there are three people, they should face one another and speak as follows:
"O two elders, please bear this in mind!"
Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha recites the Prātimokṣa; I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure.
(Recite this) three times.
The same applies to the other two.
The Method for Reciting the Prātimokṣa by Mental Intention: If there is but one person, he should mentally reflect, saying:
"Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha recites the Prātimokṣa; I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure."
The third recitation.
Regarding the legal rules for increasing or decreasing the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the Vinaya states:

"If there are bhikṣus who delight in fighting and reviling, who mutually slander one another, and whose mouths produce swords and blades, and they wish to come here to recite the precepts, one should perform two or three *poṣadha* ceremonies."
If it should be recited on the fifteenth day, one should do so on the fourteenth;
if it should be recited on the fourteenth day, one should do so on the thirteenth;
if one hears that [the assembly] will arrive today, one should immediately perform the *poṣadha* with haste.
If, after hearing [the announcement], they have already entered the boundary, they should go outside the boundary to recite the precepts.
If they can do so, it is well;
if they cannot, they should make a formal motion (*jñapti*) and then recite the precepts.
He makes this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha not recite the Prātimokṣa now, but shall do so on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight."
I have made this announcement.
If the visiting bhikṣus do not depart, a second announcement of refusal should be made.
It should be made in this manner:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time for the Saṃgha has come and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha not recite the Prātimokṣa now; it shall be recited on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon.
The announcement is made thus.

If the visiting bhikṣus still do not depart when the bright fortnight arrives, the resident bhikṣus should, in accordance with the Dharma, engage the visiting bhikṣus in formal questioning and answering.

If, during an improper time for the formal act of reconciliation, a dispute arises due to the raising of a matter, such that the accuser and the accused are at odds and the community is divided for the recitation of the precepts,
they should repent and reform their transgressions and request the Sangha to lift the suspension.
Once the suspension has been lifted, a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) is made to perform the *poṣadha* in harmony.
The announcement should be made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

On account of that matter, the Saṃgha has been embroiled in strife and slander, mutually seeking out each other's faults; it has caused the Saṃgha to be split, caused the Saṃgha to dwell separately, and caused the Saṃgha to become defiled."
That person has been formally charged by the Saṃgha with an offense, but has since been released; the impurities of the Saṃgha have been extinguished.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha perform the *poṣadha* in harmony.
The announcement is made as follows.
Having made this announcement, the *poṣadha* is performed in unison.
Regarding the method for reciting the precepts at an improper time: if it is due to strife that causes the Saṃgha to be discordant and the Saṃgha to become divided into two factions.
If one can repent within this matter and not incite others to raise the issue, this is called "harmony through the Dharma.
One should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):

The matter of dispute upon which the community of monks relies causes the Sangha to quarrel and lack harmony; it destroys the Sangha, defiles the Sangha, and causes the Sangha to become divided into two factions.
That person has personally acknowledged their transgression and has now repented, thereby removing the dust and defilement from the Saṃgha.
If the time for the Saṃgha has arrived, and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now, in harmony, recite the Prātimokṣa.
The announcement is made as follows.

Section Six: The Rain Retreat (*Varṣā*). Part One. Regarding the Method for Addressing Each Other: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should not travel among human settlements at all times throughout spring, summer, and winter.
From this day forward, I allow the bhikṣus to observe the three-month summer rains retreat.”
One should speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am dependent upon the monastery [Name]; if it is within a village, one should say:"
If one is in a certain village or in a specific room, one should say:
"In such-and-such a room, I shall observe the three-month summer retreat;
this is for the purpose of repairing dilapidated quarters."
This is recited three times.
Because the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) relies upon a fifth *vinayadhara*, one must ask:
"Upon whom do you rely to uphold the Vinaya?"
He should reply:
"I rely upon Master So-and-so.
He should further say:
"If you have any doubts, you should ask.
He replied again, "So be it."
The procedure for the latter three-month *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) is also like this.
There are two types of *varṣā*:
first, the earlier; second, the later.
If one observes the earlier retreat (*pūrvavārṣika*), one shall remain for the first three months;
if one observes the later retreat (*paścimavārṣika*), one shall remain for the latter three months.
Regarding the rule of mental recollection (*cittānuśāsana*), the Vinaya states:
From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣus who have no one to rely upon to observe the rains retreat through mental resolve (*cittotpāda*).
The ritual procedure is the same as before, with the exception of the opening statement and the subsequent question and answer.

He performed the three proclamations, but forgot to state that the *dharmatā* (the formal procedure) was established. At that time, a bhikṣu residing at a monastery wished to enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*), but he failed to inform anyone upon whom he relied and did not bring it to mind. [The question is: Is it considered established or not?
The Buddha said, "If one comes for the sake of the rains retreat (*varṣā*), it constitutes the completion of the retreat.

At the time of the formal procedures regarding boundaries, some bhikṣus went to their place of residence intending to enter the retreat; however, as soon as they entered the boundary, the dawn broke. They had doubts: "Is the retreat considered completed?"
The Buddha said:
"If one comes for the sake of the rains retreat (varṣā), one thereby establishes the rains retreat.
The same applies when entering a monastery garden; it is identical.
Next, entering a boundary or a monastery with only one foot is also treated in this manner.

Chapter Seven: Receiving the *Saptāha* (Seven-Day) Period (Part One). Regarding the rules for addressing another (*pratimukha-dharma*): if there are matters concerning the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha; if one is summoned by a donor, parents, or others; if one is to receive a confession; or due to illness, nursing the sick, seeking fellow practitioners, or other such circumstances where it is impossible to return on the same day, it is permitted to receive the seven-day period before departing.
One should act as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], having received the seven-day leave to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose, inform the Venerable One so that he may know that I shall return here to observe the rains retreat."
This is stated three times.
One should not go solely for the sake of food and drink.
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) is established because the preceding circumstances were such that one could not return within seven days.
The Buddha said:

"I allow such a matter: the practice of receiving [the robe] for more than seven days, whether for fifteen days or one month, by means of a formal motion and second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
It should be performed in this manner."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If the time for the Saṃgha has come, and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let this bhikṣu named [Name] receive the *saptāha-vartanīya* (the seven-day rule) for fifteen days or one month to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose, and then return here to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
It is announced as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu [Name], having received the seven-day, fifteen-day, or one-month *anumata* (permission), shall go outside the boundary for a certain purpose and return here to observe the rains retreat."

"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha’s authorization for the bhikṣu so-and-so to receive the 'seven-day-at-most' rule—whether for fifteen days or one month—to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose and return to observe the rains retreat within these limits, let them remain silent; whoever does not consent, let them speak."

The Sangha has already granted its consent for the bhikṣu so-and-so to receive the seven-day, fifteen-day, or one-month *anujñā* (permission) to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose, and having returned here, he shall complete his rains retreat within this area.
The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent; thus this matter is upheld. Chapter 8:

On the Pravāraṇā (Self-Examination). Part One. The Procedure for Announcing the Pravāraṇā to the Saṃgha: "From this time forward, it is permitted to perform the pravāraṇā once the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*) has concluded."
Regarding the request for permission to withhold the *pravāraṇā*: one should not seek such permission. Why?
Because the *pravāraṇā* itself is the granting of permission.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus did not know whether the *pravāraṇā* was to be held today or tomorrow.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is permitted that at the time of the morning meal or the midday meal, the Elder shall proclaim:
'Venerable Sangha, listen!'"
"Today, on the [day] of the [month], at the [time], the Sangha has assembled at [place] for the *pravāraṇā*.
The remaining ritual procedures and so forth are all the same as those for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

Regarding the method for appointing those who receive the *pravāraṇā*, the various bhikṣus performed the *pravāraṇā* all at once in a noisy and chaotic manner; furthermore, they did not seek to follow the proper sequence, leaving the Elder (*sthavira*) utterly exhausted."
The Buddha said:
"It should not be done in that way; I allow you to appoint a person to receive the *pravāraṇā* by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
One who possesses five qualities should be appointed."
If one is not biased, not hostile, not fearful, and not deluded, and knows whether the invitation has been performed or not yet performed,
such a person should be appointed.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the person to receive the invitation to self-examination (*pravāraṇā*).
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so as the person to receive the invitation to criticism (*pravāraṇā*).
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so as the person to receive the invitation to criticism should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the person to receive the invitation to admonish;
the Sangha consents, because it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the formal motion for the invitation to admonish (*pravāraṇā*), the Vinaya states:
When listening to the monks' sitting, one should ascertain whether they have arrived;
first make a formal announcement, and afterwards perform the *pravāraṇā*.
Make the announcement as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony.
The announcement is as follows.
Regarding the legal procedure for the *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha, it is said:
"It is permitted to recite the three [verses] slowly, so that the *pravāraṇā* is clearly understood."
One should not fold the robe over the back or wrap it around the neck, etc.; rather, one should expose one shoulder, etc., and speak as follows:
"Venerable Sir!"
Today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā*.
If you, Venerable Elders, out of compassion, should see, hear, or suspect any offense in me, please speak to me; if I perceive the offense, I shall confess it according to the Dharma.
This is stated three times.
If a sick bhikṣu is present, the Buddha permits him to perform the *pravāraṇā* according to his own comfort.
The procedure for announcing one's purity (*śuci*) and the method of making that announcement are identical to those for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.
Regarding the rules for the abbreviated *pravāraṇā*:
the Vinaya states that if there are the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv āpattayaḥ*) or other circumstances, an abbreviated *pravāraṇā* is permitted.
If the difficult situation is still far off and there is sufficient time to perform the full recitation, one should perform the full recitation.
If a difficult situation approaches and one cannot recite it three times, one should recite it twice;
if one cannot recite it twice, one should recite it once;
if one does not do so, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If difficult circumstances are imminent such that a single recitation is not possible, the bhikṣus should immediately make a formal announcement (jñapti):
"Let us each perform the invitation to confession (pravāraṇā) by reciting it three times together.
They should make the announcement as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha now each perform the *prātimokṣa* invitation (*pravāraṇā*) by means of three statements.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this announcement, they each perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) three times;
the same applies if it is stated twice or once.
If a difficult situation is imminent such that they cannot each perform the *pravāraṇā* three times, nor can they make the announcement, they should depart immediately on account of that matter.
The Method of *Pravāraṇā* by Mutual Declaration: If there are four persons, each should face the others and speak as follows:
"Venerable sirs, please take note!
Today is the day of the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha; I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure regarding my *pravāraṇā*."
Recite this three times.
If there are three or two people, it is also done in this manner.
Regarding the method for the *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) performed through mental recollection when there is only one person, one should mentally recite as follows:
"Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure regarding the *pravāraṇā*.
(Recite this) three times.
Regarding the legal procedure for the *pravāraṇā* with added elements, the Vinaya states:
If there are many bhikṣus who have entered the rains retreat (*varṣā*), diligently practicing the Path and attaining the realization of superior fruits (*viśeṣa-phala*), those bhikṣus might think:
"If we were to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony today, we would have to move to another location; I fear we shall no longer be able to enjoy such bliss."
That bhikṣu should immediately make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to extend the *pravāraṇā*.
He should make the announcement as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: the Saṃgha shall not perform the *pravāraṇā* today; when the four months are complete, it shall perform the *pravāraṇā*.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Having made this announcement, one shall perform the *pravāraṇā* when the four months are complete.
Regarding the legal procedure for the reduction or extension of the *pravāraṇā*:

The Vinaya states that if, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, one hears that monks from another residence who have been quarreling and living in discord intend to come here for the *pravāraṇā*, those monks should perform the *pravāraṇā* with the date reduced by two or three days.

If, after hearing [the announcement], they have already entered the boundary, one should provide them with bathing vessels and other requisites; having settled them, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* outside the boundary.
If they can act with such skillful means, it is well;
if they cannot, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* by means of a formal motion (*jñapti*) for the sake of the presiding authority.
He makes this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha not hold the *pravāraṇā* today, but shall hold the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight."
The announcement is made as follows.
Having made this announcement, the *pravāraṇā* is further extended.
If a visiting bhikṣu remains until the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, the resident bhikṣus should perform the announcement for a second further extension of the *pravāraṇā*.
Make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha not perform the *pravāraṇā* today; rather, it shall perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the latter half of the month."
The announcement is made thus.
If the visiting bhikṣus still do not depart, the resident bhikṣus should, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, forcibly bring about a harmonious *pravāraṇā*.
When receiving the *pravāraṇā* from the bhikṣuṇīs, the community of bhikṣus should assemble in its entirety; those who do not attend must provide a formal authorization (*anujñā*).
After that bhikṣuṇī has finished reciting her *pravāraṇā* within the Saṃgha, the Elder of the Saṃgha says:
"Venerable Saṃgha, we do not see any offense—whether seen, heard, or suspected—in this bhikṣuṇī community that may be brought forth."
He addressed the community of bhikṣuṇīs, saying: “Perform the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma; be diligent and do not be negligent!
Having had the bhikṣuṇīs prostrate at his feet, he sent them back. Chapter Nine:
Receiving and Purifying Robes, Alms Bowls, and Medicines (Part One). Regarding the method for receiving the three robes, according to the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*, it says:
Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, the bhikṣu [name], am receiving this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of so many strips; it is so many spans long and so many spans wide, and I shall maintain it as a robe of cut pieces.
Recite this three times.
Receiving the two lower robes follows the same procedure by analogy.
The ritual for relinquishing the three robes should be performed by reversing the formula for receiving them as follows:
Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], having received this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips—[number] long and [number] short—and having maintained it as a robe of cut pieces, now relinquish it.
Recite this three times.
The procedure for relinquishing the two lower robes is to be understood by analogy in the same way.
The ritual for receiving the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) should be stated as follows:
Venerable One, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], accept this *niṣīdana* as my auxiliary robe for the body.
(Recite three times.)
The method for receiving other auxiliary robes is the same as this.
Regarding their relinquishment, one should know that it is the reverse of the procedure for receiving them.
The Vinaya rules concerning the reception of the alms-bowl state:
There are two kinds of bowls:
first, those made of clay; second, those made of iron.
Their colors are likewise of two kinds:
The first is red, the second is black.
The large size is three *sheng*, the small size is one and a half *sheng*.
These should be kept or given as pure gifts (*pariśuddha-dāna*). Regarding their maintenance, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), it says:
Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], accept this pātra of standard measure for the purpose of long-term use.
(Recite three times.)
Regarding "relinquishing," it should be understood as the opposite of "accepting.
Regarding the legal rules for accepting non-timely medicine, the Vinaya states:
"It is permitted to drink eight kinds of syrups."
First, mango juice; second, jambu fruit juice; third, sour jujube juice; fourth, sugarcane juice; fifth, mṛdvīkā fruit juice; sixth, śālu-ka juice; seventh, pāruṣaka juice; eighth, grape juice.
If it does not intoxicate people, one may drink it at improper times;
if it intoxicates people, one should not drink it;
if one drinks it, one shall be dealt with according to the law.
Having received it from the hand of a pure person, one should then address a bhikṣu with the following formula:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!
I, the bhikṣu [name], for the reason of a certain illness, have this [type of] non-time beverage; in order to consume it outside of the proper time, I now receive it from you, venerable sir."
Recite this three times.
The procedure for receiving the other two medicines is the same.
For the seven-day medicine, one should say:
Because it is for the purpose of taking [the medicine] for seven days after having stayed overnight together,
one should say "for the purpose of long-term taking throughout one's life" when staying overnight for the duration of one's life.
Seven-day medicines are those such as clarified butter (*sarpis*).
Life-long medicines are all salty substances, fermented acids, and so forth, which are unfit to be used as food.
Regarding the ritual of "true purification" (*yathābhūta-pariśuddhi*), one should say:
Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I have this long robe which has not yet been purified; now, for the sake of purification, I relinquish it to you, venerable sir, for the purpose of true purification.
To perform the purification by truth (*bhūta-śuddhi*), one should ask the donor for permission before putting on the garment.
The same applies to the bowl and medicinal substances.
Regarding the method of purification through transmission (*paramparā-śuddhi*), it should be said as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!
This is my extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) which has not yet been purified; for the sake of purification, I give it to you, venerable sir, so that it may be purified through transfer.
The recipient who accepts the purification should say:"
"Venerable sir, attend to me with a focused mind!
You have this extra robe which has not yet been purified; for the sake of purifying it, you give it to me, and I now accept it.
Having accepted it, he says:
"To whom have you given it?
He should reply,
"I gave it to so-and-so."
The recipient of the purification says:
"Venerable one, attend to me with a single mind!
This long robe of yours has not yet been purified; for the sake of purification, you have given it to me. I now accept it."
Having received it, you give it to [Name]; this robe already belongs to [Name]. You must guard and maintain it well for [Name], wearing and using it according to the circumstances.
This constitutes a "successive purification" (*parivartaka-śuddhi*); whether he asks or does not ask, it is permitted for him to wear it as he pleases.
The bowl and the medicinal substances are similar; they differ only in their specific functions.
Section Ten: On the Collection of Objects (Part One). Section Ten: On the Collection of Objects. Regarding the legal rules for the timely distribution of present offerings, the Vinaya states:
"From this day forward, one should not seek summer robes at all times—whether in spring, summer, or winter."
Furthermore, one should not observe the rains retreat in one place and receive one's share of the summer robes in another.

Moreover, there was a bhikṣu who, having already entered the rains retreat at one residence, stayed instead in another; he did not know from which location he should take his share of the retreat provisions.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to take [the portion] from where you have stayed for the greater number of days.
If you have stayed for an equal number of days at both places, I allow you to take half from each."
It is further stated:
When the Saṃgha obtained robes for the summer retreat (varṣā), the Saṃgha split into two factions.
The Buddha said:
"One should count the number of people and divide [the property] accordingly.

Whether the summer robes have not yet been obtained, or whether some have obtained them while others have not, even when the Saṃgha is split into two factions, one should still count the number of people and divide."
Regarding these rules for the distribution of gifts made in person, there was no formal procedure established.

At that time, in Rājagṛha, when the lay devotees (upāsakas) heard that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to accept robes offered by donors, they immediately dispatched men to deliver various fine garments to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to divide it."

Not knowing how to divide it, one should count the number of people to determine the portions: if there are ten people, it is divided into ten parts; up to a hundred people, it is divided into a hundred parts;
the good and the bad are mixed together in the division.
One should not take one's own portion, but have another person take it.
One should not cast one's own voting tally, but have someone who is not present cast it.
Since this involves counting people, there is likewise no method for distributing portions.

Regarding the procedure for the distribution of gifts to the Saṃgha during the rainy season retreat: suppose a bhikṣu departs before the summer robes have been distributed. Later, when the bhikṣus distribute the summer robes, they do not dare to take a portion for the one who has departed. The bhikṣus do not know whether the distribution is valid or not.
The Buddha said:
"The portion shall be divided; they should wait for one another, and they should also entrust it to a subsequent person to receive the summer robe portion.
The Vinaya states:
If a single bhikṣu, while observing the rains retreat, obtains a large quantity of robes and requisites intended for the Sangha’s summer retreat, that bhikṣu should form this thought:
"This is my property."

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for the face-to-face method, it is identical to the rules for the untimely distribution of gifts to the Saṃgha; as there is no difference, it is not set forth here.

As for the rules for appointing a person to distribute items from the untimely distribution of gifts to the Saṃgha: when there is a settled residence, the present members of the Saṃgha obtain the divisible clothing and goods.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to divide them.
While they were dividing them, many guests arrived, and they grew utterly exhausted from the task of distributing the robes.
One person should be appointed to perform the distribution; this person must possess five qualities, which are as stated above.
It should be done in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to act as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to serve as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha.
Those elders who consent to the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of goods for the Sangha.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Distributing rice gruel for the Saṃgha, distributing light meals, *khajjaka*, assigning invitations to assemblies, spreading bedding, distributing bedding, distributing bathing robes, distributing robes, giving what may be given, taking what may be taken, appointing monks as messengers, and appointing novices as messengers—all such matters are likewise [governed by this rule].
There are five qualities by which one who distributes rice porridge for the Sangha goes to hell as swiftly as a shot arrow: namely, having craving and so forth.
There are five qualities by which one who distributes rice porridge is born in heaven as swiftly as a shot arrow: namely, being without craving and so forth.
This applies even down to the appointment of a novice as a messenger;
it is the same in all such cases. Regarding the method for entrusting items of cloth or other goods: once the person has been appointed, the items must be entrusted to them.
The entrustment is performed in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Whatever robes or non-robes are present in this residence should be distributed by the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let the Saṃgha now give these to the bhikṣu so-and-so, who shall then distribute them to the Saṃgha.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Whatever is present at this residence—whether it be robes or non-robes—the Saṃgha currently present should divide it."
The Saṃgha now gives this to the bhikṣu so-and-so, who shall give it to the Saṃgha.
Those elders who consent to this—that whatever belongs to the present Saṃgha, whether it be robe-cloth or not robe-cloth, should be divided;
and that the Saṃgha gives it to the bhikṣu so-and-so, who shall give it to the Saṃgha—let them remain silent. Whoever does not consent, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to give [the property] to the bhikṣu so-and-so; he shall now distribute it to the Saṃgha.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having performed this rite, the items shall be divided equally according to the number of persons.
If the śrāmaṇeras are in harmony, they shall share equally;
if they are not in harmony, two parts shall be given to one;
and if they are still not in harmony, three parts shall be given to one.
Furthermore, if it is not given, one should not divide it;
one-fourth should be given to the monastery attendants.
If it is not given, one should not divide it.

The Procedure for Directly Taking Charge of Objects by Four Monks: If there are only four monks, it is not possible to appoint an official nor to entrust the task; one should simply perform the procedure of taking charge directly.
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
Whatever is present at this dwelling, whether it be robes or non-robes, the *saṃgha* currently assembled should divide it.
If the time is right for the *saṃgha*, and the *saṃgha* grants its consent, let the *saṃgha* now divide these items among those present.
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Whatever belongs to this residence—whether it be cloth or not cloth—the present Saṃgha should divide it; now the present Saṃgha shall divide these items."

"Venerable sirs, those who consent to these robes or non-robes of this residence—which the present Saṃgha should divide—let those members of the present Saṃgha who approve of dividing these items remain silent; whoever does not consent, let them speak."
The Sangha has already consented; the distribution of these robes and articles by the present Sangha is now complete.
Because the Sangha consents through silence, this matter is thus upheld.
Having performed the *karmavācanā*, the method of distribution is as previously described.
Regarding the method for receiving items through face-to-face agreement: if there are three persons, they should mutually receive them by means of three utterances.
They should speak as follows:
"Venerable Elders, please bear this in mind!"
Whatever is in this residence, whether it be robes or non-robes, the present Saṃgha should divide it.
There is no Saṃgha here; this is our portion.
(Recite this) three times.
The same applies to two persons; the method for dividing the property is as previously described.
Regarding the method for mentally designating property: if there is only one person, he should mentally resolve:
"In this residence, whether it be robes or non-robes, the present Saṃgha shall divide them."
"There are no monks here; this is my portion.
(Recite this) three times.
The method of distribution is as previously described.

The Procedure for Receiving Offerings by Convening the Two Assemblies of Monks: At that time, in a certain residence, the two assemblies of monks obtained a large quantity of divisible robes and requisites; at that time, the assembly of bhikṣus was numerous, while the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs was few.
The Buddha said:
"It should be divided into two parts.
If there are no bhikṣuṇīs, but only śikṣamāṇās, it should likewise be divided into two parts.
If there are only śrāmaṇerikās, they shall also divide it into two portions;
if there are no śrāmaṇerikās, the Saṃgha should divide it.
If the bhikṣus are few and the bhikṣuṇīs are many, they shall likewise divide it into two portions.
If there are no bhikṣus and only śrāmaṇeras are present, they shall also divide it into two portions;
if there are no śrāmaṇeras, the bhikṣuṇīs should divide it.
Having divided it into two portions, each group shall go to their respective places and divide it by means of the three methods, such as performing the *karmavācanā*.
The distribution of alms received by the Saṃgha was likewise. Regarding the two types of offerings made in the presence of the assembly, these were divided among the number of persons present.

As for the rules concerning the property of deceased bhikṣus: at that time, the bhikṣus divided the monastic gardens, fields, and fruit trees; they further distinguished the rooms and the items belonging to specific rooms; they also divided the bronze jars, bronze basins, cauldrons, and other heavy articles; they also divided the rope beds, wooden beds, sitting cushions, bedding, and pillows; they also divided the *elāyanta*, *maurava*, *maudgalaka*, and woolen rugs; they also divided the carriages and the monastery attendants; they also divided the water pitchers, rinsing vessels, mendicant staffs, and fans; and they also divided the iron tools, wooden tools, ceramic tools, leather tools, and bamboo tools.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be divided; it belongs to the Sangha of the four directions.

However, woolen rugs (three cubits wide and five cubits long, with a pile three finger-widths high), razors, robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, containers for storing robes, and *kūyara* vessels should be divided among the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the present assembly)."
Having first made this preliminary distinction, one then performs the formal rite.
When the patient-care attendant relinquishes the items before the Saṃgha, he holds the objects and, having prepared the proper ritual deportment within the assembly, makes this declaration:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

If a certain bhikṣu dies in another location, it is said that he has passed away at that place of residence. Regarding his robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container—whatever six items are currently present here, the formal ritual (karmavācanā) is performed for them; if any are missing, they should be excluded.
Furthermore, if the categories of items are numerous and these words do not encompass them all, one should say:
"Whether it be robes or non-robes,
this dwelling place shall be divided by the present Saṃgha."
Recite this three times.
Regarding the legal rules for rewarding those who tend to the sick, the Vinaya states:
The Saṃgha asks the attendant to say:
“Does the sick person have any instructions left?
Who owes the sick person anything?
Or whom does the sick person owe anything?”
There are five qualities by which one should be given property for the care of a patient:
first, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not eat, and being able to provide what they may eat;
second, not loathing or despising the patient’s excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit.
3. Possessing a heart of compassion, one does not act for the sake of food or clothing;
4. being able to manage medical treatments until the patient recovers or passes away;
5. being able to preach the Dharma to the sick person, causing them to rejoice, while one’s own self increases in wholesome qualities.
If these five conditions exist, one should take the clothing and requisites of the sick person.
Regarding such items as robes and bowls, they shall be awarded according to what is currently available;
if none are present, other items must not be substituted in their place.
It should be distributed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [name] has passed away; his robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container shall be divided by the present Saṃgha."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now assign [this task] to the monk who is tending to the sick.
This is the motion.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu has passed away; his robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container should be divided by the present Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now bestows these upon the bhikṣu who attended to that deceased monk.

"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha granting the robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing container to this bhikṣu who tended to the sick, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak."
The Saṃgha has already consented to give the robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage vessel to the bhikṣu who attended to the sick.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The procedure for appointing a person to distribute robes is as follows; possessing the requisite qualities as previously described, one should appoint them in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to act as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha."
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to serve as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha.
"Whichever elders approve of appointing the bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has approved and completed the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of goods for the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is upheld as such.
Regarding the method for distributing items of clothing, once the person has been appointed, it should be handed over in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
A certain bhikṣu has passed away; whatever robes or non-robes he possessed, these should be divided by the present saṃgha.
If the time is right for the saṃgha, may the saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the saṃgha now gives [these items] to the bhikṣu so-and-so, and the bhikṣu so-and-so shall return them to the saṃgha.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so has passed away; whatever robes or non-robes he possessed, these should be divided by the present Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha now gives [this] to the bhikṣu so-and-so; the bhikṣu so-and-so shall in turn return it to the Saṃgha.

Those elders who consent that, upon the passing away of the bhikṣu so-and-so, whatever there may be—whether robes or non-robes—should be divided by the present Saṃgha, and that the Saṃgha now gives it to the bhikṣu so-and-so, who shall in turn return it to the Saṃgha: let them remain silent. Whoever does not consent, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to give [this] to the bhikṣu so-and-so; the bhikṣu so-and-so shall now return it to the Saṃgha.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The procedure for distribution is as before.
Regarding the method for four persons to directly take charge of the goods without appointing a distributor, they shall distribute them directly, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
"A certain bhikṣu has passed away; whatever robes or non-robes he possessed, these should be divided by the present saṃgha.
If the time is right for the saṃgha, may the saṃgha grant its consent: let the present saṃgha now divide these items."
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so has passed away. Whatever robes or non-robes he possessed should be divided by the present Saṃgha; now the present Saṃgha shall divide these items."

"Whichever elders consent that all the robes and non-robes belonging to the deceased monk so-and-so shall be divided by the present Saṃgha, and that the present Saṃgha now divides these items—let those who consent remain silent; whoever does not consent, let them speak."
The Saṃgha has already consented; the distribution of these robes and articles by the present Saṃgha is now concluded.
Because the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having performed the *karmavācanā*, the method of distribution is as previously described.
If there is a nurse, they should be rewarded with a verbal agreement.
Regarding the method for the communal management of property: if there are three people, they should mutually recite the acceptance three times, speaking as follows:
"Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind!
A certain bhikṣu has passed away; whatever robes or non-robes he possessed, these should be divided by the present Saṃgha.
Since there is no Saṃgha here, these are our portion."
This is recited three times.
The same applies to the other two persons; the distribution of the property is as previously described.
If there is a caregiver, they shall also receive a portion of the reward through verbal agreement.
The Method for Mentally Taking Possession of Objects: If there is a single person, one should mentally reflect, saying:
"A certain bhikṣu has passed away; whatever robes or non-robes he possessed, these should be divided by the present saṃgha."
"There is no monk here; this is my portion.
[This] is said three times.
The method of distribution is as before.
Regarding the rule for distributing items when there is no resident: At one time, a bhikṣu was traveling and arrived at a village where no bhikṣus resided. Having arrived, he passed away.
It was not known who should divide his robes and bowl, so they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If there is a faithful lay devotee (upāsaka) or a park-keeper at that place, they should be entrusted with it.
If any of the five groups of renunciants come forward, it should be given to them."
"If there is no one coming to receive it, it should be sent to a nearby monastery.
