Chapter Eleven: On the Robe of Merit (Middle). Chapter Eleven: On the Robe of Merit.
The Proclamation for Receiving the *Guṇavāsa* (Robe of Merit). The Vinaya states:
Whether it be a new robe, a robe offered by a donor, or a rag-robe— whether it be a new garment or an old one—
one should perform the ritual of *parikarmana* (purification) by attaching a patch to a new item;
if it has already been washed, one should perform the ritual of *parikarmana* after washing it and then folding it.

It must not be obtained through wrong livelihood, nor by means of signs, nor by agitation, nor by being kept overnight, nor by the rite of purification for what has been abandoned (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
It must be acquired on that very day in accordance with the Dharma; it should have a border sewn around the four sides and consist of five strips with ten sections.
Even if it exceeds these requirements, it may still be accepted.
One should personally wash, dye, stretch, and press it, then cut it into ten sections and sew them together.
One should receive it before the community of monks, making this announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
Today the community of monks receives the *guṇa-cīvara*.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the community of monks, being in harmony, shall receive the *guṇa-cīvara*.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Regarding the appointment of a person to maintain the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit), the Vinaya states:
One should ask who is able to maintain the robe of merit.
If someone says they are able, one should appoint them by means of a formal motion followed by a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the kaṭhina robe on behalf of the Saṃgha."
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Sangha, please listen!
The Sangha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the kaṭhina robe on behalf of the Sangha.
"Whichever elders approve of appointing the bhikṣu so-and-so to hold the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has approved and appointed the bhikṣu so-and-so to hold the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha."
Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having selected the person to receive the *kaṭhina* robe, one performs the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to entrust it to that robe-receiver.
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
In this residence, the Saṃgha has obtained cloth items that may be distributed; the present Saṃgha should divide them."

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; let the Saṃgha bestow this robe upon the bhikṣu [Name], so that this bhikṣu shall take this robe and, for the sake of the Saṃgha, receive it as a *kaṭhina* robe and maintain it at this residence.
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This monastery has obtained divisible robes and articles, which the present Saṃgha should divide."
The Sangha now bestows this robe upon the bhikṣu so-and-so; this bhikṣu shall take this robe for the Sangha to receive as a *kaṭhina* robe and maintain it at this residence.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha holding this robe for the bhikṣu so-and-so to receive it and make it into a *kaṭhina* robe remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
The Sangha has already consented and completed the bestowal of the robe upon the bhikṣu so-and-so."
The Saṃgha having consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the procedure for receiving the robe in the presence of the Saṃgha: the bhikṣu who holds the robe should stand up and take hold of the robe. When the hands of the various bhikṣus reach the robe and the verbal communication is clear, he should speak as follows:

"This robe the Saṃgha shall accept to make into a *kaṭhina* robe; this robe the Saṃgha now accepts to make into a *kaṭhina* robe; this robe the Saṃgha has already accepted to make into a *kaṭhina* robe."
Having spoken thus three times, those bhikṣus should say:
"The recipient has properly received [the merit]; whatever merit and renown exist herein belong to us."
The person holding the robe should reply,
"So be it. In this manner, the sequence continues down to the lowest seat.
Having received [this authorization], one is permitted to perform five things:

first, to keep extra robes; second, to stay overnight apart from one's robes; third, to eat in a separate group; fourth, to eat by successive invitations; and fifth, to enter a village without informing a bhikṣu.
Regarding the legal rules for appointing a person to make a *guṇakīva* (merit robe):
if unmade robes are obtained, the Saṃgha should appoint a person by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to make them.
The appointment should be made in this manner.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu [Name] to prepare a *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*)."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to prepare the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha.
Those elders who consent to the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] to prepare the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to prepare the *kaṭhina* robe for the Sangha.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The ritual procedure is as before.
Regarding the method for relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe: those six groups of bhikṣus did not relinquish the *kaṭhina*, thinking thus:
"We shall set aside the five privileges we have long enjoyed."
The Buddha said:
"You should not entertain such a thought. When the four months of winter have concluded, the Saṃgha should distribute the kaṭhina robe.
It should be done in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today the community of monks shall put forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha, being in harmony, now put forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
The announcement is made as follows.
If it is not relinquished, and the period for the *kaṭhina* robe expires, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are eight causes for the relinquishment of the *kaṭhina* robe:
1. Departure; 2. Completion; 3. Non-completion; 4. Loss; 5. Severance of hope; 6. Hearing; 7. Crossing the boundary; 8. Exiting together.
Furthermore, there are two ways of relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe:
if a bhikṣu who holds the *kaṭhina* robe spends the night outside the boundary, the Saṃgha may collectively relinquish it through a formal act of harmony.

Section Twelve: Elimination of Offenses (Middle). Section Twelve: Elimination of Offenses. Regarding the method for eliminating *pārājika* offenses, according to the Vinaya, there are five kinds of confession:
There may be those who commit an offense and repent through their own mental reflection;
there may be those who commit a minor offense and repent before another;
or there may be those who commit a middling offense and likewise repent before another.
Some may commit a grave offense and repent before another;
some may commit an offense that cannot be repented of—this irredeemable offense is called a *pārājika*.
Regarding the commission of a *pārājika* offense, there are three legal procedures:
first, for one who commits the offense and conceals it, the *pravāsanīyakarman* (act of banishment) is administered;
second, for one who commits the offense but does not conceal it, the *yāvajjīva-śikṣādattakarman* (act of lifelong training and repentance) is administered.

3. Regarding one who has committed a transgression while undergoing training for repentance (*śikṣādattaka*), the formal act of *parivāsa* (probation) followed by *nigarhaṇīya* (reproval) is to be performed.

If one who has committed a concealment is to be subjected to the rite of *parivāsa*, and if they have concealed a *pārājika* offense, the Saṃgha shall first perform the act of formal accusation (*codanā*), the act of calling to mind (*smṛti-karaṇa*), and the imposition of the penalty. Only after these have been granted shall the rite of *parivāsa* be carried out.
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense."

If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; the Saṃgha now performs the formal act of *parivāsa* (banishment) for the bhikṣu so-and-so for the offense of *pārājika*, such that he shall not dwell together [with the community] and shall not engage in communal affairs.
The motion is thus stated:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense."

The Saṃgha now performs the formal act of *niḥsāraṇīya-karman* for the expulsion of the bhikṣu so-and-so for the offense of *pārājika*, such that he shall not dwell together [with the community] and shall not engage in communal affairs.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *niḥsāraṇīya-karman* for the expulsion of the bhikṣu so-and-so for the offense of *pārājika*, such that he shall not dwell together and shall not engage in communal affairs, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The motion has been stated three times.

The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the formal act of *niḥsāraṇīya-karman* for the bhikṣu so-and-so for the offense of *pārājika*, such that he shall not dwell together with the community and shall not participate in communal affairs. The procedure is concluded.
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is held as such.
Regarding the legal procedure for granting *śikṣādattaka* (probationary training) for life to one who has not concealed [the offense], the Vinaya states:
If a bhikṣu has not yet committed a *pārājika* offense, he shall never commit one.

If one has already committed an offense but possesses no intention to conceal it and repents according to the Dharma, the Saṃgha is permitted to grant that bhikṣu the formal act (karmavācanā) of the *pārājika* precept.
He should, within the Saṃgha, perform the ritual with full decorum and make this request as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; having no intention whatsoever to conceal it, I now beg the Saṃgha for the pārājika-śikṣāpada.
"May the Saṃgha grant me, bhikṣu So-and-so, the Pārājika precepts; out of compassion.
(Recite this three times.
The Saṃgha should confer the dharma in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; being without a mind of concealment, he now requests from the Saṃgha the pārājika precept.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now bestow the *pārājika* precepts upon the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; being without a mind of concealment, he now begs the Saṃgha for the pārājika discipline.
The Saṃgha now grants the pārājika discipline to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha bestowing the *pārājika* discipline upon the bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
This is said three times.
The Sangha has consented and completed the bestowal of the *pārājika* discipline upon the bhikṣu so-and-so."
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is so upheld.
Having received the Pārājika precepts, one must follow and practice them accordingly throughout the remainder of one's life.
One who practices in accordance with the Dharma:
may not bestow full ordination upon others;
may not provide dependence (niśraya) to others.
One must not keep a śrāmaṇera;
if appointed to instruct bhikṣuṇīs, one must not accept the appointment;
even if appointed, one should not go to provide instruction.
One should not recite the precepts for the Saṃgha;
one should not engage in questions and answers regarding the Vinaya within the Saṃgha;
and one should not accept an appointment from the Saṃgha to serve as an administrator.
One should not accept a position of authority within the Saṃgha to adjudicate legal matters;
one should not accept a mission on behalf of the Saṃgha;
and one should not enter a village too early or return at the close of day.
One should associate with bhikṣus;
one must not associate with non-Buddhists or laypeople;
one should comply with the dharma of bhikṣus.
One must not speak other worldly speech;
one must not recite the Vinaya in the midst of the assembly, though it is permitted if there is no one else capable of reciting it;
one must not commit this offense again.
One should not commit other offenses as well—whether they are similar, derived from this, or more serious than this;
one must not participate in or perform a *karmavācanā* that is not authorized by the Saṃgha;
and one must not accept from a pure (*pariśuddha*) bhikṣu a seat-covering, water for washing the feet, a leather sandal-eraser, body massage, prostration, welcoming, or inquiries after one's welfare.
One should not accept the robes and bowl held by a pure bhikṣu;
one must not raise a pure bhikṣu for the purpose of a formal reminder (smṛti) or for a disciplinary procedure based on his own admission (svavāda-vinaya);
and one should not act as a witness in a legal matter concerning another person.
One must not obstruct a pure bhikṣu from reciting the precepts or performing the *pravāraṇā*;
one must not engage in disputes with a pure bhikṣu.

Regarding a bhikṣu who has committed a *pārājika* offense, whether he comes or does not come when the Saṃgha recites the precepts or performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*), the assembly incurs no offense.
Regarding the formal act of expulsion for one who has committed a grave offense while under probation for a previous offense, the monks asked:
"If a monk who has already been granted the *pārājika* discipline commits the offense again, may he receive the *pārājika* discipline once more?"
The Buddha said:
"It should not be done in that way; he should be expelled.
The formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and so forth should be carried out in this manner."
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; being without a mind of concealment, he has already requested the pārājika penance from the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha has already granted the pārājika penance to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
While this bhikṣu was undergoing the *śikṣādattaka* penance, he has again committed such-and-such a *pārājika* offense.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* against this bhikṣu [named] So-and-so for having again committed such-and-such a *pārājika* offense; he shall not dwell together with the community, nor shall he engage in communal affairs.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed such-and-such a pārājika offense; being without any intention to conceal it, he has already requested from the Saṃgha the pārājika-discipline."
The Sangha has already conferred the *pārājika* discipline upon the bhikṣu so-and-so.
While this bhikṣu was in the process of training and repenting, he again committed a certain *pārājika* offense.

The Sangha now confers upon the bhikṣu so-and-so the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*) for reoffending in a certain *pārājika* offense; he shall not dwell together [with the community] and shall not participate in communal affairs.

"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha’s formal act of banishment for the bhikṣu so-and-so for repeatedly committing a pārājika offense—such that he shall not dwell together with us nor engage in communal affairs—let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."
The motion has been stated three times.

The Saṃgha has already granted the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* for the bhikṣu so-and-so for repeatedly committing such-and-such a *pārājika* offense; he shall not dwell together with them, nor shall he engage in communal affairs. It is concluded.
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is upheld as such.
There are five *karmavācanā* procedures for removing the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*:
first, concealment (*praticchādana*).
2. If one commits the offense again while undergoing the penance, one must undergo the *mūlaparivāsa* (root-penance) for the period of concealment;
3. [then] the *mānatva*;
4. If one commits the offense again while undergoing the *mānatva*, one must undergo the *mūlamānatva* (root-mānatva).
5. Expiation of Offenses.
Regarding those who conceal their offenses, there are two types:
first, those who have committed a grave offense and must undergo the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for re-ordination, which may be performed either four or five times;
Second, regarding the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for not committing a transgression after having received the Dharma, there are three types of disclosure, which also consist of two categories:
first, the formal act for committing a transgression again after having received the Dharma, which has three [subdivisions];
second, the formal act for not committing a transgression again after having received the Dharma, which has two [subdivisions].
Regarding the legal rule on concealment:
if a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense—meaning he commits a pārajika, a sthūlātyaya, or even a duṣkṛta—and conceals it, this is called "not concealing."

If a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and conceals it with the intention of concealment, he should be instructed to perform a *duṣkṛta* confession; once the confession is made, the period of concealment (*paryuṣita*) is granted to him.
The same applies to offenses from *pāyattika* down to *durbhāṣita*.

If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense but does not remember the number of times it was committed nor the number of days, one should be granted concealment (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*) starting from the time of purification;
if one remembers the number of times but not the number of days, one should likewise be granted concealment starting from the time of purification;
if one remembers the number of days but not the number of times, one should grant concealment for the counted number of days.
The same applies to doubt and lack of doubt, and to recognition and lack of recognition.
That bhikṣu should perform the formal ritual within the Saṃgha and make this request:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"

There are eight matters that cause the night to be lost:

Regarding the method for expiating *sthūlātyaya* offenses, according to this [text], there are two categories of *sthūlātyaya*:
first, the root offense;
second, the derivative offense.
Within these two [categories], the stages of repentance are divided into three grades.
The first is the superior grade, which involves repenting before a great assembly;
this refers to primary offenses such as being a leader who disrupts the Wheel of Dharma, stealing the four requisites, killing a deva, and so forth.
Regarding those arising from [sexual] intercourse:
offenses from *pārājika* down to heavy *sthūlātyaya*.
Second, the medium category, which is to be confessed before a small group; that is, within the root [offenses]:
Regarding the schism of the *saṃgha* through formal act (*karmabheda*), those who obstruct the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and those who steal the three kinds of property and so forth:
among these offenses arising from birth,
those below *pārājika* are light *sthūlātyaya*, while those below *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are heavy *sthūlātyaya*.
The third is the inferior grade, which involves confessing before a single person; this refers to the following among the root offenses:
shaving the hair, going naked, wearing human skin, using a stone bowl, eating raw meat or blood, wearing the robes of non-Buddhists, and stealing one *kārsāpaṇa* or more;
as well as those arising from birth:
A *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that is minor is a light *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding the ritual for repenting the twenty-four offenses of concealment: when performing this rite of repentance, one must observe the proper protocol with utmost sincerity and earnestness, maintaining profound shame and remorse, severing the continuity of the offense forever, and requesting witness and testimony;

That bhikṣu must guard this bowl: he must not place it where tiles or stones might fall upon it; he must not place it beneath a leaning staff or beneath a leaning sword; he must not place it beneath suspended objects; he must not place it on a path, on a stone, beneath a fruit tree, or on uneven ground. He must not place it inside the threshold or beneath the door leaf; he must not place it beneath a rope bed, a wooden bed, between beds, or at the corner of a bed—except for temporary placement. Afterwards, when money or treasures are obtained, they should all be bestowed upon the donor.
If the steward (netra) dies or departs for another country, one should seek a new steward.
Furthermore, there are two ways of declaring things as pure (śuddhi):
If a layperson comes with money or precious objects to give them, the bhikṣu should simply say:
"This is an impure thing; I should not possess it. If it were pure, I would accept it."
This is pure.
If a layperson says, "Give this jewel to the bhikṣu," and the bhikṣu says:
"I should not keep it.
The attendant replied,
"I shall exchange it for pure items and then keep it."
This constitutes the act of purification (*viśuddhi*).

If a layperson does not state that they are exchanging it for a purified object, and a bhikṣu himself does not perform the declaration of purity (*viśuddhi-vācana*), but simply leaves the item to go elsewhere—if there is another bhikṣu present, he should declare his purity toward that person, regardless of how long or short the period of possession has been.
The wording is the same as above.

Regarding the rule for discarding bedding made of mixed wild silk cotton: if a bhikṣu goes personally to a silkworm-keeper’s house to beg for silk to make bedding, once it is completed, he must personally destroy it with an axe or hatchet and discard it.
One performs this rite as follows:
using either an axe or a hatchet, one finely chops and minces [the bone] and mixes it with clay, which is then used to plaster a wall or a mound.
Because one has personally destroyed and discarded it, there is no returning.
When performing the confession before a single person, the ritual procedure is the same as above.

Regarding the method for confessing the ninety *pāyattika* offenses: if one wishes to eliminate the original offense, one must first confess the concealment (*praticchādana*). The specific number of items involved should be understood according to the previous rules.
In this regard, having set aside the primary offense, one should first invite a preceptor for confession; the method of invitation is as described above.
Having invited them, one should address the preceptor with these words of repentance:
"Virtuous One, please attend to me with a single mind!"
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally uttered false speech, committing this many numerous *pāyattika* offenses—[here specify the particular category and the individual instances].
"I now confess to the Venerable One, not daring to conceal it," and so forth, as above.
The method for confessing *pāyantika* offenses regarding the category of concealment is as previously described.
Having requested the presiding master of the confession (*pratideśanā-ācārya*), perform the confession as follows:
"Virtuous one, please attend to me with a single mind!

I, Bhikṣu [Name], being free from illness, intentionally accepted food with my own hands from a Bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative while staying within a village, thereby committing such-and-such numerous *pātideśanīya* offenses—mentioning each by its specific name according to the category—and [other] matters as they apply."
"Venerable Sir!
I have committed a censurable offense, which ought not to have been done.
I now repent before the Venerable Sir and do not dare to conceal it."
The same as above.
One explanation states:

Regarding the method for repenting *duṣkṛta* offenses, this applies to all *duṣkṛtas*, whether they are primary or derivative, intentional or accidental, concealed or subsequently concealed; their categories and numbers are as previously described.
With utmost sincerity and earnest self-reproach, pledging to forever sever such faults, I perform this confession:
I, Bhikṣu [Name], intentionally failed to wear the saṃghāṭī robe in a neat and orderly manner, thereby committing this many numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Because it was done intentionally, one further commits as many numerous *dukkaṭa* offenses of improper conduct (*anācāra*).
If committed through negligence, there is no offense of improper conduct committed intentionally.
One should say:

"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have inadvertently worn the saṃghāṭī robe in a disarrayed manner; I have committed this many, numerous *duṣkṛta* offenses—[specifying] the remaining according to their respective names and designating each instance separately."
"I now confess, and dare not conceal it," and so forth, as above.
Regarding the legal procedure for all monks who have collectively committed an offense and disclose it: the Vinaya states:
Listen well!
The community of monks has gathered in one place intending to recite the precepts. At the time of the recitation, the entire community of monks has committed offenses.
Each of them thinks to themselves:

“The World-Honored One has established the precepts: one who has committed an offense shall not recite the precepts, shall not hear the precepts, shall not confess toward one who has committed an offense, and one who has committed an offense shall not accept the confession of another.”
After that bhikṣu has made this announcement, he shall perform the confession.
He should make the announcement in this way:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This entire assembly of monks has committed an offense.
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha permits it, let this entire Sangha perform confession.
Thus is the motion.
Having made this announcement, the precepts are then recited.
Regarding the rule for when the entire Saṃgha has collectively committed a doubtful offense and must confess it, the Vinaya states:
"Listen well! You all should listen attentively!"
If the Saṃgha assembles in one place intending to recite the precepts, and at the time of the recitation, the entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding their offenses,
each of them thinks to themselves:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that those who have committed an offense are not permitted to participate in the recitation of the precepts, and so forth, as previously stated."
After the entire Saṃgha has made the formal motion (jñapti), they should declare his offense.
The motion should be made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding an offense.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let this assembly of monks confess their offenses themselves.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this announcement, the precepts are then recited.
Regarding the method for an individual who recognizes a transgression to disclose it: one should approach a pure bhikṣu, observe the proper decorum, and say:
"Venerable sir, please take note!"
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such offenses, numbering so many and being numerous.
I now disclose them before the Venerable One; hereafter, I shall perform repentance according to the Dharma.
Once this has been said, one receives the hearing of the precepts (*śīla-śravaṇa*).
Regarding the method for a person to confess a doubtful offense (*āpatti-vicikitsā-prakāśana*): returning to a single pure bhikṣu, one should perform the formal ritual and speak as follows:
Venerable sir, please bear this in mind!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have developed a doubt regarding a certain offense.
I now declare it to you, venerable sir; when the time comes that I am free from doubt, I shall perform the confession according to the Dharma.
Once this has been said, one is permitted to hear the precepts.
Regarding the legal rules for recognizing an offense within the assembly for the recitation of the precepts and confessing it through mental reflection (*cittena āviṣkaraṇa*): [the text continues].

When the *poṣadha* is being recited, if there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense—whether he has been accused by others or not, whether he has been reminded of it or not—if that person himself remembers the offense and discloses it, that bhikṣu should say to those nearby:
"I have committed such-and-such an offense; I now confess it before the Elder."
Again, he should think:
"If I speak to others, I fear it will disturb the assembly of monks and prevent the recitation of the precepts.
That bhikṣu should then reflect in his mind, saying:
"I have committed such-and-such an offense; I must first leave my seat and perform repentance according to the Dharma.
Having done so, I shall be permitted to hear the recitation of the precepts.

The conditions for the method of mentally disclosing a doubtful offense while seated during the recitation of the precepts are the same as those previously described, with the sole difference being that it concerns a doubtful matter.
He thinks to himself:
"I have doubts regarding a certain offense; once I have ceased sitting and am free from doubt, I shall perform confession according to the Dharma.
Having done this, he may listen to the recitation of the precepts.
*Saṃghakarmavastu*, Middle Volume;
*Saṃghakarmavastu*, Lower Volume. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Huaisu of the Western Taiyuan Monastery, based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Chapter Thirteen: Governing People (Part Two). Chapter Thirteen on Governing People:
On the *Karma* of Reprimand. According to the Vinaya, there are two matters for which the Saṃgha should perform the *karma* of reprimand:
speaking what is not Dharma as Dharma, and speaking Dharma as not Dharma; this applies likewise to cases of speaking and not speaking.
The same applies even to the *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension).
Furthermore, there are three matters for which the Saṃgha should perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure):
namely, violation of the precepts (*śīla*), violation of views (*dṛṣṭi*), and violation of conduct (*ācāra*).
The same applies even to the *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension).
Furthermore, there were monks who delighted in quarreling and disputing with one another, reviling each other, and speaking words like swords and blades as they sought out each other's faults.

If there were other monks who, upon seeing such disputes, went to encourage and assist them, this caused disputes to arise where none had existed before, and disputes that already existed to remain unresolved.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to perform a formal motion with a four-part proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman) to carry out a reprimand.
He then assembled the Saṃgha.
Once they have assembled, one should perform the formal act of censure;
once the censure has been performed, one should perform the act of calling to mind;
once the act of calling to mind has been performed, one should impose the offense.
Having confessed the offense, he should act as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, delights in quarreling and disputing, reviling one another, and uttering words like swords and blades, seeking out each other's faults."
Having already engaged in mutual strife themselves, if there are other bhikṣus who are also quarreling, they immediately go to them and urge them, saying:
"Exert yourselves! Do not be inferior to others!"
"You possess great learning and wisdom, your wealth is superior, and you have many friends;
we shall act as your allies.
Thus they cause disputes to arise where none existed before, and they fail to resolve those that already exist.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall perform a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu so-and-so; if he should again engage in quarreling or mutual abuse hereafter, the community of monks shall further increase his punishment.
The motion is thus stated.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, delights in engaging in quarrels and disputes, reviling one another, uttering words like swords and blades, and seeking out each other's faults.
Having already engaged in mutual strife themselves, if there are other bhikṣus who are also quarreling, they immediately go to them and urge them, saying:
"Exert yourselves; do not be inferior to others!"
"You possess great wisdom and extensive learning, your wealth is superior, and you have many friends;
we shall act as your allies.
Thus they cause disputes to arise where none existed before, and they fail to extinguish disputes that already exist.
The Saṃgha is performing the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu [Name].

Which elders approve of the Saṃgha’s performance of the *tarjanīya-karman* against the bhikṣu [Name], such that if he should again engage in quarreling or mutual abuse hereafter, the Saṃgha shall further increase his punishment?
The monks who approve remain silent; those who do not approve should speak.
This has been said three times.
The Sangha has approved and completed the *karman* of censure for the bhikṣu [Name].
The Saṃgha having consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having obtained the Dharma, he practiced the seven groups of five conducts.
These seven groups of five conducts are fully explained as above.

The Procedure for the Karman of Censure: If the community of monks is gathered for the morning meal, the afternoon meal, for a Dharma discourse, or for the *poṣadha*, the person subject to the karman of censure shall adjust their robes, remove their leather sandals, stand to one side, kneel with palms joined, and address the assembly as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha!"
"Accept my confession.
From this day forward, I shall reproach myself and cease from such actions forever.
The Buddha said:

"If one conforms to the Saṃgha and does not oppose it, seeking the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman* (reproach), the lifting shall be granted through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
The Saṃgha should examine [the candidate] and should not grant the lifting if five conditions are present; namely, if they violate the aforementioned seven sets of five practices.
There are five things that should be done for the purpose of resolving a formal reprimand (*tajjanīya-karman*); namely, one must not transgress the aforementioned seven sets of five practices.
One should go before the Saṃgha, assume the proper deportment, and make this request as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of formal rebuke (tarjanīya-karman).
Now, in full compliance with the Saṃgha and without any opposition, I beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of this act of formal rebuke.
"May the Sangha, out of compassion, perform the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman* for me.
(Recite this three times.
The Sangha should grant the procedure in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the *karman* of censure.
That bhikṣu has complied with the Saṃgha and has not opposed it; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *karman* of censure.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to revoke the *karma* of censure against the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has had the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) performed against him by the Saṃgha.
That bhikṣu has complied with the Saṃgha without opposition and now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha's lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman* for the bhikṣu [Name] should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This has been said three times. The Sangha has consented and the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman* for the bhikṣu [Name] is completed."
The Saṃgha, by remaining silent, consents; thus this matter is upheld.
Regarding the procedure for the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment): at that time, there was a bhikṣu who engaged in evil conduct and defiled the families of lay supporters.
"Evil conduct" refers to such acts as planting flower trees oneself or instructing others to do so.
"Defiling the household" consists of four types of matters:

first, defiling the household by relying on the family; second, defiling the household by relying on material gain; third, defiling the household by relying on relatives and friends; and fourth, defiling the household by relying on the monastery.
"This bhikṣu has committed evil deeds and defiled families; this is known through both what has been seen and heard.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to perform the formal motion of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for his banishment."
The procedures for this formal act (*karman*) and its revocation are as explained in the Vinaya.

Regarding the method for the *niśraya-karman*: if a bhikṣu is deluded and ignorant, frequently commits many offenses, dwells in close association with laypeople, and does not accord with the Buddha’s Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the purpose of providing a formal reliance (*niśraya*).
This means that one should be sent to rely upon a person of virtue; one must not designate a direction, a country, or other such locations as the place of reliance.
The performance and the revocation of this [act] are also as set forth in the Vinaya.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* for the formal act of prohibiting someone from entering the homes of laypeople (*avadhyāna-karman*), there are five conditions under which the Saṃgha should perform this prohibition against a layperson:
if this person respectfully honors his father, mother, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, and firmly maintains and does not abandon that which ought to be upheld.
If a bhikṣu possesses ten qualities, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of *karmavācanā* to prohibit him from entering the homes of laypeople:

he speaks ill of and reviles the families of laypeople; he employs means to cause the decline of the families of laypeople; he acts to their disadvantage; he acts to their detriment; he incites strife among the families of laypeople; he slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha in the presence of laypeople; he utters insults regarding lowly matters in the presence of laypeople; and he promises laypeople something according to the Dharma but does not fulfill it.
These procedures for performing the act, assigning duties, sending forth, and the rituals for confession and release are also as set forth in the Vinaya.
Regarding the *karmavācanā* for censuring one who has not acknowledged an offense: when a bhikṣu commits an offense and another bhikṣu says to him, "Do you see that you have committed an offense?"
He replied, “I did not see it.
The Buddha said:
"Listen, the Saṃgha shall perform the formal motion with one proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha*) to raise the charge against him for not seeing his offense.
This procedure for both the enactment and the lifting [of the charge] is also as prescribed in the Vinaya.
Regarding the ritual for raising a charge against one who does not repent their offense: if a bhikṣu commits an offense, the other bhikṣus say to him:
"You have committed an offense;
you must confess it. He replied, "I will not confess."
The Buddha said:
"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal motion with a proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to suspend [the monk] for the offense of refusing to repent.
The procedures for both this suspension and its subsequent resolution are also as set forth in the Vinaya.
The procedure for the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of suspending a monk who does not relinquish an evil view: If a certain bhikṣu gives rise to such an evil view and speaks thus:
"I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha that the commission of sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path."
The Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to perform a formal admonition through a jñapti-caturtha-karman.
The method of admonition is as set forth in the text.
The community of bhikṣus gave him a formal admonition, yet he did not relinquish his evil view.
The Buddha said:
"Perform the formal motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) for the suspension of one who does not relinquish an evil view."
The performance and the rescinding of this [act] are also as stated in the Vinaya.
Regarding the ritual for the *unmattaka-karman* (the act for those who are insane or deluded), there are three types of insanity or delusion:

first, at the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), one either remembers or does not remember [the offense], and either attends or does not attend; second, one remembers and attends; third, one neither remembers nor attends.
These are called the three types of insanity.
Among them, the latter two should not have [legal acts] performed for them;
for the first one, a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) should be performed.
It should be granted in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is mentally deranged and insane; he may or may not remember the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, and he may or may not come."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, grant this formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the bhikṣu so-and-so who is mentally disturbed and insane, such that the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act and recite the Prātimokṣa whether he remembers or does not remember, or whether he comes or does not come.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is mentally disturbed, deranged, and insane; he may or may not remember the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, and he may or may not come."

The Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*kamma*) for the bhikṣu so-and-so regarding his disturbed mind and insanity; whether he remembers or does not remember, whether he comes or does not come, the formal act and the recitation of the precepts shall proceed.

"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha performing the formal act (*kamma*) for the bhikṣu so-and-so—who is mentally deranged and insane—whether he remembers or does not remember, whether he comes or does not come, for the purpose of reciting the Prātimokṣa, please remain silent. Whoever does not consent, please speak."

The Sangha has already consented to perform the formal act (kamma) for the bhikkhu so-and-so who is mentally disturbed, insane, and deluded—whether he remembers or does not remember, whether he comes or does not come—and the kamma is concluded.
Since the Saṃgha has remained silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the method for revoking the *karmavācanā* for those who are insane or deluded: if the madness ceases, one should revoke it by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
The individual concerned should perform the proper ritual and make the following request.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], previously suffered from the illness of insanity.

At the time of the recitation of the precepts, I sometimes remembered and sometimes did not remember; I sometimes came and sometimes did not come. The Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for me regarding my insanity.
Once it has been performed, the illness shall cease. Now, [the monk] requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *unmattaka-karman* (the ritual for those who are insane).
This is said three times.
The Saṃgha should grant the formal act (*dharma*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, was previously afflicted with the disease of insanity.

When the *Poṣadha* was being recited, he sometimes remembered and sometimes did not remember; sometimes he came and sometimes he did not come. The Saṃgha has therefore performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for one suffering from insanity upon him.

After the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) was performed for him, his madness and delusion were brought to a halt; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *karmavācanā* for madness and delusion.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant it, let the Saṃgha lift the *karmavācanā* for madness and delusion.
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, was previously afflicted with the disease of insanity; when the *poṣadha* was being recited, he sometimes remembered and sometimes did not remember, and sometimes came and sometimes did not come. The Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for him regarding his insanity."
After the formal ritual (kamma) was performed for him, his madness and delusion were brought to an end. He now requests the Saṃgha to revoke the ritual for madness and delusion.
Whichever elders among you consent to the Saṃgha revoking the ritual for madness and delusion for this bhikkhu named [Name], remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already consented; the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the formal act against the bhikṣu so-and-so for his madness and delusion is concluded.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The Buddha said:
"One performs the *karma* for one who has fallen into madness;
when the madness ceases, it is revoked.

Regarding the method for performing the *karma* with a family of householders: there was once a householder’s home where both husband and wife had attained faith and joy, becoming disciples of the Buddha.
It is the constant law for the disciples of the Buddhas who have realized the Truths:
they cherish nothing among the bhikṣus, even unto their own flesh.
If bhikṣus come to their homes, they always provide them with food, drink, and various offerings; thus, [the householders] are rendered poor, their clothing and food exhausted.
The Buddha said:
“I allow the Saṃgha to perform the *karmavācanā* for that householder as a ‘family under training’ (*śikṣādattaka*).
It should be performed in this manner.”
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
In a certain city, at the home of a certain lay devotee, a husband and wife have gained faith and become disciples of the Buddha until their wealth is exhausted.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of designating them as a "family under training" (*śikṣādattaka*), such that no bhikṣus shall accept food or eat at that household.
The announcement is as follows:
Venerable Sangha, please listen!
In such-and-such a city, at the home of such-and-such a lay devotee, a husband and wife have attained faith and become disciples of the Buddha; their wealth has been entirely exhausted.
The Saṃgha now performs the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for this person; no bhikṣus shall accept food from this family to eat.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha performing the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for this layperson remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented to perform the *karmavācanā* for the householder [Name] as a "family under observation.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

There is no offense if one has previously accepted an invitation, if one is ill, if the gift is placed on the ground, if it is received from another person, or if, after the family under observation has given, their wealth subsequently increases again.

The Procedure for Rescinding the *karmavācanā* for a Family under Restrictions: If the wealth of a family has increased again and they request the Saṃgha to rescind the *karmavācanā* for that family, the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) to rescind it.
It should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

In such-and-such city, at the house of such-and-such lay devotee, husband and wife have attained faith and become disciples of the Buddha; they are fond of giving until their wealth and goods were completely exhausted, and the Saṃgha previously performed the *kula-karma* (formal act regarding a family) for them."
Now that their wealth has returned to abundance, they request from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *kula-karma* (formal act regarding a family).
If it is the time for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the *kula-karma* be lifted.
The motion is thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
In such-and-such a city, at the house of such-and-such a lay devotee, husband and wife have attained faith and become disciples of the Buddha; their wealth is still abundant."
The Saṃgha now grants the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the "householder's discipline" (*śikṣādattaka*) to the lay follower [Name].
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the householder's discipline to the lay follower [Name], remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented; the *karmavācanā* for the revocation of the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for the lay follower [Name] is concluded.
Because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
While the *karmavācanā* for the *anyavāda* (speaking otherwise) was being performed, a bhikṣu committed an offense. The bhikṣus asked him:
"Do you know for yourself that you have committed an offense?
He then replied to the bhikṣus with another matter:
"To whom were you speaking?"
What matter do you speak of?
What principle do you discuss?
Are you speaking to me?
To whom are you speaking?
Who has committed the offense?
From what does the offense arise?
"I do not see any offense!
Why do you say that I am guilty?
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is permitted that after the formal announcement (jñapti) has been made, one may speak of 'other matters' (anyavāda).
The announcement should be made as follows:
'May the venerable Saṃgha listen!'"
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense.
The bhikṣus ask him:
"Do you yourself now recognize that you have committed an offense?"
That bhikṣu then replied to the other bhikṣus with some other matter, saying:
"To whom were you speaking? What was it that you said?"
In discussing what principle,
are you speaking for my sake,
or are you speaking for the sake of others?
Who commits the offense?
From what does the offense arise?
I do not perceive an offense!
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the monk named So-and-so be designated as one who speaks evasive words.
This is the motion.
Having made this motion, he is designated as one who speaks evasive words.
If one utters extraneous speech before the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, it is entirely *duṣkṛta*;
if one utters extraneous speech after the formal announcement has been made, it is entirely *pāyattika*.

When the formal act of *takkara-kamma* (the act of causing annoyance) was being performed, there was a bhikkhu who, after the Saṅgha had established a rule that he must not engage in further talk, proceeded to annoy the Saṅgha:

when told to come he did not come; when not told to come he came; when he should have risen he did not rise; when he should not have risen he rose; when he should have spoken he did not speak; and when he should not have spoken he spoke.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to perform a formal motion (jñapti-karman) for this bhikṣu; having done so, he shall be designated as one who causes disturbance.
The motion is made as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having been designated by the Saṃgha as one who speaks evasively, has subsequently provoked and disturbed the assembly:
when told to come he does not come, and when told not to come he comes;
He should rise when he ought to rise, yet does not; he rises when he ought not to rise.
He speaks when he ought to speak, yet does not; he speaks when he ought not to speak.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha enact a formal act of censure against this bhikṣu, naming him "The Troublemaker."
The announcement is made as follows.
Once the announcement has been made in this manner, it is termed "causing disturbance to the Saṃgha.
If one causes disturbance to the Saṃgha before the announcement has been made, it constitutes an offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in all cases.
If, after the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, one causes disturbance to the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
Regarding the method for disciplining a "bad horse," there was once a bhikṣu who was of a wicked nature and would not accept admonition, frequently committing many offenses against the community.
Other bhikṣus said to him,
"Do you see that you have committed an offense?
He replied:
“I do not see it.
The Saṃgha should abandon the matter and not inquire further, speaking thus:

“Since you do not now see your offense, wherever you go, they there shall also raise your offense against you and act as your own accuser; you shall not be permitted to perform an *ānuvartana*, nor shall you be permitted to participate in the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*.”
It is like a horse trainer who, when a wicked horse is difficult to tame, discards the tethering rope and stake;
you, O bhikṣu, who do not see your own faults, are just the same—you shall be entirely cast aside.
To the place where you go, you shall not even be permitted to participate in the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*.
This person should not seek permission; this itself constitutes permission.

Regarding the method of disciplinary action by the *brahmadaṇḍa*: at one time there was a monk who was of evil character and violated the precepts, yet refused to accept admonition; therefore, he was subjected to the disciplinary measure of silent exclusion (*tūṣṇīka-pravāsanīya-karman*).
It should be done in this manner:
all the bhikṣus shall silently ostracize him and not speak with him; this is the punishment of brahmadanda.

If he still does not reform, he shall be brought before the assembly, where everyone shall join in censuring and expelling him, and neither allow him to recite the precepts nor participate in the communal affairs of the Dharma.

When the rules for the dismissal of those who instruct bhikṣuṇīs were being established, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇerikās, and śikṣamāṇās came into the monastery and stayed together with the bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras; they teased one another, sang together, wailed together, or laughed and joked together, thereby disturbing the bhikṣus who were practicing meditation.
The Buddha said:
"She should be summoned and punished.
If she does not reform, you should perform the formal ritual of 'renouncing instruction' (śikṣā-pratyākhyāna-karman) against her preceptor (upādhyāyī) and instructors (ācāryā)."
Regarding the ritual procedure for performing the *pātra-nyubja* (turning down the bowl) against a lay household, the Buddha said:
"If a lay household possesses five qualities, one should not perform the *pātra-nyubja* against them:
being unfilial toward one's father, being unfilial toward one's mother, not revering śramaṇas, not revering brāhmaṇas, and not providing service to bhikṣus."
There are five things that should not be done; these are the opposites of the aforementioned [five].
Furthermore, there are ten things for which the Saṃgha should perform the ritual of overturning the alms-bowl (*pātra-ovadana*):

reviling or slandering a bhikṣu; acting to the detriment of a bhikṣu; acting to his disadvantage; employing means to deprive him of a dwelling place; inciting strife among bhikṣus; speaking ill of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha in the presence of a bhikṣu; slandering a bhikṣu with groundless charges of unchastity; or having committed an offense against a bhikṣuṇī.
"In this manner, down to nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one, the *pātra-ovaddha* (the overturning of the bowl) shall be granted.
It should be granted in this way:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This person, [Name], though pure, has been slandered by the bhikṣu [Name] with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now perform the act of overturning the alms-bowl (*pātra*) against this person, [Name], so that there shall be no mutual social intercourse.
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, has slandered the bhikṣu so-and-so, who is pure, with groundless charges of a pārājika offense;
Now the Saṃgha shall perform the act of "turning over the alms-bowl" for [Name], such that there shall be no mutual coming and going.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha performing the act of turning over the alms-bowl for [Name] so that there shall be no mutual coming and going, let them remain silent; those who do not consent, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the *pātra-āvṛti* (turning over of the bowl) for so-and-so, such that they shall no longer associate with one another.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the procedure for appointing a bhikṣu to inform a layperson, the Buddha said:
"A formal motion with one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) should be made to appoint one bhikṣu as a messenger to inform the layperson.
That messenger bhikṣu must possess eight qualities.
These eight qualities and the procedure for appointment are explained in detail in the Vinaya.
This messenger-monk should go to that household and must not accept offerings such as seats, food, or drink; he should simply say:
"The Sangha has now performed the 'inverted bowl' rite for you, and we shall no longer have mutual dealings."
If they do not understand, you should explain it to them extensively.
If that person should say:
"By what means can my bowl be uncovered so that we may once again go and come together?"
That messenger should say:
"You ought to go and confess before the Saṃgha.

If you confess, follow the Saṃgha, and do not dare to oppose them, but instead request from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-nikubjana* (the overturned bowl) so that we may once again come and go between us, the Saṃgha should lift it for you."
The explanation of the text follows the Vinaya.

Chapter Fourteen: On Offering Admonition (Part Two). Chapter Fourteen: On Offering Admonition. Regarding the Method for Admonishing One Who Splits the Saṃgha: If a bhikṣu, through skillful means, desires to split the harmonious Saṃgha, accepts the methods for splitting the Saṃgha, and obstinately persists without relinquishing them.
That monk should admonish this monk, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not accept the practices that lead to a schism, nor persist in them without relinquishing them."
"Venerable sir!
You should be in harmony with the Saṃgha, living in joy without dispute, like water and milk blended as one; thus you will find increase in the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace and happiness."
"Venerable sir!
You should abandon this matter so that the Saṃgha does not proceed with a formal reprimand and you do not incur a grave offense.

If you follow our advice, it is well; if you do not follow our advice, we shall further seek out bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as kings, ministers, and various heretical śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas from other regions who, having heard of this person, trust and credit their words—they should come here."
If they accept the proposal, it is well; if they do not accept the proposal, one should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Having performed the announcement, one should further request:
"Venerable sirs!"
I have finished the motion; the formal act (*karmavācanā*) remains.
You should now relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform the formal act against you and you further commit a grave offense.
If they accept the instruction, it is well; if they do not accept the instruction, one should perform the first *karmavācanā*.
Having performed the first *karmavācanā*, one should further request:
"Venerable Sir!"
I have already finished the first *karmavācanā* of the formal motion; two more remain.
You should relinquish this matter so that the Saṃgha does not perform further *karmas* against you, causing you to incur a grave offense.
If they accept what has been said, it is well; if they do not accept what has been said, one should perform the second *karmavācanā*.
Having performed the second, one should again request them, saying:
"Venerable sirs!"
I have already completed the first of the two *jñapti-dvitīya* formal acts; only one formal act remains.
You should relinquish this matter so that the Saṃgha does not perform another formal act against you, whereby you would incur a grave offense.
If she is able to relinquish it, that is well; if she is unable to relinquish it, the third *karmavācanā* is recited to her.
When the third *karmavācanā* is finished, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one renounces [the offense] after the second motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) have been completed, there are three *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one renounces it after the first motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-ekakarma*) have been completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If, after the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been completed, one abandons [the intent], it is one *sthūlātyaya*.
If one abandons it before the initial announcement is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If, prior to any announcement whatsoever, one employs the means to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, accepts the method for causing a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, and persists in holding to it without relinquishing it, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The essential nature of the *karmavācanā* procedure is fully explained in the Vinaya.

Regarding the method for admonishing those who assist in causing a schism in the Saṃgha: when the community of monks is admonishing that monk who has caused a schism, there may be other monks belonging to an unlawful faction—whether one, two, three, or many—who say to the monks:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Do not admonish this bhikṣu; this bhikṣu is a speaker of the Dharma, a speaker of the Vinaya;
what this bhikṣu has said, we accept."
The monks should say to him:
"Do not speak these words, saying:
'This monk is a monk who speaks according to the Dharma, a monk who speaks according to the Vinaya;'"
"What this bhikṣu has spoken, we accept and approve.
Yet this bhikṣu is one who speaks what is not in accordance with the Dharma and one who speaks what is not in accordance with the Vinaya.
Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should support the harmony of the Saṃgha.
"Venerable One!
Be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing and not disputing," and so forth,
as before.
The essential nature of the *karmavācanā* procedure is also as clarified in the Vinaya.

Regarding the method of admonishing one who has been expelled for slandering the Saṃgha: at that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed evil deeds and defiled the families of others, such that both his actions were seen and heard by all.
When the Saṃgha performed the formal act of banishment, he slandered the Saṃgha, saying:
"The bhikṣus have favoritism, hatred, fear, and delusion; for there are bhikṣus who have committed such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not."
The bhikṣus should say to him:
"Venerable sir,
we have both seen and heard that you have defiled families, and we have both seen and heard that you have engaged in evil conduct."
"Venerable one!
You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; you should abandon this matter so that you do not incur the censure of the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense.
It would be well if you follow these words."
If one does not comply with the instruction, it is to be repeated up to the third time, as described above.
The formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.

Regarding the legal procedure for admonishing one of bad character who does not accept advice: if a bhikṣu is of bad character and does not accept the words of others, and while the other bhikṣus instruct him according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, he himself acts in a manner that makes communal discourse impossible and says to the bhikṣus:
“Venerable sirs!
Do not speak to me of what is good or what is bad, nor shall I speak to you venerable sirs of what is good or what is bad.
Venerable sirs, please desist!”
"There is no need to admonish me.
That monk then said to this monk:
"Venerable sir!"
Do not make yourself one with whom it is impossible to converse; rather, you should become one with whom it is possible to converse.
Venerable sir, you should admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, and the bhikṣus should likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma.
"In this way, the community of the Buddha’s disciples attains increase as they instruct one another, admonish one another, and repent with one another.
Venerable sir, you should abandon this matter; do not be censured by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense."
If they comply with what has been said, it is well;
if they do not comply, this is repeated up to the third time, as described above.
The formal procedure (karmavācanā) consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman), as well as its essential nature, is also as clarified in the Vinaya.
Admonishing against the teaching of evil views that claim sensual desire does not obstruct the path to enlightenment: That bhikṣu speaks thus:
"I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual desire is not a dharma that obstructs the path."
The virtuous bhikṣus should admonish this bhikṣu, saying:
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the Blessed One. It is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One; the Blessed One does not speak such things."
The World-Honored One has, through countless skillful means, taught that engaging in sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
You should now abandon this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and commit further offenses.
If they comply with what has been said, it is well;
if they do not comply, it shall be repeated up to the third time as above.
The formal substance of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is also as clarified in the Vinaya.
The method for admonishing a śrāmaṇera who speaks of sensual desires as not being an obstacle to the Path is identical to this and no different.

When the time comes to admonish one who has committed an offense, if there is a bhikṣu who intends to commit a pārājika or even a pāyattika offense, the other bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable One!"
"Do not say that this is right; this should not be so.
What the Venerable One has done is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha's teaching.
Yet this bhikṣu, refusing to heed the lawful admonitions of the virtuous bhikṣus, has immediately committed an offense."
If this bhikṣu knows for himself that what he has done is right and that the admonisher is wrong, yet persists in his action, he commits a root offense;
if he does not comply with the instruction, it is a duṣkṛta.
If this bhikṣu knows for himself that what he has done is wrong and clearly recognizes that the other’s admonition is right, yet he persists in his action, he commits a root offense;
if he does not comply with their words, it is a pāyattika.
If there is an ignorant person who does not know the method of admonition, one should say to them:
"You should ask your preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya); further study and recite the scriptures until you understand the method of admonition, and only then offer your admonition."

15. Chapter on the Settlement of Disputes (Part Two). Chapter Fifteen: The Settlement of Disputes. Regarding the Dharma of the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the accused): at one time, various bhikṣus performed a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) even though the person concerned was not present.
The Buddha said:
"One should not perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) in the absence of the person concerned.
From this day forward, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement by presence) to extinguish disputes; you should explain the *sammukhavinaya* as follows.
There are, however, five things that must be present before one:
namely, the Dharma, the Vinaya, the person, the Saṃgha, and the boundary.
What is meant by the presence of the Dharma?
That which is held as the Dharma for settling disputes is this:
what is the presence of the Vinaya?
That which is held as the Vinaya for settling disputes is this.
What is "presence before the person"?
It refers to one who engages in the exchange of words regarding the meaning [of the matter].
What is "presence before the Saṃgha"?

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed with the assembly gathered in one place; those who do not attend have given their authorization (*anuśrāvaṇa*), and those present who ought to be reproved are not reproved—this is [the definition].
What is "presence before the boundary" (*sīmā-sammukhatā*)?
This refers to one who, within the boundaries of the *sīmā*, performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to impose disciplinary measures.

When the rule for the *smṛtivinaya* (verdict based on memory) is being granted, there are monks who have not actually committed grave offenses such as *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or *sthūlātyaya*, yet all the monks claim they have committed grave offenses.
He asked,
"Do you remember committing a grave offense?
Since he did not remember committing one, he replied:
"I do not recall committing such an offense.
He then spoke to the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Do not continue to interrogate me.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to interrogate him without ceasing.
The Buddha said:
“Listen, the Saṃgha shall perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the purpose of instituting the *smṛti-vinaya*.
Request it as prescribed in the text.
From this day forward, when establishing the *smṛti-vinaya* to settle disputes among the bhikṣus, the *smṛti-vinaya* should be proclaimed in this manner.”
What is the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection)?
When a bhikṣu has committed such an offense, he should no longer be formally accused (*codanā*) nor should he be subjected to the procedure of recollection.

At the time when the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one who was not insane) is being granted, there was a bhikṣu who was deranged and mentally disturbed; he committed many offenses against the rules, which were contrary to the dharma of a śramaṇa. His speech was unrestrained, and his coming and going, entering and exiting did not accord with the proper decorum.
Later, when he regained his mind, the bhikṣus said,
"You have committed a grave offense, a pārājika or a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
He asked them:
"Do you remember committing grave offenses?
He replied, "In the past, when I was deluded and my mind was deranged, I committed many offenses; these were not done intentionally by me, but were merely due to madness and folly."
"Venerable elders, there is no need for you to repeatedly challenge and interrogate them.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to challenge and interrogate them without ceasing.
The Buddha said:

"Listen, the Saṃgha shall grant him the *amūḷhavinaya* (the discipline for one who was not insane) by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
He should request it according to the text.
From this day forward, when establishing the *amūḷhavinaya* as a means of settling disputes for the bhikṣus, the *amūḷhavinaya* should be recited in this manner.
What is the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who is no longer deluded)?
In this case, that bhikṣu’s offense should not be further raised, nor should it be brought to mind.

When a bhikṣu who has been granted the *svavāda-vinaya* (the discipline of confession) sees with his purified divine eye that another bhikṣu has violated the precepts, he does not accept the latter's own confession, but drags him out of the monastery.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be done in this way.
Even at another time, it should not be done in this way."
“One must cause them to confess their guilt before imposing the penalty; one should not impose a penalty upon someone who has not confessed their own guilt.

From this day forward, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish the *pātimokkha* rule of confession (*sāmīci-vinaya*) for the settlement of disputes. It should be recited as follows: “The *sāmīci-vinaya*.”
Among these people, those who appear before one are the recipient of the confession and the one who performs the confession.
What is meant by "speaking for oneself"?
It refers to the one who confesses by stating the name of the offense and the category of the offense.
How is it settled?
One should reproach one's own mind and give rise to weary detachment.

Regarding the *vinaya* rule for settling disputes through discussion with many people: if a dispute among the bhikṣus arises and cannot be extinguished, one should seek out many bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma to perform a *śalākā* (lot) to settle the dispute, using the majority of voting sticks as the expression of their decision.

From this day forward, I shall establish for the bhikṣus the legal procedure for settling disputes by means of the majority decision (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*). It should be proclaimed as follows regarding the use of the majority decision:
What is the majority decision?
If one relies on the explanations of many people— those who uphold the Dharma, those who uphold the Vinaya, and those who uphold the Mātikā—
and when granting the *āpattiyā tiṭṭhanā-vinaya* (the legal procedure for resolving offenses), the bhikṣus commit offenses that are contradictory from beginning to end.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for that bhikṣu to designate the place of his offense.
It should be performed in this manner:"
He assembles the Sangha;
having assembled them, he performs the formal act of *ukkhepana* (suspension);
having performed the *ukkhepana*, he grants him the act of *sativinaya* (reinstatement through recollection).
Having performed the formal recollection, one shall impose the penalty according to the ritual procedure as set forth in the text.
Once this has been done, one should practice the seven sets of five observances in due order.

From this time forward, for the sake of all bhikṣus, I shall establish the legal procedure for settling disputes through formal adjudication (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). It should be proclaimed as follows: What is the legal procedure for formal adjudication? [It is] as follows: [The Buddha said: "From this day forth, for the sake of all bhikṣus, I shall establish the Dharma for settling disputes through formal adjudication.
It should be proclaimed as follows: What is formal adjudication?"
Regarding that offense of the bhikṣu, it is one for whom the formal act of *codanā* (reproval) and *smṛti* (remembrance) have been performed.
When the *tṛṇaprastāraka-vinaya* (the method of covering with grass) is granted, the various bhikṣus reflect:
"We have transgressed many communal precepts; these are not the dharmas of a śramaṇa. We have both committed them and spoken of them, entering and exiting [the community] without restraint."

If we were to return and discuss this matter among ourselves, it might cause this dispute to become even more serious and protracted over months and years; we would fail to settle the dispute in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions, thereby depriving the Sangha of peace and happiness.
The Buddha said:
"This dispute should be settled by the method of 'covering over with grass,' as it were.
From this day forward, I shall establish for the bhikṣus the legal procedure for settling disputes by covering over with grass; it should be recited as follows: 'Covering over with grass.'"
What is the "covering with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*)?
It refers to one who confesses a fault without further specifying the name of the offense or its category.

There are four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*): disputes concerning speech (*vāda*), disputes concerning investigation (*anveṣaṇa*), disputes concerning transgressions (*āpatti*), and disputes concerning formal procedures (*kṛtya*).
What is verbal dispute?
It is when bhikṣus engage in verbal disputes with one another, citing eighteen grounds for dispute:
from "Dharma" and "non-Dharma," up to "speaking" and "not speaking."
If, by means of such characteristics, they engage in mutual verbal dispute and subsequently fight with one another, this is called a dispute over speech (*vāda-vivāda*).
What is a dispute over searching for faults (*anuvāda-vivāda*)?
If a bhikṣu seeks out the offenses of another bhikṣu by means of three types of formal charges (*karma-vastu*):

Having violated the precepts, violated the views, or violated the decorum, and having acted upon what was seen, heard, or suspected, one seeks out an offense by manifesting such characteristics. One does not speak falsely when conversing, seeks companions and support, and comforts their mind. Whether one brings forth a formal charge or calls for mindfulness, whether one establishes this matter or does not establish it, provided one is neither deluded nor exempted—this is called "seeking a dispute" (*utkṣepa-vivāda*).
What is a dispute concerning offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*)?
Committing the seven kinds of offenses, from the *pārājika* down to the *dubbhāsita*, constitutes a dispute concerning offenses.
What is a dispute concerning matters (*kicca-adhikaraṇa*)?

Matters arising from disputes over speech, matters arising from disputes over accusations, and matters arising from disputes over offenses constitute "disputes concerning matters" (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).

The methods for settling these through formal procedures (*yācanā*), medicinal remedies (*bhaiṣajya*), and face-to-face reconciliation (*sammukha-vinaya*) are explained extensively in the Vinaya texts.
16. Section on Miscellaneous Practices (Part II). Section on Miscellaneous Practices, Chapter Sixteen. Regarding the concluding remarks on the *Poṣadha* hall, the Vinaya states:
