[The monks] did not know where they should perform the *Poṣadha*.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct a hall for the recitation of the precepts.

A single bhikṣu, having performed the formal ritual, should announce: 'This is the Great Hall,' or 'the upper story of the hall,' or 'the walking path,' or 'by the riverbank,' or 'under a tree,' or 'beside a rock,' or 'a place of growing grass.'"
"It should be done in this manner:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let us establish a Poṣadha hall at such-and-such a place.'"
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
Now the community of monks is establishing a hall for the recitation of the precepts at a certain location."
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha establishing a Poṣadha hall at such-and-such a place, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has approved and consented to establish the Poṣadha hall at such-and-such a place."
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is upheld as such.
When the rules for establishing a *poṣadha-śālā* (confession hall) are being explained, the bhikṣus first established a *poṣadha-śālā*, yet they now wish to establish one in another location.
"Listen, Venerable Saṃgha! Having first dissolved the previous boundary for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, it shall then be re-established.
It should be dissolved in this manner:
'Listen, Venerable Saṃgha!'"
If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, grant permission to dissolve the boundary of the Poṣadha hall at such-and-such a place.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now the Saṃgha dissolves the boundary for the Uposatha hall at such-and-such a place.
Those elders who consent to the dissolution of the boundary for the Uposatha hall at such-and-such a place by the Saṃgha should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented to the completion of the recitation of the Prātimokṣa in the hall at [place name].
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the procedure for securing the storehouse: if a visiting bhikṣu arrives while it is being secured, he may move his belongings to another room, as they would not be safe otherwise.
The Buddha permitted the construction of storehouses from separate rooms.
A single bhikṣu should announce: "In such-and-such a room, or a heated hall, or an upper story, or a place for walking meditation, a storehouse shall be constructed."
Having recited this, one should act as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha designate a certain room as a storehouse."
The motion is as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha shall designate a certain room as a storehouse.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha’s designation of such-and-such a room as a storehouse remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented and completed the designation of such-and-such a room as a storehouse."
Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If the storehouse is not secure, it is permitted to appoint a person to guard the storehouse, provided they possess the aforementioned qualities.
If he is unwilling, give him a portion of the offerings and some gruel.
If he still refuses, then two shares of all the clothing and food he receives should be given to him.
If they still refuse to comply, they shall be dealt with according to the law.
Regarding the procedure for releasing the storehouse, the text is abbreviated and lacks the formula for release; it should be expanded from the formula for binding as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!..."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha release the room and storehouse of [Name].
This is the motion.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha dissolves the assignment of the room, storehouse, and treasury of [Name].
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s dissolution of the assignment of the room, storehouse, and treasury of [Name] should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
The Sangha has already consented to the resolution regarding the storehouse and storeroom of [Name]’s cell.
Because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the method for constructing a cell for oneself when there is no owner: after that bhikṣu has inspected a site that is free from difficulties and obstacles, he should perform the formal ritual within the Sangha and make this request:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], am personally begging for materials to build a house; it is without an owner and is for my own use. I now request from the Saṃgha the assignment of a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.
This is said three times.
The Sangha should examine whether this bhikṣu is trustworthy;
if he is trustworthy, one should then permit him to act.
If he is not to be trusted, the entire Saṃgha should go there to investigate.
If the Saṃgha does not go, they should send someone from among the Saṃgha who is trustworthy to investigate.
If that place is dangerous or obstructed, one should not grant the formal authorization (*jñapti*).
If there is no danger but there is an obstruction, or if there is danger but no obstruction, one should not grant the site.
If there is neither danger nor obstruction, one should grant the site.
The motion is made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The bhikṣu so-and-so is seeking to build a hut for himself; it is ownerless and intended for his own use. He requests from the Saṃgha a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now assign a place free from difficulties and hindrances to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu, seeking to build a dwelling for himself, without an owner and for his own use, has requested from the Saṃgha a site that is free of difficulties and free of obstructions;
the Saṃgha now grants this bhikṣu a site that is free of difficulties and free of obstructions.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha’s granting of a site free from difficulties and hindrances to the bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to grant a site free from difficulties and hindrances to the bhikṣu so-and-so."
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is upheld as such.
The procedure for constructing a dwelling with an owner is identical [to the previous rules], differing only in that it specifies "with an owner.

At the time when the rule for the non-loss of the *saṃghāṭī* robe was being established, there was a bhikṣu who suffered from consumption. He possessed a *pāṃśukūla-saṃghāṭī* which he found burdensome, and he thought to himself:
“The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus that one must not sleep apart from one’s robe.

I am now afflicted with the disease of consumption; my paṃsukūla saṃghāṭī is extremely heavy, and because of certain circumstances I wish to travel among the people, yet I am unable to carry it while traveling.”
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit the Saṃgha to perform a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to establish for this sick bhikṣu the 'non-loss of robes' (*acchinna-cīvara*).
He should go before the Saṃgha, assume the proper decorum, and make his request in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], am afflicted with the disease of consumption. This saṃghāṭī robe made of discarded rags is heavy; having a necessary reason to travel among the people, I am unable to carry it while traveling. I now request from the Saṃgha the formal authorization for the "non-loss of robe" (acchinnacīvara) procedure.
Recite this three times.
The Saṃgha grants it thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

A certain bhikṣu has contracted the disease of consumption; he possesses a heavy *saṃghāṭī* robe made of discarded rags, and because of certain business he wishes to travel among the people, he is unable to carry it with him. He requests from the Saṃgha the authorization to employ the "non-loss of robes" (*acīvarāpatti*) rule.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha establish for this bhikṣu the rule regarding the non-loss of robes.
This is the motion.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

A certain bhikṣu has contracted the disease of consumption; he possesses a heavy *saṃghāṭī* robe made of discarded rags, and because he wishes to travel among the people for a necessary purpose, he is unable to carry it with him. He requests from the Saṃgha the authorization to practice the "non-loss of robes" rule (*acchinna-cīvara-dharma*).
Now, the Saṃgha grants this "non-loss of robes" rule to the bhikṣu [Name].
"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha's conferring of the 'not losing the robe' rule (*akālacīvara*) upon this bhikṣu [Name], remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already consented to confer the 'not losing the robe' rule upon this bhikṣu [Name]."
The Saṃgha having consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the procedure for making new bedding: at that time, there was a bhikṣu who suffered from consumption; he possessed some very heavy discarded bedding and thought to himself, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must keep new bedding for six years."
If, when less than six years have passed, one does not discard old bedding but instead makes new bedding, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
I am now afflicted with the disease of consumption; these bedding materials are heavy and I am unable to carry them while traveling.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to grant that bhikṣu the formal act by white-and-second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
You should go before the Saṃgha, observe the proper decorum, and make this request as follows."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], am afflicted with the disease of consumption. Having a minor matter requiring me to travel among the people, I possess a refuse-rag bedding that is extremely heavy and cannot be carried on my journey. I now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the preparation of new bedding."
Recite this three times.
The Saṃgha grants it thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has contracted the disease of consumption and wishes to travel among the people; however, his discarded bedding is heavy, and he now requests from the Saṃgha the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for the preparation of new bedding.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of providing new bedding and seating for this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has contracted the disease of consumption; his discarded bedding is heavy, and he wishes to travel through the human world. He now requests from the Saṃgha the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for making new bedding;
the Saṃgha grants this bhikṣu, so-and-so, the formal ritual for making new bedding.

"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha performing the formal act (*kamma*) for this bhikṣu so-and-so to have a new bedding and seat made for him, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already consented and completed the formal act for bhikṣu so-and-so to have a new bedding and seat made."
The Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is upheld as such.
Regarding the method for providing a staff and a bowl-pouch: at one time there was a bhikṣu who was weak and old, unable to walk without a pouch to hold his bowl or a staff.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to perform a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) to provide a staff and a carrying pouch for that elderly bhikṣu.
One should go before the Saṃgha, assume the proper decorum, and make this request as follows.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am aged and infirm; I am unable to walk without a staff and without carrying my bowl in a pouch. I now request the Saṃgha for permission to possess a staff and a pouch.
"May the Saṃgha listen as I, the bhikṣu [Name], out of compassion, keep a staff and a bag for carrying requisites.
(Recite this three times.
The Saṃgha should grant the formal authorization in this manner.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is weak and aged; he is unable to walk without a staff and without carrying his bowl in a bag. He now requests from the Saṃgha a staff and a bag for his bowl.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant permission, let the Saṃgha give a staff and a staff-pouch to the bhikṣu [Name].
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so by name, is weak and old; he is unable to walk without a staff and a carrying net. He now requests a staff and a carrying net from the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha now grants this bhikṣu, so-and-so by name, a staff and a carrying net.
"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha giving a staff and a pouch to the bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak up.
The Sangha has already consented and completed the granting of the staff and pouch to the bhikṣu so-and-so."
The Saṃgha consents, as they remain silent; thus this matter is upheld.
Regarding the Dharma of the Six Recollections, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the first recollection is:
This means knowing the number of days, the length of the months, and whether they are "white" or "black.
One should state:
"This month is large" or "this month is small," and for a small month, count from the first day of the white fortnight up to the fifteenth day.
Regarding the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), it should be stated as:
"the first day of the dark fortnight, up to the fourteenth and fifteenth days.
According to the original system of the West (India), the month has both a bright and a dark fortnight; the bright fortnight is always full, while the dark fortnight may be either short or long.
In this land, the month consists of thirty days.
Therefore, one who practices mindfulness should understand both the long and short months and accordingly establish the lunar system according to local custom;
yet, when specifically mentioning the white and black phases or the first and second days and so forth, one again follows the original Western (Indian) system for calculating days and months.
The second mindfulness:
this refers to knowing the place of eating.
Since the place of eating is not fixed, one speaks according to that specific place of eating:
One may eat the regular food of the Sangha, or always beg for food, or accept invitations from others, or eat what one has obtained oneself.
If there is no place to eat, one should say:
"Today I mindfully refrain from eating in response to an invitation."
The third mindfulness:
This refers to knowing the date and the number of years since receiving the precepts.
It is recited as follows:
On such and such a year, month, day, and hour, when the shadow of a one-foot gnomon measured such a length, I received full ordination;
I have no summer retreats. If there are summer retreats, they should be stated accordingly.
The fourth mindfulness:
This refers to knowing whether the requisites for robes and alms-bowl are present or absent, complete or deficient.
If there are deficiencies regarding the robes and bowl, one should state them accordingly:
Regarding the robes and bowl:
if one possesses some but lacks others, one should state:
"I possess such-and-such robes and a bowl, but lack the remainder; I shall attend to them when they are available."
If one possesses them all, one should say:
"The three robes and bowl are complete.
As for other surplus robes, medicine, or bowls, one should remain mindful and aware of whether they have been purified or not yet purified.
If there are any items that have not been purified, one should say:
"I have such-and-such an extra robe (*cīvara*) and medicinal bowl (*pātra*) that have not yet been purified; I shall now declare them as pure.
If there are none, one should say:
There are no extra robes, medicine, or alms bowls.
The fifth mindfulness is:
knowing whether food is common or private.
Exhorting others to join in the meal, one says:
"This is not eating apart from the assembly.
The sixth reflection:
That is to say, does one know that there is illness?
One who has an illness says:
"I now have an illness; I must attend to its treatment."
The one who is not ill says:
"I am currently free from illness and am practicing the Path in reliance upon the community.

Regarding the relinquishing of invitations: if a bhikṣu who is not ill and has no reason for receiving robes receives many invitations on a single day, he should personally accept one invitation and transfer the remainder to others.
He spoke these words:
"Venerable sir!
A certain family has invited me to partake of the five kinds of formal meals; I ought to go there, so I now give this to you as an offering."
If one does not relinquish a prior invitation but accepts and eats food at a subsequent invitation, for every swallow, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not relinquish a subsequent invitation but accepts and eats food at a prior invitation, for every swallow, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the practice of the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for leftover food), there are two kinds of food:
first, proper food (*bhojana*); second, improper food (*abhojana*).
Improper food refers to:
Roots, stalks, and so forth—
these are not proper food and are not sufficient.
Proper food refers to:
Rice, parched grain, boiled rice, fish, and meat.
If, when the gruel has first come out of the cauldron, one draws a line with a blade of grass and it does not join together, this is considered "proper food" (bhojana) and must not be eaten.

Among the five kinds of food, if one eats any one of them until fully satiated, then changes one's posture and, without performing the *yavaddhika* (remaining-food) ritual, continues to eat, there is an offense of *pāyattika* for every swallow.
If one wishes to eat, one should take the food to a bhikṣu who has not yet finished eating and say to him:
"Venerable sir, I have already finished my meal; please look at this and acknowledge it. This constitutes the ritual for making leftover food permissible.
That bhikṣu, having taken a small portion of food, should say to this bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
I have finished eating; you may take and eat it."
He should reply, "Yes.
Having performed this rite, one may eat at will.
The procedure for announcing and entering or exiting when eating apart from the community: "Eating apart from the community" refers to four or more persons.
If there are two or three persons, one may eat as one pleases.
If there are four people or more, they should divide into two groups and eat alternately with one another.
If a bhikṣu has a reason for eating separately from the group and wishes to enter and eat, he should rise and announce:
"I have a certain reason for eating separately; I wish to join you."
The Buddha said:
"You should be permitted to enter according to the order of seniority.

Regarding the circumstances for eating separately from the assembly: when one is ill; when making robes; when receiving donated robes; when traveling on a journey; when traveling by boat; when the great assembly has gathered; and when śramaṇas are distributing food.
If a bhikṣu has no reason for taking food separately from the community, that bhikṣu should immediately rise and say:
"I have no reason for this separate meal; I wish to leave."
The Buddha said:
"I permit [you] to go out.
If a bhikṣu eats apart from the community, for every swallow there is a pāyattika offense.
If there is a reason for not announcing it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

At that time, because the various bhikṣus had many invitations for meals both before and after eating, they were apprehensive and did not dare enter the city. They followed the rule of entrusting their presence to other households when visiting them.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to enter the city after having entrusted one another;
if there is only one person in a room, he should entrust himself to a bhikṣu in an adjacent room."
He should speak thus:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have already accepted an invitation from [Name]."
Now, if there is a certain circumstance where one enters a certain village and goes to a certain person's house, one should inform a virtuous elder so that they may know.
Exceptions are permitted during times of illness, when making robes, or when receiving robes as a gift.
If, after having entrusted [the robes], one wishes to go to a destination but returns midway;
or if one does not go to the entrusted place but goes instead to another house, even to a storehouse, a lodging on the outskirts of a village, or a *ni-kalāma* (monastery);
or if one goes to the house of a layperson to whom the robes were entrusted and then returns; [in these cases, the entrustment is considered invalid].
In such cases, the previous authorization is forfeited; if one wishes to go, one must receive authorization anew.

Regarding the method of authorization for entering a village at an improper time: if there is business concerning the Saṃgha, the stūpa or monastery, or the care of a sick bhikṣu, one is permitted to enter the village after having received authorization.
If one stays alone in a room, one should entrust oneself to a monk in an adjacent room,
saying: "Venerable sir,
please attend to me with a single mind!"
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have entered a certain village at an improper time and have gone to the house of [Name] for a certain reason; I inform the Elder so that he may know.

There is no offense if the path passes through a village, or if there has been a formal announcement, or if one is summoned, or if one accepts an invitation, or if one is held by force, bound, and so forth.
Chapter Seventeen: On Cultivation and Service (Part Two). At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!"

If a bhikṣu speaks words that are merely superficially similar, obstructing the Dharma and the Vinaya, this bhikṣu causes many people to fail to obtain benefit, creates various karmas of suffering, and thereby extinguishes the True Dharma.

If a bhikṣu follows the authentic words and does not violate the Dharma and the Vinaya, such a bhikṣu benefits many people, prevents them from creating various karmas of suffering, and causes the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
"Therefore, monks, you should follow these words and phrases; do not add to or subtract from them, nor violate the Dharma or the Vinaya. You should train yourselves in this way.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the monks heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he perceives the faults of the multitude; therefore, for the sake of the śrāvakas, he establishes the precepts based on a single principle:
to bring the Saṃgha into harmony.”
"For this one reason, the Tathāgata has established the precepts for the śrāvakas.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, filled with joy, faith, and delight, they received and upheld it.
This applies to every sentence up until the long endurance of the True Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Tathāgata appears in the world for a single purpose: to establish the *karma* of censure for the bhikṣus."
"He is included within the Saṃgha.
For this single reason, the Tathāgata has appeared in the world to establish the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) for the bhikṣus.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, accepted and upheld it.
This applies to every single phrase until the True Dharma remains for a long time.

Likewise, this applies to the *karma* of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), the *karma* of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), the *karma* of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople (*apravāsanīya-karman*),

the *karma* of censuring one who does not acknowledge an offense (*adarśana-utkṣepaṇīya-karman*), the *karma* of not allowing repentance (*apratikarmārhā-karman*), and the *karma* of not relinquishing evil views (*pāpikā-dṛṣṭi-anutsarga-karman*).

Examining the regulations established by the legal authorities: the regulation for receiving dependence (*niśraya*); the regulation for the *brahmadaṇḍa* penalty; the regulation for formal accusation (*codanā*);
the regulation for calling to mind (*smṛti*); the regulation for requesting permission (*śravaṇa*); the regulation for self-accusation (*svavacana*); the regulation for prohibiting the *anuśrāvaṇā*;

the regulation for prohibiting the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*); the regulation for prohibiting the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*); the regulation for the precepts; the regulation for the recitation of the precepts; and the regulation for the *poṣadha* ceremony.
The establishment of the *poṣadha* ritual; the establishment of the *pravāraṇā*; the establishment of the *pravāraṇā* ritual; the establishment of the *jñapti-karman*;
the establishment of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*; the establishment of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; the establishment of granting the *parivāsa*; the establishment of granting the *mūlāpakarṣa*;
the establishment of granting the *mānāpya*; the establishment of granting the *āvarhaṇa*; the establishment of the four *pārājika* offenses.
The thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, the two *aniyata* rules, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules,
the ninety *pāyattika* rules, the four *pratideśanīya* rules, the *śaikṣaka* rules, and the seven methods for settling disputes—
each individual clause is to be treated according to the *tarjanīya-karman*.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two views that those who have left the household life should not practice:
regarding what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and regarding the Dharma as not the Dharma."
Furthermore, there are two views:
regarding what is Vinaya as non-Vinaya, and regarding what is non-Vinaya as Vinaya.
Furthermore, there are two views:
Not seeing an offense as an offense, or seeing an offense as not an offense;
furthermore, there are two other views:
regarding what is light as heavy, and regarding what is heavy as light.
Furthermore, there are two views:
the view that there is remainder where there is no remainder, and the view that there is no remainder where there is remainder.
Again, there are two views:
One views what is coarse and evil as not coarse and evil, and views what is not coarse and evil as coarse and evil.
Furthermore, there are two other views:
one views established doctrines as not established doctrines, and views what are not established doctrines as established doctrines.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing what is prescribed as not prescribed, and viewing what is not prescribed as prescribed.
Furthermore, there are two views:
To speak of seeing is not to speak; to speak of non-seeing is to speak of seeing.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing wine as non-wine, and viewing non-wine as wine.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing what is drink as non-drink, and viewing what is non-drink as drink.
Again, there are two views:
They perceive food as non-food, and non-food as food.
Furthermore, there are two views:
they perceive the timely as untimely, and the untimely as timely.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing the pure as impure, and viewing the impure as pure.
Again, there are two views:
One sees what is not heavy as heavy, and one sees what is not heavy as heavy.
Furthermore, there are two views:
seeing what is difficult to see as not difficult, and seeing what is not difficult as difficult.
Furthermore, there are two views:
seeing no insects where there are insects, and seeing insects where there are no insects.
Again, there are two views:
One who destroys views does not destroy [the truth], nor does one who does not destroy views destroy [the truth].
Furthermore, there are two kinds of views:
viewing what is a seed as not a seed, and viewing what is not a seed as a seed.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing what has already been understood as not yet understood, and viewing what has not yet been understood as already understood.
Furthermore, there are two views:
One may see what is trustworthy as untrustworthy, and see what is untrustworthy as trustworthy.
Furthermore, there are two other views:
seeing what is fearful as fearless, and seeing what is fearless as fearful.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing what is not the path as the path, and viewing what is the path as not the path.
Again, there are two views:
One views what is conducive to practice as not conducive to practice, and views what is not conducive to practice as conducive to practice.
Furthermore, there are two other views:
viewing what leads to liberation as not leading to liberation, and viewing what does not lead to liberation as leading to liberation.
Furthermore, there are two views:
the view that what is abandoned is not abandoned, and the view that what is not abandoned is abandoned.
Furthermore, there are two views:
They see the world as eternal; they see the world as impermanent.
Furthermore, there are two other views:
they see the world as finite, and they see the world as infinite.
Furthermore, there are two views:
that the body is the life-principle, and that the body and the life-principle are different.
Furthermore, there are two views:
There is the view that there is the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata, and the view that there is no parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there are two views:
the view that there both is and is not the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata, and the view that there neither is nor is not the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata.
"Within the Buddha-dharma, there are these two views which those who have left the household life should not practice;
if they do practice them, they shall be dealt with according to the law.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it, and with joy, faith, and delight, they received and upheld it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two kinds of people who dwell in unease:
first, those who delight in anger; second, those who harbor resentment."
Furthermore, there are two qualities:
first, a quick-tempered nature; second, difficulty in relinquishing.
Furthermore, there are two qualities:
First, stinginess; second, jealousy.
Furthermore, there are two other factors:
first, deceit; second, sycophancy.
Furthermore, there are two things:
first, self-exaltation; second, delighting in contention.
Furthermore, there are two things:
First, fondness for ornamentation; second, heedlessness.
Furthermore, there are two other dharmas:
first, pride; second, overweening pride.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
first, greed; second, hatred.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
First, praising oneself; second, disparaging others.
Furthermore, there are two other dharmas:
first, wrong view; second, extreme view.
Furthermore, there are two qualities:
first, being difficult to instruct; second, not accepting guidance and admonition.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"One who breaks the precepts falls into two realms:
the hells and among the animals."
Observing the precepts gives rise to two destinies:
birth among gods or among humans.
Committing evil deeds in secret leads to birth in two [unfortunate] destinies: [the realms of animals and hungry ghosts].
Those who perform virtuous deeds in secret while in the realms of hell or as animals will be reborn in two paths:
among the devas or among human beings.
Wrong view gives rise to two destinies:
that of hell-beings and that of animals.
Right view gives rise to two destinies:
They are born among gods and humans;
the noble disciples of the Buddha are the most honored among devas and men.
There are two things by which one does not attain liberation:
First, transgressing the precepts; second, not seeing one's transgression.
There are two factors by which one attains liberation for oneself:
first, not transgressing; second, seeing one's transgression.
There are two things that prevent one from attaining liberation:
first, committing an offense and not seeing it as such; second, seeing an offense and failing to repent according to the Dharma.
There are two things by which one attains liberation for oneself: [the opposite of the above].
First, seeing an offense; second, having committed one, being able to repent according to the Dharma.
There are two conditions by which one does not attain liberation:
first, seeing an offense and failing to repent according to the Dharma; second, if one repents according to the Dharma, but the other party does not accept it.
There are two dharmas by which one attains liberation for oneself:
first, seeing one's transgressions and being able to repent according to the Dharma; second, those who repent according to the Dharma being able to receive [the precepts] according to the Dharma.
It is the same regarding bondage and non-bondage.
"There are two kinds of purification:
first, non-transgression; second, repentance.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are two assemblies:
first, the assembly that speaks according to the Dharma; second, the assembly that speaks contrary to the Dharma.”
What is an assembly that speaks what is not the Dharma?

It is an assembly that does not employ the Dharma and the Vinaya, does not speak according to the Buddha’s teachings, persists in not teaching what should be taught, and persists in not extinguishing what should be extinguished; this is called an assembly that speaks what is not the Dharma.
What is the assembly that speaks according to the Dharma?

It is an assembly that employs the Dharma and the Vinaya, speaking in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions; it abides by teaching what should be taught and abides by extinguishing what should be extinguished—this is called the assembly that speaks according to the Dharma.
"Of these two assemblies, I praise the assembly that speaks according to the Dharma as being supreme.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
Furthermore, there are two assemblies:
"the assembly that acts according to the Dharma" and "the assembly that does not act according to the Dharma.
What is the assembly that does not act according to the Dharma?
If among the assembly those who act contrary to the Dharma are powerful while those who act according to the Dharma are weak;
if those who act contrary to the Dharma gain companions while those who act according to the Dharma do not;
and if they perform illegal *karmavācanā* rather than legal *karmavācanā*.
They perform formal acts that are contrary to the Vinaya and do not perform those that accord with the Vinaya;
they carry out what is illegal and do not carry out what is legal;
this constitutes an assembly that is non-Dharmic.
What is a community that acts in accordance with the Dharma?
It is when those who act in accordance with the Dharma have power within the assembly while those who act contrary to the Dharma have none;
when those who act in accordance with the Dharma find companions while those who act contrary to the Dharma do not.
They perform legal *karmas*, not illegal *karmas*;
they perform *vinaya* *karmas*, not non-*vinaya* *karmas*;
thus, what is in accordance with the Dharma prevails, while what is contrary to the Dharma is extinguished.
"This is what constitutes a community that accords with the Dharma.
Between these two types of communities, I praise the one that accords with the Dharma as being supreme.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, filled with joy, faith, and delight, they accepted and upheld it.
There are two kinds of assemblies:
equal assemblies and unequal assemblies; it is also thus.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"If the power of the Dharma-king in his kingdom is weak and the various bandits are rampant, then at that time the Dharma-king will not be able to enter or exit with peace and happiness; the subordinate kings of the borderlands will not obey his commands, and the people within the realm will likewise not be able to enter or exit with peace and happiness. Their livelihoods will come to a standstill and fall into ruin; they will suffer from anxiety and affliction, experience decline, and fail to obtain any benefit."
Thus, the bhikṣus who act contrary to the Dharma are powerful, while the bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma are powerless.
The bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma find no peace and happiness; even when among the assembly, they are not permitted to speak.
If they dwell in a secluded place, at that time they perform illegal *karmavācanā* and do not perform legal *karmavācanā*;
they perform non-disciplinary (*avinaya*) *karmavācanā* and do not perform disciplinary *karmavācanā*;
thus, what is illegal is carried out, while what is legal is not carried out.

If he does not apply himself with diligent effort to attain what has not yet been attained, to enter what has not yet been entered, and to realize what has not yet been realized, then he will cause gods and humans to fail to obtain benefit and to suffer for a long night.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, accepted and upheld it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If, according to the laws of a kingdom, the power of the king is strong and the strength of the bandits is weak, they will all come to submit or flee away."

At that time, the Dharma King entered and exited in peace and security, free from anxiety; the minor kings of the borderlands obeyed his commands, and the people within his realm likewise enjoyed peace and happiness. They engaged freely in their livelihoods without any sorrow or suffering, gaining great benefit and experiencing no decline.

In this way, when a bhikṣu who acts according to the Dharma gains power and a bhikṣu who acts contrary to the Dharma lacks power, the bhikṣu who acts contrary to the Dharma comes before the bhikṣu who acts according to the Dharma; he follows his instructions and does not dare to disobey them, and even if he were to flee, he would commit no further evil deeds.
At that time, the bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma dwell in peace and attain happiness;
whether they are among the Saṃgha or dwelling in a secluded place, they perform legal (dharmic) karmas and do not perform illegal (adharmic) karmas;
they perform karmas according to the Vinaya and do not perform non-Vinaya karmas.
One practices this Dharma and does not practice what is not the Dharma;

through diligent and energetic cultivation, one attains what has not yet been attained, enters what has not yet been entered, and realizes what has not yet been realized, thereby bringing great benefit to the devas and the people.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Venerable elders!..."

If there is a dispute, and one raises the matter of another bhikṣu or a bhikṣu who has committed an offense without examining oneself, you should know that this dispute will further increase; it cannot be settled in accordance with the Dharma or the Vinaya, and the bhikṣus will not find peace and happiness.

If monks are engaged in a dispute, and those who have accused another monk as well as the one who has committed an offense each examine their own faults, you should know that this dispute will no longer increase or become grave; it will be settled in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and the monks will then dwell in peace and happiness.
How do the bhikṣus observe their own faults?
A bhikṣu who has committed an offense reflects thus:
"I have committed such an act; he sees my transgression. Had I not committed it, he would not have seen my transgression; because I have committed it, he has seen me."
"I should now personally repent my transgression so that he will no longer reproach me with harsh words; if I act in this way, it will cause wholesome dharmas to increase.
This is what is meant by a bhikṣu being able to observe his own faults.
How does one, by censuring another bhikṣu, examine one’s own faults?
One forms this thought:
"That bhikṣu has committed an offense, which allows me to see it; had he not committed an offense, I would not have seen it. Because he has committed an offense, I am able to see it."
"If he is able to sincerely repent on his own, he will not cause me to utter harsh words; in this way, wholesome dharmas will increase.
This is called observing one's own faults while addressing another bhikṣu.

If there is a dispute among bhikṣus, and a bhikṣu who has been accused—or a bhikṣu who possesses an offense—is able to thus examine his own faults, it should be known that these faults will no longer increase; acting in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, the bhikṣus will dwell in peace and happiness.
When Śāriputra had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir, you are the Master of this Dharma. You have spoken of 'training' (śikṣā); what constitutes training?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"One trains in the precepts, therefore it is called 'training.
How does one train in the precepts?"
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—this is why it is called "training.
When one trains in these higher trainings of virtue, mind, and wisdom, one attains the subduing and total exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Having attained the exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion, one does not commit unwholesome deeds and does not associate with evils; this is why it is called "training."
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
At that time, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"How do you train?"
"What is meant by 'training'?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir, you are the root of the Dharma and the master of the Dharma. As the World-Honored One has just explained, we receive and uphold it; therefore, we speak of 'training.'"
Furthermore, there are three trainings:

the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. By training in these three trainings, one attains the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; therefore, one should diligently apply oneself with vigor to train in these three trainings.
At that time, Ānanda was staying in the Kukkuṭārāma monastery at Pāṭaliputra. Then the brahmin Mayūra came to where Ānanda was; after exchanging greetings, he sat to one side and said to Ānanda:
"For what reason has the śramaṇa Gautama established for the bhikṣus the training in higher morality, the training in higher pure conduct, and the training in higher prātimokṣa?"
Ānanda replied:
"The reason for this is that the World-Honored One has established the precepts for the bhikṣus in order to subdue greed, hatred, and delusion so that they may be brought to an end."
He asked again:
"If a bhikṣu has attained arhatship and exhausted all outflows, what is it that he trains in?
Ānanda replied:

"When greed, hatred, and delusion are exhausted; when one no longer commits unwholesome deeds and stays far from all evils; and when what was to be done has been accomplished—one is called an Aśaikṣa (One Beyond Training)."
The brahmin asked,
"Is one who acts as you have just described considered to be one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Ānanda replied:
"So be it," replied the Brahmin Mayūra-cūḍa, having heard this; he rejoiced with faith and joy, and took it to heart.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣu Kāśyapa, saying:

"If the Elder neither trains in the precepts nor praises the precepts, and if there are other bhikṣus who delight in training in the precepts and praising the precepts, he likewise fails to exhort, encourage, and praise them at the proper time."
Kāśyapa Bhikṣu!
I do not praise such an elder. Why is that?
If I were to praise them, it would cause the bhikṣus to associate with them;
if they associate with them, it would cause others to study their teachings;
and if they study those teachings, they will suffer for a long night.
"Therefore, Kāśyapa Bhikṣu!
Because I see such faults in these elders, I do not praise them.
This applies equally to those of middle rank and those of lower rank.
Next, there are those of superior, middling, and inferior standing who act according to the Dharma; the opposite of the preceding phrases applies to them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“It is like a donkey walking together with a herd of oxen, saying to itself:”
"I am also an ox! I am also an ox!

Yet the donkey's fur does not resemble that of an ox, its feet do not resemble those of an ox, and its voice likewise does not resemble that of an ox; yet it walks together with oxen and claims for itself, "I am an ox."
In this way, there is a deluded person who follows after a bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma and claims for himself, "I am a bhikṣu.
This deluded person lacks the higher morality, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom possessed by a virtuous bhikṣu; yet he travels together with the Saṃgha and declares, "I am a bhikṣu!"
"Therefore, you all should diligently practice and cultivate the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.”
What is the training in higher virtue?
It is when a bhikṣu respects virtue and takes virtue as his primary focus,
yet does not respect meditative concentration and does not take meditative concentration as his primary focus.
They do not value wisdom, nor do they take wisdom as their primary focus.
Regarding these precepts, if they commit a minor offense, they confess it; why is this?
Because in this case, it is not like a broken vessel or a shattered stone.
If it is a grave precept, one should uphold it firmly, dwell well within the precepts, practice with intimacy, practice without violation or deficiency, and practice without defilement.
By constantly practicing in this way, one severs the five lower fetters (*paryavasthāna*), attains *nirvāṇa* in the higher realms, and does not return to this world again.
If a bhikṣu values the precepts and takes the precepts as his primary focus;
values meditative concentration and takes meditative concentration as his primary focus;
He does not value wisdom nor take wisdom as primary;
as stated above.
If a bhikṣu values the precepts and takes the precepts as primary;
He values concentration and takes concentration as his primary focus;
he values wisdom and takes wisdom as his primary focus.

Having exhausted the taints, he attains the liberation of mind that is free from taints and the liberation by wisdom, realizing for himself in the present life: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further returning to this state."
For one who practices with fulfillment, there is the accomplishment of fulfillment;
for one who practices without fulfillment, there is the accomplishment of non-fulfillment.
I say that this precept is never in vain.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
"Furthermore, there are three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom."
What is the training in higher morality?

If there is a bhikṣu who fulfills the practice of morality, but practices concentration little and practices wisdom little, he severs the five lower fetters and attains nirvāṇa in the intermediate state, never again returning to this world.
If one cannot reach such a state, yet can attenuate the three fetters—
lust, hatred, and delusion— one attains the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) and returns to this world once more before making an end to suffering.

If one cannot reach such a state, yet is able to sever the three fetters and attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, one will not fall into the evil destinies; being certain of attaining the Path, one will undergo seven births in the heavens and seven births among humans, after which the limit of suffering is exhausted.
If a bhikṣu is fully endowed with the practice of morality and fully endowed with the practice of concentration, yet practices wisdom only to a small degree, it is also as described above.
If a bhikṣu is fully endowed with the practice of morality, fully endowed with the practice of concentration, and fully endowed with the practice of wisdom, it is also as described above.
“Furthermore, there are three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
What is the training in higher virtue?”

If a bhikṣu fully maintains the prātimokṣa precepts, accomplishes dignified conduct, and out of fear and caution treats even minor precepts as heavy as a vajra, training equally in all the precepts—this is called the training in higher virtue.
What is the training in the higher mind?
If a bhikṣu is able to abandon sensual desires and evil states, up to attaining entry into the fourth dhyāna, this is called the training in the higher mind.
What is the training in the higher wisdom?
"If a bhikṣu thus knows the truth of suffering, and knows [the truths of] its origin, its cessation, and the path, this is called the training in increased wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the city of Bhaja in the country of Vatsa, and he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall speak of four kinds of detailed expositions; listen well, and I will explain them for you."
The bhikṣus said:
"Venerable Sir!
We wish to hear it with joy."
“What are the four?
If a bhikṣu speaks thus:
‘Venerable elders!...’”
‘In such-and-such a village or such-and-such a city, I personally heard and received this from the Buddha: “This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha.

If you hear what that bhikṣu says, you should not immediately give rise to suspicion or doubt, nor should you rebuke him; rather, having carefully examined the words and phrases, you should investigate the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and verify them against the legal codes.

If, upon listening to that bhikṣu’s discourse and investigating the Sūtras and Vinaya to examine the legal codes, one finds that it does not correspond with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the legal codes, and contradicts the Dharma, one should say to that bhikṣu:
"What you have spoken was not spoken by the Buddha; or perhaps the Elder has not carefully grasped the Buddha's words."
Why is this? Having investigated the sūtras, the vinaya, and the legal codes, I find that [this] does not accord with the sūtras, the vinaya, and the legal codes, but rather contradicts the Dharma.
"Elder! There is no need to recite or study this, nor should you teach it to other bhikṣus; you should now abandon it.

If, upon hearing what that bhikṣu says, one investigates the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the legal codes, and finds that it is consistent with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the legal codes, one should say to that bhikṣu:
"What the Elder has spoken is what the Buddha spoke; he has truly grasped the Buddha’s words. Why is this?
For when I investigate the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Dharma and Discipline, they correspond with his teaching and do not contradict it."
"Elder! You should maintain this well through recitation and study, and teach it to other bhikṣus so that it is not forgotten.
This is the first detailed exposition.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu speaks thus:
"Venerable sirs!
In such-and-such a village or such-and-such a city, I heard this before the elders in a harmonious Saṃgha: 'This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha.'"

"When you hear what that bhikṣu says, you should neither harbor suspicion nor reprimand him; rather, you should carefully determine the words and phrases, investigate the Sūtras and Vinaya, and examine the legal codes."
If, upon hearing what that bhikṣu says and investigating the sūtras, the vinaya, and the legal codes, one finds it inconsistent with them and contrary to the Dharma, one should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"This was not spoken by the Buddha; it is that assembly of monks and the elders who have not carefully grasped the Buddha’s words, and the Venerable Ones are likewise at fault.

Why is this? Having investigated the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the legal codes, I find that this does not correspond with them and contradicts the Dharma. Venerable Ones, you need not recite or study this, nor should you teach it to other bhikṣus; you should now discard it."

If, upon hearing those words of that bhikṣu, one investigates the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the legal codes, and finds them to be consistent with them and not contrary to the Dharma, one should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable One!..."
This was spoken by the Buddha, and the elders and senior monks of that assembly have also correctly understood the Buddha’s words.
Why is this? Because when I investigate the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the legal codes, they are found to be in accord with them, without any contradiction.
"Elder! You should maintain this through diligent recitation and study, and you should also teach it to others so that it is not forgotten.
This is the second detailed exposition.
The third phrase is likewise when one hears from many bhikṣus who know the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā.
The fourth phrase is likewise when one hears from a single bhikṣu who knows the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā.
"These are the four detailed expositions.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
There are five matters by which the Vinaya is answered:
First, the introduction; second, the enactment; third, the re-enactment; fourth, the sūtra; fifth, that which accords with the sūtra.
There are five qualities by which one is called a holder of the Vinaya:
knowing what constitutes an offense, knowing what does not constitute an offense, knowing what is light, knowing what is heavy, and extensively reciting the two sections of the precepts.
Furthermore, there are five qualities:
four are the same as before, and the fifth is to recite the Vinaya extensively.
Furthermore, there are five qualities:
The four dharmas are the same as before; the fifth is to abide in the *vinaya* without wavering.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas:
the four dharmas are the same as before; the fifth is to be skillfully able to eliminate disputes when they arise.
There are five ways of upholding the Vinaya:
reciting the introduction to the Prātimokṣa, the four pārājika offenses, the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, the two aniyata rules, and reciting the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules in detail;
this is the first way of upholding the Vinaya.
If one recites the ninety matters extensively, this is the second way of upholding the Vinaya.
If one recites the Vinaya of the precepts extensively, this is the third way of upholding the Vinaya.
If one recites the Vinaya of the two sets of precepts extensively, this is the fourth way of upholding the Vinaya.
If one recites the entire Vinaya, this constitutes the fifth way of upholding the Vinaya.
Among these, during the spring, summer, autumn, and winter, one should rely upon the aforementioned four ways of upholding the Vinaya;
if one does not abide by them, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
During the summer retreat (varṣā), one should rely on a fifth person who maintains the Vinaya;
if one does not so abide, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
A person who maintains the Vinaya possesses five merits:

Firm in the precepts, he excels over all adversaries; he is fearless in making definitive judgments among the assembly; he can resolve the doubts and regrets of others; and by skillfully upholding the Vinaya, he ensures that the True Dharma endures for a long time.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of offenses:
*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *duṣkṛta*;
these are also called the five kinds of established precepts, or the five aggregates of offenses.
If one does not know and does not see these five offenses, I say that such a person is deluded regarding the *pārājika* down to the *duṣkṛta*.
Furthermore, there are five undesirable qualities of a dead person:

first, impurity; second, a foul odor; third, being a source of fear; fourth, causing others to fear and providing an opportunity for malevolent spirits; and fifth, being a dwelling place for evil beasts and non-human beings.
A person who violates the precepts has five faults:
their actions of body, speech, and mind are impure, just as a corpse is impure;
I say that such a person is likewise so.
If there are those whose actions of body, speech, and mind are impure, and whose evil reputation spreads abroad like the stench emanating from a corpse,
I say that such persons are likewise.
If there are impurities of bodily, verbal, and mental karma, virtuous bhikṣus will fear and avoid them, just as a corpse causes terror in people;
I say that such a person is exactly like this.
There are impurities of bodily, verbal, and mental karma that cause virtuous bhikṣus who see them to give rise to evil thoughts, saying:
"How is it that I have come to see such an evil person?"
"Just as when a person sees a corpse and gives rise to fear, it allows evil spirits to find an opportunity;
I say that such a person is exactly like this.
One whose actions of body, speech, and mind are impure and who dwells together with unwholesome people is like that corpse dwelling among wild beasts and non-humans."
I say that this person is likewise so.
These are the five faults of one who has violated the precepts, like that corpse.
There are five faults in breaking the precepts:
Self-harm is censured by the wise; it results in the spread of an evil reputation, gives rise to regret at the time of death, and leads to rebirth in the evil realms after death.
There are five merits of upholding the precepts, which are the opposites of the aforementioned points.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, one cannot obtain things not yet obtained;
second, once obtained, one does not maintain them.
In whatever assembly one may find oneself—whether an assembly of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or bhikṣus—one will feel shame and remorse;
for countless yojanas around, śramaṇas and brahmins will proclaim one’s evil deeds;
and as a person who has broken the precepts, one will fall into the evil realms after death.
There are five merits of upholding the precepts.
Conversely, there are five kinds of pure fruits:
those purified by fire, those purified by the knife, those purified by a wound, those purified by birds, and those unfit for planting.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of impurity:
if the skin is partially stripped, if it is entirely stripped, if it is putrefied, if it is torn, or if it is bruised.
There are five factors that cause the True Dharma to perish quickly; what are these five?
There was a bhikṣu who did not carefully receive or recite [the teachings]; being prone to forgetfulness and error, he taught others with incomplete texts;
since the texts were incomplete, their meaning was deficient.
This is the first way in which the True Dharma is swiftly extinguished.

Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu who is a preeminent person among the Saṃgha, an elder (sthavira), or one venerated by an entire nation; yet he frequently fails to uphold the precepts, cultivates only various unwholesome dharmas, abandons his ascetic conduct, and lacks diligent effort. He claims to have attained what he has not attained, to have entered what he has not entered, and to have realized what he has not realized.

Later, young bhikṣus who emulated his conduct likewise frequently violated the precepts, cultivated unwholesome dharmas, and abandoned their monastic discipline; they were neither diligent nor energetic, claiming to have attained what they had not attained, entered what they had not entered, and realized what they had not realized.
This is the second way the True Dharma is swiftly extinguished.

Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu who is learned, upholding the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā; yet he does not teach what he has memorized to other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, and then he passes away.
Once he has passed away, it causes the Dharma to be cut off and extinguished.
This is the third way in which the True Dharma is swiftly extinguished.
Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu who is difficult to instruct, who does not accept wholesome words, and who is unable to practice patience; other virtuous bhikṣus will then simply abandon him.
This is the fourth way in which the True Dharma is swiftly extinguished.

Furthermore, there may be bhikṣus who delight in strife and quarreling, mutually reviling one another with contentious speech; their mouths are like swords and blades as they seek out each other's faults.
This is the fifth cause for the rapid extinction of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there are five other dharmas by which the True Dharma may abide for a long time;
these are the opposites of the aforementioned points. At that time, a certain bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“Venerable Sir!
By what causes and conditions does the True Dharma quickly perish and not endure for long?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"If a bhikṣu has gone forth within the Dharma and Vinaya, yet does not wholeheartedly preach the Dharma for others, nor wholeheartedly listen to and retain the Dharma; even if he should maintain it with persistence, he cannot contemplate its meaning and intent. Not knowing the meaning, he cannot practice according to the teaching; he fails to benefit himself and likewise fails to benefit others."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are these causes and conditions that cause the Dharma to perish quickly and not abide for long.
[The bhikṣus asked: "Venerable Sir!"
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions will the Dharma endure for a long time?
This is the inversion of the preceding sentence. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“When a bhikṣu enters the midst of the Saṃgha, he must first possess five qualities:”
One should act with a mind of loving-kindness;
one should humble oneself like a cloth for wiping dust;
one should be well-attentive to sitting and rising: if one sees a senior, one should not sit down comfortably; if one sees a junior, one should not stand up.
When he has entered among the Sangha, he should not engage in miscellaneous talk concerning worldly matters; rather, he should either preach the Dharma himself or request another to preach it.
If he perceives anything improper within the Sangha that his mind cannot endure, he should remain silent. Why is this?
"Lest there be division among the Saṃgha, a bhikṣu should first possess these five qualities before entering the midst of the Saṃgha.

At that time, the World-Honored One was at the side of the Gaṅgā Pond in the city of Campā; on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight during the recitation of the precepts, he sat in the open air, surrounded by the assembly of monks before and behind him.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who charged another bhikṣu with an offense based on what he had seen, heard, or suspected.
While the charge was being made, that bhikṣu answered with evasive remarks and gave rise to anger.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should interrogate that person with careful scrutiny.

That person is incapable of anything within the Buddha-dharma and makes no progress; he is like a farmer whose field crops are interspersed with weeds. The stalks and leaves are so similar they cannot be distinguished, yet they cause harm until the grain has ripened, at which point one finally knows the difference between the true crop and the weed."
Once it is known that they are not grain, their roots are immediately weeded out.
Why is this? For fear that they might harm the sprouts of goodness.
It is the same with the bhikṣus: when evil bhikṣus come and go, sit and rise, and carry their robes and bowls, they are indistinguishable from virtuous bhikṣus, and thus no offense is revealed;
only when their offense has been exposed do people finally recognize the difference between them and the tares and weeds among the bhikṣus.
Once you have recognized their heterodoxy, you should join together to carry out their formal expulsion and removal.
Why? For fear that they might obstruct the virtuous bhikṣus.
It is like a farmer processing grain: when winnowing it in the wind, the good grain remains gathered beneath, while the chaff and husks are carried away by the wind. Why is this?
Fearing that they might defile the good grain,
such wicked bhikṣus— whether coming or going, entering or leaving— are not distinguished from virtuous bhikṣus, nor are their offenses exposed;
only when their offenses have finally been revealed is it known that they are chaff and husks among the bhikṣus, foul and evil.
Once this has been known, one should act in unison to carry out their formal exclusion and expulsion.

It is like a man who needs wood to make a well-railing; he goes out from the city, carrying a sharp axe in his hand, and travels to that forest, striking every tree. If the tree is solid within, its sound is firm and real;
if it is hollow within, its sound is empty and rattling.
Now, the roots, trunk, branches, and leaves of that hollow tree were no different from those of a solid one; it was only when struck that one knew it was empty within.

Once the internal emptiness was known, it was immediately felled and cut down; the branches and leaves were stripped away, the coarse outer bark was first removed, and then it was carefully pared and trimmed with adzes until both inside and out were clean, to be used as a well-railing.
In this way, these evil bhikṣus come and go, enter and exit, carrying their robes and bowls with a deportment no different from that of virtuous bhikṣus, until their offenses are finally exposed;
only when their offenses have been revealed do people realize they are the filth, the tares, and the hollow trees within the community of śramaṇas.
Once this is known, one should immediately act in concert to carry out the formal act of banishment. Why?
For fear that it may cause harm to virtuous bhikṣus.
And he spoke in verse:
"Living together, one knows their character and conduct: They are jealous and delight in anger;
They speak kind words among people, But commit unrighteous acts in private."
Those who employ skillful means to speak falsehoods can be discerned by the wise;
like weeds and tares, they should be removed and discarded, as well as trees grown from the air.
Those who claim for themselves to be śramaṇas while being false and deceitful should be expelled.
When the formal act of *tarjanīya* (reproval) has been completed against one who acts wickedly and contrary to the Dharma,
and he dwells together with those who are pure— know that this is a manifestation of glory;
through concordant action, he is formally expelled, and through concordance, he reaches the end of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
*Saṃghakarmavastu*, Vol. II.
